cia-0000119740: A CIA report gives the Hungarian situation with information as of 11:30 p.m. during the 1956 crisis. The late edition caught events at their most fluid, and it preserves the picture the overnight watch passed to the president's advisers. The late hour marks the edge of the reporting day in Washington, when the watch summed up a night of cables for the morning's first readers.
cia-0000132240: Situation report 557, dated January 1991, covers political developments, its subtitle repeating the same words before breaking off. The doubled phrase is a small mark of the daily grind of the crisis watch. The report covers the politics as filed. High-numbered sitreps blur in wording because the watch produced them around the clock; the doubled heading is the grind showing through the file's formal surface.
cia-0000132440: Changes inside the Cuban government fill a CIA document dated November 4, 1959. Ministers were coming and going as Castro tightened his hold on power. Each change moved the government further from the broad promises of its first weeks. The short document tracks the reshuffles one by one, giving readers a dated record of who rose and who fell during the revolution's first year in office.
cia-0000132740: World reactions to Cuba fill a CIA item dated March 4, 1961. The item sorts them into three piles: the Free World, the Sino-Soviet bloc, and the United Nations. That three-way split was the Cold War drawn in miniature. Nearly every government on earth had a stance on Cuba by then. The short item gathers the reactions in one dated place.
cia-0000134340:
Events in Indochina fill a CIA paper dated August 3, 1972. The Paris peace talks were still months from their end, and the fighting in Vietnam had not stopped. American troops were drawing down while the war's endgame took shape around them.

The paper surveys the latest events across the region that summer. Battles, talks, and supply lines all fed into the account. For readers, it is a snapshot from the war's last full year of heavy fighting. The accords that closed the American role came the following January, and this paper dates from the hard months just before them.
cia-0000135940: Dated 5 January 1954, a declassified CIA cable deals with a request that headquarters alone concur in any clearance or clarification the station sought. Lincoln handled the field traffic of PBSUCCESS, the agency effort against the Arbenz government in Guatemala in the early 1950s. For readers of the coup, the value lies in the plain wording, written before anyone knew how the story would end.
cia-0000136040: The cable dated 6 February 1954 in the CIA files, now open, deals with information on a thing the heading calls this one man force function. As the Lincoln station file, it forms part of PBSUCCESS, the CIA plan that ended with President Arbenz driven out in June 1954. Later books on the coup rest on stacks of paper exactly like this, dated, coded, and only partly opened.
cia-0000136140: One CIA cable dated 2 April 1954 handles instructions for teams targeting bridges, typos and all, the orders breaking off at the end. Lincoln was where PBSUCCESS staff worked the Guatemala operation day to day, under code names, in 1953 and 1954. The file rewards slow reading, since its short heading is often the only summary the agency ever gave it.
cia-0000136240: The declassified CIA cable dated 4 May 1954 takes up Instructions 7 for the Sherwood broadcast, sent to a name the heading spells as Lagevin. In these files Lincoln names the field station of PBSUCCESS, the covert CIA plan to topple President Arbenz of Guatemala. The heading alone tells a reader the topic, the channel, and the moment, even where names stay deleted.
cia-0000136340: Do not be influenced by the cry of hoax, LINCOLN tells CADICK in this June 1954 cable, because the power of retaliation will be retained until CALLIGERIS's position is secure. The station regrets it cannot fully inform him of every detail and demands complete compliance with an earlier message. Aircraft use is modified: he may resupply field forces as needed to maintain effectiveness while awaiting developments. Secrecy and obedience are the cable's twin themes.
cia-0000139040: A lecture on Germany's future draws a small crowd in New York. This OSS report covers a September 1945 meeting at a workers' hall. Attendance was 126. The speaker addressed Germany's eastern territories. Annexation by Poland and Russia was explained as a security need. Those lands were principally Germanized Slavs, he argued. They could not be trusted at this time. The garbled transcription keeps the outline, not the wording. The report records communist-line speaking in America. The war had ended only days before.
cia-0000139440: The capture of two Israeli soldiers in Lebanon complicates the hostage situation, the DCI Hostage Location Task Force report of January 1986 states in its highlights. Israeli sweep operations in southern Lebanon continue and have produced a number of clashes with Shia forces, the excerpt adds before cutting off. The task force existed to find the Americans held hostage in Beirut during the Lebanon hostage crisis. The surviving sample is brief; the full report's reporting on hostage locations does not appear here.
un-ga-res-40:
Strains over the big-power veto showed up early at the United Nations. Resolution 40 was passed on 13 December 1946. It notes the rows that had grown up around Article 27 of the Charter. That clause gives the five permanent members of the Security Council their veto. Small states feared the veto would slow the Council or block it outright.

The Assembly begs the permanent members to take care, in talks with each other and with fellow members, that the veto not bar swift Council action. It also urges the Council to adopt habits of work, within the Charter, that ease the strain. The veto fight, as this text shows, is as old as the UN itself.
un-ga-res-140:
Nauru, a tiny island in the Pacific Ocean, passed from League of Nations rule to UN trusteeship under Resolution 140, adopted on 1 November 1947. Under the old League mandate, Australia had run the island on behalf of itself, New Zealand, and the United Kingdom. The UN Charter of 1945 had since set up a Trusteeship System for just such lands.

The three states agreed to place Nauru under that system and to run it on the terms set out here. The Assembly, acting under Article 85 of the Charter, approves those terms in place of the old mandate. Nauru stayed a trust land for two more decades, until its freedom in 1968.
un-ga-res-a-69-40:
Nuclear arms are named the gravest threat to mankind in Resolution A/69/40, from the General Assembly's sixty-ninth session. Any use or threat of such arms, the text holds, would breach the Charter. It argues that the spread of these arms in any form would deepen the risk of nuclear war. Full nuclear disarmament, and the end of such arms for good, are held up as the sole sure guard.

Till that day comes, states with nuclear arms are pressed to shield states without them from use or threat of use. The hair-trigger alert of ready arms is singled out: it carries an unfit risk of a launch by error or without leave, with ruin for all mankind.
un-sc-res-140: Madagascar, then styled the Malagasy Republic, asked to join the United Nations in 1960. The Council took up the request at its 870th meeting. That meeting fell on 29 June 1960. Members raised no objection. In a single sentence, the Council says it has examined the application. It then recommends admission to the General Assembly. Brief as it is, the text marks the formal UN welcome for a newly independent state.
un-sc-res-240: Formal action by the Council in its numbered series produced Resolution 240, which the catalog dates to 1967. These short legal texts often sit at turning points, since the Council acts when peace or security is at stake. The text here follows the English Wikisource transcription of the official record, so readers get the Council's own wording. It sits in this library among other public records in the DECLASSIFIED group.
un-sc-res-540: Entered in the record as Resolution 540, this Security Council text is catalogued at 1949. Behind each numbered text lies a meeting, a draft, and a vote, even when the final wording runs to a few lines. Read in sequence with its neighbours, it helps trace how Council practice grew across the postwar decades. No summary replaces it; the record itself is the content of the entry.
un-sc-res-1040: The official series of Council decisions runs through Resolution 1040, catalogued here for 1996. A resolution may address a conflict, a court vacancy, a new member, or the running of the United Nations itself. Anyone studying UN practice can read the decision itself here, in the Wikisource transcription of the official record. The catalog places it in the DECLASSIFIED group of official public records.
un-sc-res-1340: Council action recorded as Resolution 1340 appears in this catalog under the year 2001. Formal decisions of this sort guide UN staff, peacekeeping forces, and governments in the years that follow. What is preserved is the exact formal wording, transcribed on English Wikisource from the official record of the Council. Its place here reflects the library's aim of keeping primary records readable.
cia-0000132640: Filed as section III, The West - Cuba, this CIA paper of May 1, 1960 survives as a fragment of a larger regional survey. Its place in that survey puts Cuba among the Western Hemisphere concerns Washington tracked that spring, rather than as a stand-alone study. The declassified fragment is preserved through the CIA Reading Room mirror at the Internet Archive, cataloged under document number 0000132640.
cia-0000135740: Dated 6 March 1961, a Spanish document from the declassified archive of Brigade 2506. The exile force was then weeks from its April landing in Cuba, in the last phase of training and planning. The catalog names no subject for this item. It is held in the original Spanish through the CIA Reading Room. The record is one of the brigade's final-month documents, described by its date and file rather than by any guessed content.
cia-0000136640: A Spanish document dated 4 March 1961, from the declassified papers of Brigade 2506, the exile force the CIA built against Castro. March was the brigade's last full month of preparation. The catalog record gives this item no subject heading. It survives in the original Spanish, one of the March records of the operation, released through the CIA Reading Room for direct study.
cia-0000136740: This Spanish document, dated 1 November 1960, is filed with the 2506 Brigade papers released by the CIA. plos-pone-0000040:
Michael Forgber, Rajatava Basu, Kaushik Roychoudhury, and co-authors mapped what the immune system sees during a parasitic infection in 2006. Leishmania donovani causes visceral leishmaniasis, a deadly disease spread by sand flies. Antigenicity is the measure of which parasite proteins the human immune system actually attacks.

Using proteome serology, testing patient blood serum against the parasite's full set of proteins, the team mapped those targets across the proteome. A map of what the body recognizes is a shortlist for vaccines and for blood tests that could diagnose the disease early. For a neglected illness of the poor, that shortlist is where practical defenses begin.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d40: Roosevelt wrote to Chiang Kai-shek on October 13, 1943, and the letter stands as Document 40 of the Cairo and Tehran volume. Chiang was to join Roosevelt and Churchill at Cairo in November, the only meeting of the three that China attended as an equal. Letters like this one kept that plan warm through the autumn. The record names no subject; the text in the Foreign Relations series is the place to find it.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d140: General Eisenhower wrote to President Roosevelt on November 18, 1943, and his letter is Document 140 of the Cairo and Tehran volume. The president had just passed through Eisenhower's North African command on the road to Cairo, and theater commanders wrote to their commander in chief with care. The record gives the date and the two men and no topic. The letter is part of the Foreign Relations series.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d240:
Secretary of State Cordell Hull sent President Roosevelt a long secret digest from Washington on 20 November 1943, gathering reports from Ankara, Algiers, and Madrid. It is a snapshot of half a dozen side issues of the war in a single message.

British and Turkish officers, Ankara reports, differ wildly on Axis striking power against Turkey, and a compromise estimate will set the aid Turkey needs. From Algiers come orders to hold German prisoners accused of atrocities for later trial, and news of Yugoslav partisans interned on the Italian mainland. Madrid reports a protest over the many German agents working in Spain. It also reports pressure to shut the German consulate at Tangier. Washington wishes to let the Laurel incident rest if Spain proves itself by deeds.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d340:
A draft agreement prepared by the American delegation at Cairo on 30 November 1943, marked secret, sets the liaison rules between the European Advisory Commission and the Combined Chiefs of Staff. It grew out of John McCloy's talks with Eden, and its heading shows it was accepted at the Sextant Conference.

The Moscow conference had created the commission and sent it civil affairs questions closely tied to military matters of prime interest to the chiefs. Under the draft, the commission's tentative recommendations go to the chiefs for comment before final submission to the three governments. Approved recommendations return to the chiefs, who prepare the final directives for commanders in the field. British members of the civil affairs committee are to take full part in all its work, without limit as to area.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d440:
Agreed minutes, signed off by both the American and British sides, record a United States-United Kingdom meeting of December 4, 1943, during the Second Cairo Conference. Unlike a single nation's notes, an agreed text is the version both delegations accepted as accurate. The State Department printed it in the Cairo-Tehran conference volume.

Inside, the reader finds the shared record of what the two allies discussed and settled that day, in the middle of a conference called to finish the work begun at Tehran. Agreed minutes carry special weight for historians, because neither side could later rewrite them. They mark the points where London and Washington truly stood together.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d540:
Ambassador Averell Harriman wrote to Secretary of State Hull on January 6, 1944, using the formal channel to the department rather than his direct line to the President. Harriman's Moscow embassy was then Washington's main window on the Soviet Union. The message appears in the State Department's Cairo-Tehran volume.

Harriman wrote to Hull on departmental business and to Roosevelt on the great questions, and the choice of channel itself is a clue to a message's weight. Six weeks after Tehran, Soviet-American relations were entering their working phase. For readers, this cable shows the alliance being run through proper diplomatic form as well as summit friendship.
frus-1944-quebec-d40:
Wilson Brown, the President's naval aide, wrote to A. J. McFarland, secretary of the Joint Chiefs of Staff, on August 31, 1944. Brown managed the President's military household and map room. The message appears in the State Department's Quebec 1944 volume.

Staff traffic between the White House military office and the Joint Chiefs' secretariat arranged the soldiers' part of the coming conference: papers, attendance, and the movement of plans. Brown and McFarland were the kind of officers whose names rarely reach print but whose work made summits run. For readers, the note shows a conference's military skeleton being assembled.
frus-1944-quebec-d140:
Numbered C.C.S. 654, this top-secret memorandum from the United States Chiefs of Staff is dated August 22, 1944. It proposes the basic policies the Combined Chiefs should adopt for the next Anglo-American staff conference, the meeting that became the Quebec Conference. The paper states the coalition's whole strategy in a few numbered paragraphs.

The over-all objective is the unconditional surrender of the Axis, in cooperation with Russia and other allies. Europe comes first; meanwhile pressure on Japan must never slacken. Once Europe is defeated, the full resources of both nations turn on Japan. The listed undertakings include aiding Russia and China, assisting French and Italian forces, and moving troops from Europe to the Pacific as a first priority.
frus-1944-quebec-d240:
Hopkins wrote to Roosevelt on September 13, 1944, about "the Italian business." He had talked with O'Dwyer, Crowley, and the State Department. He urged the president to take the initiative at Quebec. Roosevelt should win Churchill's approval for a course of action announced publicly. The machinery for quick relief and rehabilitation purchases, he said, was already available.

Italians could pay for goods, other than emergency relief, from funds accruing from American soldiers' pay in Italy. Two matters needed clearing up fast: the prisoner of war question, and amendment of the armistice terms. An attached memorandum argues Italy must return quickly to political and economic independence, free from domination by any powerful neighbor, with shipping, trucks, and payment as the immediate problems.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d40: Another Roosevelt message to Churchill followed on 3 January 1945, the second in two days. Filed as document 40 in the Foreign Relations of the United States volume on Malta and Yalta, it belongs to the final weeks of written preparation. frus-1945-malta-yalta-d140:
Harriman watched, but took no part, when Stalin and Churchill pressed the Polish premier in Moscow. His report to the President of 14 October 1944 describes the meeting with Mikolajczyk and his associates the day before. Molotov and Eden were present. The cable is printed in the Malta and Yalta volume.

Mikolajczyk first laid out the proposals of his August memorandum. Stalin found two great defects in it. It ignored the Polish Committee of National Liberation, the rival body set up at Lublin. And it failed to accept the Curzon Line as the Soviet-Polish boundary. Churchill backed Stalin on the Curzon Line without reserve. Stalin did allow that the memorandum had good points, friendly relations with the Soviet Union among them.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d240:
The Iranian minister came to plead his country's case on 18 January 1945. Stettinius recorded the conversation in a memorandum printed in the Malta and Yalta volume. It shows a small nation looking to Washington on the eve of the Big Three meeting. The minister called at his own request.

He had been instructed, he said, to draw attention to the Persian people's great concern over Russia's attitude and actions toward their country. His people hoped the United States would take a firm hand in insisting on a strong, independent Iran at the coming conference. Stettinius assured him that Persia's welfare was constantly in mind. The President, he was confident, would keep Iranian interests before him in the talks with Churchill and Stalin. The minister then offered his government's facilities for the meeting itself.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d340: Why not agree to a French zone now, Harry Hopkins asked the President in a note slipped across the Yalta table on February 5, 1945. The question of French membership in the Control Commission for Germany could be weighed later. Or, Hopkins added, Roosevelt might say that French participation could be considered later. Then he could leave it at that. The slip survives in Hopkins's papers, printed word for word. It captures a decision being shaped in real time, in pencil, while Stalin and Churchill waited.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d440:
Ties between the powers close the Polish formula, and this paper of February 10, 1945, preserves Molotov's draft of the final paragraph. His text notes that the Soviet state already kept ties with the Polish government then in place. Britain and the United States would now open ties with the new Polish Provisional Government of National Unity.

frus-1945-potsdam-1-d40:
Truman kept his options open in this telegram to Churchill of May 29, 1945. Churchill's Number 58 had been received. He was now making a study of a possible date for the three-party meeting. He hoped to have further information on the subject in the not distant future.

The wire is short and commits to nothing. Read beside Churchill's eagerness for mid-June, it looks deliberate. Stalin had signaled readiness after June 27. Washington would name the day when its own calendar, and its reading of Moscow, were ready. The caution fits a president six weeks into the job, holding the alliance's timetable in his own hand.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d140:

The printed passage covers procedure. Cadogan asked whether Potsdam would follow the Yalta pattern of foreign ministers meeting from noon to one and heads of government in the afternoon. frus-1945-potsdam-1-d240:

The message is document 240 in the Foreign Relations volume on the Potsdam Conference. The recommendation was that, once Italy declared war on Japan, the United States publicly back her admission in due course to the world security organization.

The recommendation already lay before the President in the Big Three briefing papers, Grew notes. But Italy may now declare war before the meeting opens. The value of the American move, at home and abroad, may depend on announcing it promptly after the declaration. He proposes proceeding at once: if Byrnes agrees and the President approves, Winant will be told to inform the British and ask whether they will support the American position.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d340:
A new state map for western Germany is reported in Murphy's despatch of June 30, 1945, on state organization in the American area. Army headquarters had directed the Twelfth Army Group to organize the Western Military District for military government on the basis of three German states, or Laender. The order held pending final fixing of the French zone.

The three states were Hessen-Nassau, with its capital at Kassel, Hessen, and a third built from the region's old units. frus-1945-potsdam-1-d440:
American views on minority transfers are restated in a State Department memorandum to the British Embassy dated July 11, 1945. The Department had considered the Foreign Office telegram of June 22 and the draft instructions for Ambassador Nichols in Prague. It answers by quoting its own note to the Czechoslovak government of January 31, 1945.

In that note Washington said it fully appreciated the injuries Czechoslovakia had suffered at the hands of Germany and of the German minority over the past decade. It was prepared to examine the problem in search of a satisfactory solution. Any solution, though, must weigh the broader aspects of the problem, and its relation to Europe's future peace.

frus-1945-potsdam-1-d640:

Bidault, the minister said, had told him France had firmly decided two things. The Troupes Speciales would be turned over to the Lebanese government. All French forces would leave the Levant as soon as British forces left theirs. France had also dropped, for now, its plan for a naval base there. It would revive that plan only if the new world organization allowed it. The minister added that Syria's mood ran much hotter than Lebanon's, and that few Frenchmen were left in Syria at all.

frus-1945-potsdam-2-d940:

Bombing had done little damage, Pauley writes. After the armistice, Russian teams removed nearly all the machinery, plus process records and plans. A few foremen were persuaded to go to Russia with the gear. Two plants belonged to International Telephone and Telegraph and were almost fully American owned. Sending it through the Moscow embassy would not reach the Kremlin in time. Since Ambassador Harriman was traveling to Berlin, the matter could be raised there in person. frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1140:

arxiv-2606-00040: Students writing with AI leave interaction patterns worth tracing. This paper uncovers them through epistemic network analysis. The patterns reveal how GenAI literacy develops. Writing alongside AI is an emerging literacy. Interaction patterns show how it develops. Educators should pay attention.
arxiv-2606-07640: Synthetic images under data scarcity — there's no free lunch. This paper proves it. The result tempers expectations for generative augmentation.  Generative data augmentation has real limitations. Understanding the no-free-lunch result tempers unrealistic expectations appropriately. Practitioner expectations become much more realistic.
tob-10040:
Evelyn Underhill, the scholar who brought mysticism to modern English readers, devoted a full study to Jan van Ruusbroec. Ruusbroec was a fourteenth-century Flemish mystic, among the great voices of medieval Dutch spirituality. Underhill follows him from parish priest to prior of a religious community.

Beyond the life, she explains his vision of the soul's ascent toward God, in language meant for readers outside a monastery. His teaching stressed an active life of love joined to deep contemplation. Underhill treats him not as a curiosity but as a serious guide, and her study remains a short, sympathetic entry into his thought.
tob-13340:
R. H. Charles's classic translation presents the Book of Enoch, an ancient apocalypse attributed to Noah's great-grandfather. Quoted in the New Testament letter of Jude, Enoch was nevertheless left out of most Bibles. Preserved whole only in Ethiopia's canon, the text survived in Ge'ez while its Hebrew and Aramaic forms largely vanished.

Its central story tells of the Watchers, angels who descended for human women, fathered giants, and taught forbidden arts, bringing judgment on heaven and earth. Visions of the end times follow. Enoch shaped early Christian and Jewish ideas of demons, fallen angels, and final judgment more deeply than its excluded status would suggest.
tob-4140:
Elias Ashmole, astrologer and collector, saved England's alchemical verse in the Theatrum Chemicum Britannicum of 1652. He printed the poetic pieces of the famous English philosophers of the hermetic art: George Ripley, Thomas Norton, and masters whose names are lost.

The poems teach the Great Work in allegory and riddle, in the spelling and music of their age. Ashmole, whose gifts founded Oxford's Ashmolean Museum, knew these texts might vanish without him. He was right. Checked from the 1919 printing, his collection remains the great storehouse of English alchemy in verse, and a monument to one collector's foresight.
tob-4240:
William Hone, the radical London printer who beat blasphemy charges in famous trials, published his Apocryphal New Testament in 1820. His collection prints the writings the early church left outside its canon. Infancy gospels of Jesus stand here, and the Gospel of Nicodemus. Letters ascribed to Paul and others fill out the set.

Hone meant the book for freethinkers' shelves, and it stayed in print for that audience all century. The translations are old ones, gathered rather than made fresh. Checked from the 1919 printing, his volume shows how apocrypha reached ordinary readers: cheaply, boldly, and under a fighter's imprint.
tob-0040:
Rob Arndt compiled German Disc Programs and Occult Origins, a research file on the claims of Nazi disc aircraft and their supposed occult roots. It treats the Haunebu and Vril craft of postwar legend and the Thule and Vril societies of early Nazi lore. The work dates from 2016 and circulates as a fringe-history dossier.

Arndt gathers the saucer stories, secret-society genealogies, and wonder-weapon tales into one documented survey of the mythos. No reliable evidence supports the disc programs as real aircraft; historians class them as postwar legend. The compilation's value lies in showing the legend whole: how occult societies, wartime rumor, and flying-saucer culture fused into a lasting story.
stukeley-stonehenge-temple-restord-1740:
Antiquary William Stukeley surveyed Stonehenge and read it as a Druid temple. His book Stonehenge, A Temple Restor'd to the British Druids came out in 1740. Stukeley was a doctor and cleric who loved old Britain.

He measured the stones and the avenues around them with care. Then he built a grand theory of Druid rites upon the plan. That theory is now doubted, but his records hold real value. Later diggers destroyed much that he drew in place. His dream of Druids shaped how Britain saw the stones for two centuries.
vyse-operations-pyramids-gizeh-vol-1-184:
Richard William Howard Vyse blasted his way into the Great Pyramid in 1837, and Vol. 1 of his Operations, out in 1840, tells how. Vyse was a chief of troops with funds and zeal. With the aid of Perring, he forced the hid rooms past the king's hall. There he found the name of Khufu writ in red paint.

That find fixed who built the heap for good. Logs, costs, and tales of the dig crowd the tome. His rough means drew scorn, yet his finds changed the field. This is the first full tale of a dig there.
vyse-operations-pyramids-gizeh-vol-2-184:
Richard William Howard Vyse pushed his dig past the great heap in Vol. 2 of his Operations, out in 1840. The first tome told of the forced rooms and the name of Khufu. Here the work spreads to the next heaps, the Sphinx, and tombs in the sand. Perring's fine plans and cuts fill page past page.

Those plans are the tome's chief worth. Digs since then still cite their sums and lines. The log prose is dry, yet the scale of the work stuns. Read as a pair, the tomes found the dig of the heaps.
machiavelli-prince-dacres-1640:
Niccolò Machiavelli wrote The Prince in Italian, and Edward Dacres made the first English version in 1640. Dacres gave English readers Machiavelli's masterpiece a century after it stirred Italy in print there. The slim book of counsel on power still starts fights about ends and means.

Machiavelli tells a new prince how to gain a state and keep it by force. Fear, he argues, beats love when a ruler must choose, and cruelty has its uses. He praises Cesare Borgia's ruthless craft and blames mercy that breeds disorder in a state. Fox and lion, fraud and force, are his paired tools of rule in the text. The name Machiavellian for cold statecraft starts with this blunt little book's fame.
lermontov-hero-of-our-time-1840:
Mikhail Lermontov published A Hero of Our Time in 1840, a Russian novel made of five linked tales. The hero is Pechorin, a young officer serving in the Caucasus. He is clever, bored, and often cruel to those who love him. Other narrators describe him before his own diary speaks.

The tales include a kidnapping, a smugglers' plot, a duel, and a wager on fate. Pechorin treats life as a game and leaves harm behind him. Lermontov died young, yet this book secured his fame. It gave Russian fiction one of its first great antiheroes and a sharp portrait of a restless generation.
ranke-history-popes-vol-1-1840:
Leopold von Ranke's History of the Popes, Volume 1, appears in Sarah Austin's translation of 1840. Ranke is called the father of modern historiography for his use of archives. This volume covers the papacy from its medieval height through the Reformation era. Popes, cardinals, and Italian courts come alive from state papers.

Ranke aimed to show the past as it actually was, in his famous phrase. His calm tone toward Catholic and Protestant alike was new and striking. The work made the seminar method of history famous abroad. Austin's version carried it through the English-speaking world. Volume 1 opens a classic of both church and political history.
whitefield-journals-1740:
George Whitefield was the most famous preacher of the eighteenth century, whose voice could reach crowds in open fields. His Journals, first published in 1740, record his preaching tours across Britain and America in his own words. Whitefield wrote them partly to answer his critics.

He describes packed churches, weeping hearers, journeys by horse and ship, and his break with John Wesley over doctrine. The entries mix frank self-praise with real wonder at the crowds his message drew. Historians of the Great Awakening treat the Journals as a prime source written from the movement's center.
shelley-defence-of-poetry-1840:
Percy Bysshe Shelley wrote A Defence of Poetry in 1821, answering a friend's playful claim that poetry was fading in a practical age. Shelley left the essay unfinished, and it stayed in manuscript until 1840. By then Shelley had been dead for eighteen years.

Shelley argues that poets shape the moral and social imagination of their age. Reason counts and measures, he says, but imagination gives knowledge its human worth. Poetry strengthens sympathy, the root of all moral good. The essay closes with the famous claim that poets are the unacknowledged legislators of the world. It became the most quoted defense of poetry of the whole century.
cooper-pathfinder-1840:
James Fenimore Cooper returned to Leatherstocking after a long break and published The Pathfinder in 1840. He set it on Lake Ontario during the Seven Years' War, when his hero is in his prime as a scout. Cooper had always insisted Natty needed a love story, and this is the volume that gives him one.

Natty, called Pathfinder for his unerring woodcraft, guides young Mabel Dunham to her father's island fort. He falls quietly in love with her, though a dashing rival and his own honest nature stand in the way. French and Indian attacks, a blockade, and a storm on the lake supply the action. Cooper's lake scenery is among his finest writing. The Pathfinder is the essential middle volume of the Leatherstocking Tales.
townshend-facts-in-mesmerism-1840:
Chauncy Hare Townshend made the literary case for mesmerism in Facts in Mesmerism, printed in 1840. Townshend was a poet and man of letters, not a doctor. His book records cases he witnessed and tested himself. The subtitle pleads for a dispassionate inquiry into the subject.

He asks readers to weigh evidence before they mock or believe. Mesmeric sleep, painless operations, and clairvoyant claims enter his record. The work became the most cited early English defense outside medical journals. It shows mesmerism winning cultured friends in its first British years. Townshend's tone is curious, candid, and measured. His cases still anchor histories of the movement.
plos-pone-0003440:
Peter V. Lovell and colleagues read gene activity in the songbird brain in this 2008 paper. Songbirds learn their songs, much as children learn speech. A set of brain nuclei, called the song system, drives that learning. The team used high-throughput methods to profile genes across that system.

The profiles revealed chemical specializations in the song nuclei. Certain signals and receptors stood out against the rest of the brain. Those traits may support vocal learning, a rare skill among animals. The results offer clues to the molecular basis of learned song and speech.
plos-pone-0003540:
Tetsuya Kimura and co-authors studied an enzyme tied to memory in this 2008 paper. GSK-3β is an enzyme suspected in Alzheimer's disease. That disease starts with memory disturbance in its early stages. The enzyme's normal role in the adult brain was not well understood.

The team showed GSK-3β is required for memory reconsolidation. That process restabilizes a memory after it is recalled. Blocking the enzyme kept recalled memories from settling again. The finding names a molecular step in how memories persist. Recalled memories are not fixed files, and this work shows one way they shift.
plos-pone-0003640:
Till Bärnighausen, Claudia Wallrauch, Alex Welte, and colleagues published this methods study in PLOS ONE in 2008. Counting new HIV infections is hard, so surveys use a blood test meant to flag recent ones. The team checked that test, called cBED, in rural South Africa.

They compared incidence estimates from one-time survey testing with estimates from following the same population over years. There was concern the assay wrongly classifies some long-standing infections as recent, inflating the count. The head-to-head check shows how far the shortcut can be trusted for planning HIV programs.
plos-pone-0003740:
Dimitrios Iliopoulos, Konstantinos N. Malizos, Pagona Oikonomou, and colleagues published this arthritis study in PLOS ONE in 2008. Osteoarthritis wears down joint cartilage and affects more than 100 million people worldwide. Its causes mix genes, mechanics, and environment, and its gene list was incomplete.

The team combined microRNA data with proteomic data, the full set of proteins in tissue. Together the two approaches flagged new osteoarthritis genes. They also mapped how the hits work together in metabolic and inflammatory networks, showing the disease as a joint effort of many genes. Worn joints are a top cause of pain in older adults.
plos-pone-0003840:
Simani Gaseitsiwe, Davide Valentini, Shahnaz Mahdavifar, and colleagues published this tuberculosis study in PLOS ONE in 2008. Hunting antigens by reading serum antibodies had been used to find targets in cancer. A similar approach can flag meaningful targets in tuberculosis infection. The team applied it with a high content peptide microarray.

Their chip carried peptides from 61 proteins of Mycobacterium tuberculosis. Antibody binding patterns in patients' blood defined recognizable patterns of tuberculosis. The pattern recognition approach borrows tumor-antigen hunting for the fight against TB, aiming at better tests and vaccine targets.
plos-pone-0003940:
H. Artee Luchman, Hallgrimur Benediktsson, Michelle L. Villemaire, and co-authors timed a gene loss in mouse prostate in 2008. Loss of PTEN, a tumor-blocking gene, is common in human prostate cancer. It is most common in advanced disease. PTEN also gates a major growth signal path in cells.

Their PLOS ONE article removed Pten at set times in the mouse prostate. The pace of early abnormal growth depended on when the gene was cut. Early lesions grew at rates set by that timing. The work shows the order of gene losses shapes how prostate cancer starts.
plos-pone-0004040:
Manos Tsakiris asked how we know a mirror face is our own in a 2008 PLOS ONE article. A reflection looks like us, but looks may not be the whole story. The reflection also moves when we move. We see it touched exactly when we feel touch ourselves.

The study tested how current multisensory input alters self-face recognition. Matching sight and touch cues shifted judgments of what counts as self. That shows self-recognition is built live from several senses. The work informs research on body ownership and its disorders. It appeared in PLOS ONE, and the full text is free for any reader to check.
plos-pone-0004140:
Richard Cudney-Bueno and colleagues published this marine study in PLOS ONE in 2009. Marine reserves, sea areas where fishing is banned, are promoted around the world as tools for conservation and fishery management. Supporters argue that reserves protect sea life and also help fisheries, as extra adults spill out and larvae drift into fishing grounds.

Solid proof for those benefits, especially the larval route, had been thin. The authors present evidence that reserves can produce rapid effects through the spread of larvae to nearby waters. Their findings support the idea that a reserve can repay nearby fisheries quickly, not just in the long run.
plos-pone-0004240:
Takahiro Fujimoto and colleagues published this obesity study in PLOS ONE in 2009. Obesity and its metabolic disorders are leading causes of adult illness and death. KRAP is a protein tied to the cell's actin skeleton, found in tissues throughout the body and first identified as a cancer-related molecule.

The team studied mice lacking KRAP and fed them a fattening diet. They report altered energy homeostasis and resistance to diet-induced obesity in these mice. A protein that, when missing, keeps mice lean on rich food is a clue to how the body sets its weight.
plos-pone-0004340:
Marco José and colleagues published this theory paper in PLOS ONE in 2009. The standard genetic code translates DNA into proteins in nearly all life. The authors ask how it evolved from a primeval RNA code in the RNA world. That was an early era when RNA did both information and chemistry jobs.

They derive two candidate ancestral codes, one built from codons of the type RNY, purine, any base, pyrimidine, plus related codons. They argue the modern code keeps vestiges of critical scale invariance from that RNA world in current prokaryote genomes. The code itself, on this view, is a fossil.
plos-pone-0004440:
A small self-building peptide slowed scrapie, a prion disease, in hamsters, report Robert Hnasko and Cathrin Bruederle in PLOS ONE in 2009. Scrapie is caused by a warped protein that forces healthy copies to warp too. The team injected hamsters in the brain with scrapie material mixed with the peptide, called RADA. The peptide assembles itself into tiny scaffolds.

Hamsters given the mix got sick later and lived longer than expected. The benefit grew with the dose of peptide and with time spent mixed with the bad protein before injection. The authors say the peptide disrupts the build-up of the warped protein. For diseases with no cure, even a delay points to a new way of blocking prions.
plos-pone-0004540:
Tuberculosis bacteria from New Delhi are profiled in depth by Ruth Stavrum, Vithal Prasad Myneedu, Virendra Arora, and co-authors in PLOS ONE in 2009. India carries the highest estimated burden of tuberculosis in the world, about a fifth of all cases. Yet the genomic diversity of the bacterium in India had not been systematically mapped with multiple markers.

The team's molecular characterization of isolates from New Delhi found a predominance of drug-resistant isolates of the so-called modern type, marked by the loss of a region called TbD1. That pattern has practical weight. Drug resistance changes which medicines can be used, and strain types differ in how they spread. A clear local profile helps clinics and control programs plan.
plos-pone-0004640:
Genetic switches can now be flipped on command in zebrafish, show Stefan Hans, Jan Kaslin, Dorian Freudenreich, and co-authors in PLOS ONE in 2009. The method uses an enzyme called Cre to cut and rejoin DNA at set sites. It is a strong tool in mouse genetics, but it was nearly absent in other backboned animals. In this fish, early tries at Cre-based switching worked very poorly.

Using jumping genes to deliver the parts, the team achieved timed, controlled switching in the fish. Scientists can now turn genes on or off in chosen tissues at chosen times. These fish are cheap, clear-bodied, and fast-breeding. Giving them mouse-grade gene control widens the range of disease and development questions they can answer.
plos-pone-0004740:
Kyle Young, Jos Snoeks, and Ole Seehausen asked what drives shape diversity in African cichlid fish radiations, in PLOS ONE in 2009. When one line splits into many forms fast, three forces may be at play. Fixed rules may push like forms, past history may limit options, or chance may rule the outcome.

The team compared repeated radiations in a shared shape space. Like shapes in distinct lakes point to fixed rules, while scatter points to chance or history. Their test helps weigh those forces in a classic case. Cichlids are a key model for how new species arise.
dupotet-cours-magnetisme-sept-lecons-184:
Jules Dupotet teaches animal magnetism in seven lessons in his Cours de magnetisme, in French from 1840. The leading French magnetizer of his day instructs step by step. Students learn how to induce the trance, what signs to expect, and how the magnetic cure claims to heal the sick.

Clear, practical, and fully confident, the course served as the textbook of high mesmerism. Dupotet writes as a master sure of his art and its laws. Passes, rapport, and somnambulism each get their ordered place here. The book shows mesmerism as a teachable craft in its prime, the standard course by which a generation of magnetizers learned their trade.
dupotet-magnetisme-oppose-medecine-1840:
Dupotet declares war on the doctors in Le magnetisme oppose a la medecine, in French from 1840. The magnetic cure, he argues, heals where learned physicians fail. Regular medicine answers with scorn, and the pamphlet war between the schools burns hot on every page of his polemic.

Combative, earnest, and utterly sure of itself, the book speaks for the magnetizers' cause. Dupotet mocks degrees, latin, and fees with a pamphleteer's glee. Patients' cures are his chosen weapons in the fight. The work stands as a founding manifesto of alternative healing in nineteenth-century France, a shot in a long war over who may heal.
mueller-handbuch-physiologie-1840:
Johannes Muller sums up the science of the body in his Handbuch der Physiologie, in German from 1840. The handbook served as the nineteenth century's bible of physiology. Senses, blood, nerves, and voice all fall under Muller's vast and orderly learning, drawn from his Berlin lectures and his own tireless trials.

His students included Helmholtz, Virchow, and Du Bois-Reymond, founders of modern medicine in their turn. Muller taught them to test every claim on living tissue. Few teachers have ever shaped a science so deeply through pupils. The book stands behind a whole era of German medicine, the seedbed from which its golden age grew.
teste-manuel-pratique-magnetisme-1840:
Alphonse Teste wrote his Practical Manual of Animal Magnetism in French in 1840. French healers who used magnetic passes and trance soon treated it as their standard guide. Teste aimed to make a disputed art look calm, skilled, and safe.

Step by step, the manual shows how to induce a trance in a patient. It then explains how to read illness during magnetic sleep and how to treat it. Clear rules, case notes, and warnings fill the pages. The book shows what a trained magnetizer in France was expected to know and do each day.
savigny-system-heutigen-roem-rechts-1840:
Savigny's System of Modern Roman Law began appearing in German in 1840, the summa of his career. He had led the historical school for a quarter century, and the System gathers its doctrine into one ordered account of private law. Lawyers call the approach pandectist, after the Pandects, the Roman Digest at its core.

The volumes order the whole of private law: persons, property, obligations, and family, each concept defined and placed by historical light. Savigny's method treats law as a system whose parts explain each other, growing from a people's life rather than a legislator's whim. The System became the bible of nineteenth-century jurisprudence in Germany. Its concepts passed into the German Civil Code of 1900, so its fingerprints rest on the private law of many nations today.
cia-0000007540:
Spring 1965 produced volume 9, number 1 of Studies in Intelligence, the CIA's journal for its own officers. A heading in the issue points to intelligence treated in recent publications, a sign officers tracked outside writing about their field. The journal's readers were practitioners, not the general public.

Pages like these record a profession pausing to examine itself: its books, its methods, and its mistakes. That habit matters because secret work rarely gets open debate. Now declassified, the issue helps historians see what concerned American analysts as the Vietnam War widened. The text survives through the CIA reading room release.
cia-0000008640:
A crashed US Air Force F-105 was sighted in Hai Hung province, North Vietnam, in a report dated July 1973. The F-105 Thunderchief flew many of the war's hardest bombing missions over the north. Hai Hung lies in the Red River plain east of Hanoi.

By mid-1973 American combat flights had stopped, so wreck sightings mostly aided the accounting for lost crews. A located crash site could confirm what happened to a pilot who never returned. The report shows that work proceeding through local observation after the ceasefire. It is one entry in the air war's long final ledger.
cia-0000009440:
Americans remaining in South Vietnam, and detention of Americans in the north, fill a CIA paper dated January 1976. Saigon had fallen eight months earlier, ending the war and stranding questions about who stayed or was held. Some Americans had remained by choice, others by circumstance.

The paper takes stock of those cases a year into the new order. Washington had little access and less leverage, so reporting ran thin. Families and officials still needed names, numbers, and best judgments. The file shows the accounting moving into its postwar phase, where diplomacy at last replaced wartime channels entirely.
cia-0000009640:
Enemy prisons and facilities near Khang Khay, plus results of airstrikes in the area, fill a January 1969 CIA item. Khang Khay sits on Laos's Plain of Jars, a much-fought-over plateau in Xieng Khouang province. The pairing of prisons and strike results in one file is striking.

Planners needed prison locations marked clearly, not least so bombs would not fall on captives. Strike reports, meanwhile, recorded what air attacks had done nearby. Holding both subjects together shows the terrible closeness of bombing and captivity in Laos. The file preserves that tension in a single dated record.
cia-0000009740:
Southeast of the junction of Routes 911 and 9113 stood a prison housing Lao inmates, an October 1969 report states. The routes ran through southern Laos, along the infiltration network toward Vietnam. Most prisoners in such sites were Lao, held by one side or the other in a civil war.

Lao-held prisons rarely drew the attention given to American cases. Yet mapping them showed the war's full carceral reach inside Laos itself. Local inmates' fates also tested which side controlled the countryside. This file keeps a Lao prison, not an American one, on the permanent official record.
cia-0000009840:
A Viet Cong prison built for American prisoners inside Cambodia is described in a February 1967 report. A prison meant for Americans alone marks a step beyond holding captives in mixed camps. Cambodia's border sanctuaries gave such a site shelter from South Vietnamese forces.

Purpose-built prisons implied the captors expected a long war and many prisoners. For officials, the report proved planning, not improvisation, behind cross-border captivity. It also fixed a target for watching in a country officially at peace. The file stands early in the record of Cambodia's hidden role in the prison war.
cia-0000012340:
Conversations with a contact whose name is blacked out fill a CIA record from 1962. The talks took place in London in March and in Geneva days later. The London talks ran March 8 to 11; the Geneva talks, March 14 to 25. Two cities in one month place an allied dimension of the Penkovsky case squarely on the calendar.

Meeting records like this one fix the operation's British and Swiss chapters in dates. Allies conferred, compared, and coordinated around a source neither could run alone. For readers, the page shows the cousins' work: quiet, dated, and essential to the case.
cia-0000013940: Four American prisoners came through the fight unhurt, in a CIA note dated February 1, 1968. The note places the four in Gia Lai Province, in South Vietnam. Their sound health was the kind of detail families and officials scanned for first. Short notes like this carried the small facts that kept prisoner files current.
cia-0000015340: Recent sightings of unexplained objects fill a CIA file dated June 2, 1952. A memo is attached, dated December 2, on the same subject. June 1952 opened the summer that made saucers a national fever. A file of fresh sightings from that month catches the wave as it began to rise. The sightings file and its memo rest in the CIA Reading Room.
cia-0000020440: Orlando Letelier is noted as a lecturer at American University in a redacted CIA record dated in 1975. Letelier had served Chile's fallen Allende government as a senior envoy. In Washington he taught, spoke, and pressed the case against Chile's new rulers. Parts of the note were cut before release, so the surviving fact is his campus role that year.
cia-0000020340: Colonel Carlos Castillo Armas appears as a Guatemalan exile in a CIA record dated in 1951. Exile was his lot after a failed rising, years before he took power in 1954. Files on exiles helped officials judge who might lead next in a troubled land. Read today, the early profile gains weight from all that followed for the man and his country.
cia-0000022340: Powers was to be released, a CIA record dated in 1962 reports in its short heading. The release came in February 1962, when he was swapped for Rudolf Abel in Berlin. Word of a coming release would have raced through the agency that winter. The bare heading holds the hopeful turn after two years of prison and hard bargaining.
cia-0000027940: Hunt J. is the whole title of a CIA item dated in 1970. The catalog gives a surname and one initial, nothing more, so this account adds nothing. A file this bare could hold a contact note, a check, or a warning about a man. It stands as the thinnest kind of personal record the archive keeps, a name and a year.
cia-0000036540:
A CIA daily report on Latin America, dated October 3, 1978, notes that ORIT declared a boycott against Chile. ORIT was a regional labor body, and its boycott targeted Chile's military government. The item appears inside the day's wider roundup of Latin American news.

The report gives the boycott a place among the day's main regional stories. Labor action against Chile drew notice because it crossed borders and unions. Daily digests like this preserve small items that later histories often leave out entirely. A boycott call by a labor federation was a pressure tool that stopped short of force.
cia-0000036640:
Photo comparison results for William Johnson fill a CIA record dated January 2, 1971. The case number is 12478, and the file belongs to the MIA and POW effort. One prisoner photograph was at the center of the comparison work.

Analysts set the prisoner photograph beside known pictures and judged whether they matched. A match could confirm that a missing man was alive and held in captivity. The record holds the outcome of that careful check for one named serviceman. Johnson's case was one of hundreds worked through the same careful process during those years. A single photograph could carry the whole weight of a family's hopes for news.
cia-0000045240:
An agreement was reportedly reached for the Duarte release, in a CIA record dated September 2, 1985. Reportedly leaves the door open, as careful wire writing does. The release it promised was the ending the whole country awaited.

Inside, the reported breakthrough in the case is recorded. A reached agreement should have meant terms settled and a date set. In this crisis, such hopeful reports had risen and fallen before, sometimes within a single week of hard and silent waiting. The file preserves this one at its hopeful hour, leaving readers to set it beside the harder and slower records that surround it in the series.
cia-0000049140: Reporting requirements, the rules for how officers in the field had to file their reports, fill a CIA item from 1989. The item sits in the Truth Commission file series, a piece of office machinery among the war records. Even the paperwork had a paper trail, and this is part of it: how the flood of reports was ordered.
cia-0000049240:
Political violence and insurgent propaganda in El Salvador are paired as the subject of a CIA paper from 1983. The pairing was the point: the guerrillas fought with words as deliberately as with rifles, and the state answered in kind. The paper survives in the files later gathered for the Truth Commission.

Inside, the subject splits in two: the violence itself, counted and sorted, and the printed and broadcast war that framed it. Analysts tracked leaflets, radio, and slogans because belief moved recruits and money as surely as battles did. The paper shows the war read as a contest for minds, not only ground.
cia-0000049340: Declassified CIA document 0000049340, dated March 5, 1981, is titled El Salvador: More Political Problems and marked for the Truth Commission. The heading signals further political trouble in El Salvador without naming a single cause. Readers get a brief agency item whose general title reflects a running watch on the country's politics, preserved as filed in the declassified collection.
cia-0000078940: On the Trail of Submarine Disasters is the title of declassified CIA document 0000078940, dated September 15, 1992. The heading suggests an account following submarine losses rather than a routine report. Readers get a short declassified item whose literary title sets it apart from the catalog's plainer files. The record itself gives no further detail in its heading.
cia-0000096940: Program Objectives, Special Operations Group, Counter Intelligence Staff is the heading of declassified CIA document 0000096940, dated May 4, 1972. The title reads like an internal office label, naming the group and staff. The brief file is an internal objectives record, preserved as a glimpse of how one counterintelligence unit stated its own program aims.
cia-0000098740: CAD software for the GDR's K-1845 computer is described in declassified CIA document 0000098740, dated March 5, 1990. The heading names the software type, the country by initials, and one machine model. Readers get a short technical description record on East German computing, part of the agency's close tracking of bloc computer equipment.
cia-0000102940: Denied, plus prison labor used for pipeline construction from 1968 to March 1979, form declassified CIA document 0000102940, dated November 5, 1982. The first numbered topic is a single word, Denied, left unexplained. Readers find a short pipeline labor record with the cluster's longest date span in its heading, from the late sixties onward. The catalog keeps the record under its original subject heading.

plos-pone-0004840:
Sabine Stegemann and colleagues showed increased risk to pneumococcal superinfection during influenza is not caused by TLR7 mediated lymphopenia, in PLOS ONE in 2009. Influenza A causes respiratory infections with recurring epidemics and high morbidity and mortality. In the past century it induced several pandemics. The most aggressive in 1918 with a death toll estimated at twenty to fifty million cases including many microbe complications.

Secondary microbe pneumonia drives much flu mortality. Ruling out one step narrows the search. Lymphocyte loss via TLR7 is not the explanation. Other immune disruptions must be responsible. These findings offer a firm starting point for the next round of testing. The team also set out clear next steps for work in this field.
plos-pone-0005440:
Tobias Kind, Martin Scholz, and Oliver Fiehn asked a basic question in a 2009 PLOS ONE study. How large is the set of small chemicals in a living thing? Guessing that set from genes alone misses products made by genes no one has yet described. So the full set has to be measured in the lab, not just predicted.

The authors looked hard at how chemical data are shared and named between labs. Poor sharing makes it hard to know whether two labs found the same chemical. Their critique pushes for clearer data habits so the true size of the chemical set can be pinned down.
plos-pone-0005540:
Fumiaki Sato and co-authors tested the reliability of microRNA chip tests in a 2009 PLOS ONE report. Chip tests that read thousands of genes at once had already been put through large quality checks. Chips for microRNAs, the small strands that tune genes, came later and needed the same checks.

The team ran the same samples many times on one chip type and across different types. They measured how well repeats agreed and whether platforms told the same story. Solid agreement gives labs confidence to use these chips in cancer and disease studies.
plos-pone-0005640:
Matthew Dye, Peter Hauser, and Daphne Bavelier studied visual attention in deaf people in a 2009 PLOS ONE report. People deaf from early life pay sharper attention to the edges of vision. Whether that helps in daily life is less clear, since they are also more easily distracted by side events.

The team used a test of the useful field of view, which measures how much a person takes in at a glance. Their results weigh the gains against the costs. The balance matters for schooling and workplace design for deaf people. Deaf people's wider field may be a strength in jobs like sport and surveillance work.
plos-pone-0005740:
Anton Simeonov and co-authors screened for compounds that block a key DNA repair enzyme in 2009. The enzyme, APE1, cuts out damaged spots in DNA so they can be fixed. Cells rely on this repair path to survive daily wear from oxygen and chemicals.

Blocking APE1 could make cancer cells more sensitive to drugs that damage DNA. The team found and profiled several blockers of the enzyme. They describe how each compound acts and how strong it is. Such blockers are leads, not drugs yet, but they give chemists a start. The work also helps probe what APE1 does beyond repair.
plos-pone-0005840:
Gregory Bowman and Vijay Pande asked in 2009 what really limits computer prediction of protein shapes. Knowing a protein's folded shape from its sequence is a grand challenge. Their earlier work suggested the popular Rosetta program's rough energy scores can actually mislead the search.

Here they weigh entropy and kinetics, the odds and speed of folding paths, in prediction success. Shape prediction may fail not from bad scoring but from never visiting the right shape. That shifts effort toward smarter sampling of possible folds. The paper speaks to anyone building the next generation of folding tools.
plos-pone-0006440:
Kaushal Parikh and colleagues compared two signaling enzymes in a 2009 PLOS ONE paper. Kinases are enzymes that tag other proteins with phosphate groups, and they steer much of cell life. The human genome holds more than five hundred of them. Each kinase tags only certain substrates, but the rules behind that choice are only partly known.

Using peptide arrays, grids of short protein pieces, the team measured which pieces each enzyme tags. They compared c-Raf with a kinase known as MAP kinase kinase kinase 8. Side-by-side profiles show where their tastes match and differ. That helps decode how signaling networks stay specific instead of blurring together.
plos-pone-0006540:
Celia Ravel and co-authors tested folate pathway genes in unexplained infertility for PLOS ONE in 2009. The metabolic pathway of folate is thought to influence DNA stability. It can induce breaks in DNA or produce low levels of a key methyl donor. The team examined genetic polymorphisms in enzymes associated with folate metabolism.

Their title reports a lack of association between those polymorphisms and unexplained infertility. A clear negative result saves couples and clinics from useless genetic tests. It also steers research toward other causes. Negative findings like this are essential ballast for a literature biased toward positive claims.
plos-pone-0006640:
Dong Hu, Xiuli Bi, Wenfeng Fang, and colleagues studied cross-talk between two signaling enzymes in PLOS ONE in 2009. They had recently reported that the MAP kinase JNK1 downregulates beta-catenin signaling and plays a critical role in regulating intestinal homeostasis. Beta-catenin drives growth programs in the gut and in cancers. The team now examined GSK3 beta in relation to JNK2.

Their title reports GSK3 beta is involved in JNK2-mediated beta-catenin inhibition. Two kinases cooperate to restrain a growth signal. Layered restraint suggests the pathway is heavily guarded. Losing those guards is a known route to colorectal cancer.
plos-pone-0009440:
An Vo, Engeline van Duijkeren, and Wim Gaastra surveyed Salmonella germs from Vietnam in PLOS ONE in 2010. Some of these germs no longer respond to common drugs. The team gathered close to three hundred samples from people and from animals. They tested which drugs still worked on each sample.

They also looked for mobile bits of DNA that can carry drug resistance from one germ to the next. Such bits include class 1 integrons and a region called genomic island 1. The survey maps where resistance sits and how it might spread. That map can guide efforts to slow the loss of useful drugs.
plos-pone-0009540:
Mark Sommerfeld and colleagues examined a long acting insulin in the lab in PLOS ONE in 2010. Insulin glargine, sold as Lantus, gives people with diabetes steady sugar control for a full day. After injection under the skin, part of it is changed into two breakdown products. The team studied how the drug and those products signal inside cells.

They separated signals that handle sugar from signals that push cell growth. The products behaved much like the parent drug in these tests. That detail matters, because growth signals have raised safety questions for insulins. Knowing exactly what circulates and acts helps doctors judge the drug's long term use.
plos-pone-0009640:
Marina Panova and co-authors documented extreme mating in a small marine animal in PLOS ONE in 2010. The animal is a non social invertebrate, a group where mates meet only briefly. Females of this species mate with a very large number of males. That level of female promiscuity is rare in such animals. The team used genetic tests to count how many fathers contributed to each female's offspring.

Genetic counts confirmed mating rates far beyond the norm for like species. The authors explore what could drive such excess, from sperm competition to genetic variety in offspring. The case challenges tidy claims about mating systems. It shows that even simple animals can evolve mating lives of surprising intensity.
plos-pone-0010440:
Corey Bradshaw, Xingli Giam and Navjot Sodhi ranked countries by their harm to nature in PLOS ONE in 2010. Protecting ecosystems keeps services people depend on, from clean water to pollination. Ranking countries can expose the worst performers and highlight good models. Earlier rankings were often rough or based on few measures. The team built fresh metrics combining several kinds of impact.

Their rankings weigh harm both at home and in total scale. Big countries can rank badly by sheer size even with moderate habits. Fair metrics must state which view they take. The study gives policy makers a sharper comparison tool. It also gives the public a way to ask leaders hard questions.
plos-pone-0010540:
Akhilesh Mishra and colleagues reported that the 2009 pandemic flu caused severe disease in India in PLOS ONE in 2010. The new H1N1 strain posed a worldwide challenge that year. Early on, nations lacked solid data on how severe it really was. Without severity data, responses risk being too weak or too drastic. The team analyzed laboratory-confirmed cases from India to gauge severity there.

Their results showed the pandemic strain could indeed cause severe illness in that setting. Local severity data help hospitals plan beds, oxygen, and staffing. They also help officials communicate risk honestly to the public. India-specific evidence matters in a country of India's size and diversity. This study supplied an early, grounded severity picture.
plos-pone-0010640:
Tony Buchanan, David Bibas, and Ralph Adolphs ran a large outdoor experiment on emotion reading, in PLOS ONE in 2010. People judge feelings from faces every day. The question was whether our own felt emotions shape how well we read happiness and fear in others.

Hundreds of participants took part outside the lab. Their own emotional states were measured alongside their judgments of faces. Feeling and judging were linked, but not in a simple copycat way. The results suggest personal experience trains emotion reading over time. That matters for understanding conditions where reading feelings goes wrong.
plos-pone-0010740:
Samyra Lacerda and colleagues sped up germ cell transplantation in Nile tilapia, in PLOS ONE in 2010. Moving sperm-making stem cells from one fish to another lets a host father offspring with the donor's genes. The technique is the main way to study these stem cells in fish, but surgery made it slow.

Their method delivers the cells without surgery, through the fish's natural opening. Recipient males later produced donor-derived offspring. A fast, gentle method opens the door to banking genes of valuable or endangered fish in common hosts. Fish farms and conservation programs both need that kind of living storage.
plos-pone-0010840:
Lennert Slobbe, Jeanette Doorduijn, Pieternella Lugtenburg and colleagues ran this clinical trial, published in PLOS ONE in 2010. Patients with blood disorders often need a tunnelled central line for treatment, and bacteria growing inside the line can cause serious bloodstream infection. The trial tested a daily ethanol lock, where alcohol sits briefly inside the catheter to kill germs.

Hundreds of adult patients were assigned at random to an ethanol lock or a placebo lock, each used for fifteen minutes a day. Infection rates inside the catheter were lower with ethanol, but the gap was not large enough to rule out chance. Slobbe and colleagues report a cautious result: the approach looked safe and promising, yet this trial alone could not prove it prevents infection.
plos-pone-0010940:
Brett Hilton and Roland Wolkowicz published this HIV methods study in PLOS ONE in 2010. HIV keeps escaping drugs, so new antivirals and faster ways to find them are both needed. The virus's protease enzyme, which snips viral proteins into working parts, is a proven drug target, and the authors built a living test that reports its activity.

They engineered T cells, the very cells HIV infects, carrying a switch: the viral protease is fused inside a protein that turns on a glowing reporter gene. Only when an effective protease inhibitor blocks the enzyme does the glow appear. Hilton and Wolkowicz thus turn drug action into a light signal readable by standard cell-sorting machines. Screening inside real target cells should weed out compounds that fail where it matters.
plos-pone-0011040:
Pascal Meier, Emmanouil Brilakis, Roberto Corti and co-authors published this heart stent meta-analysis in PLOS ONE in 2010. Bypass grafts made from leg veins develop aggressive narrowing, and whether drug-eluting stents beat plain bare-metal stents for reopening them was unproven. The authors pooled the controlled studies comparing the two stent types in vein graft lesions.

Their search gathered twenty-nine studies covering more than seven thousand patients, though only a few were randomized trials and those were small. The primary question was whether the treated vessel needed reopening again, with heart attack, stent clotting, and death as secondary measures. The need for repeat procedures tended to favor drug-eluting stents, but the evidence base was thin. Meier and colleagues show where the balance of evidence leans while exposing how few strong trials support a common procedure.
plos-pone-0011140:
Secchiero, Zorzet, Tripodo and colleagues tested stem cells against lymphoma in PLOS ONE in 2010. They used human bone marrow stem cells in mice carrying spread out human lymphoma. These mice lacked a working immune system, so human cells and tumors could survive in them.

The stem cells showed anti cancer activity against the spread lymphoma in the mice. That surprising effect hints at a new kind of cell based therapy. Much more testing is needed to learn how the effect works and whether it is safe. Still, the result turns a repair cell into a possible cancer fighter worth studying.
plos-pone-0011240:
Peddinti, Memili and Burgess modeled cow egg development in PLOS ONE in 2010. A cow egg matures inside a cluster of helper cells that feed and signal to it. Using protein wide measurements and systems modeling, the team mapped how egg and helper cells interact at an early stage.

The model reveals the joint program that prepares an egg for fertilization. Better grasp of that program could raise success in cattle embryo production. Breeding gains flow to dairy and beef herds alike. The approach also shows how protein data can be turned into a working model of two cell types talking.
plos-pone-0011340:
Martin Hosking and co-authors used a mouse model in 2010 to study how a virus strips insulation from nerve fibers. Mice infected in the brain with a weakened mouse hepatitis virus first get brain inflammation, then lose myelin, the fatty coat that helps nerves carry signals fast. The team tested one chemical signal and its receptor on immune cells.

Signaling through that receptor protected the cells that make myelin and limited how much insulation was lost. Mice with the signal intact kept more healthy myelin-making cells during the illness. The finding matters because multiple sclerosis involves similar myelin loss in people. A pathway that shields myelin-making cells during viral attack offers a lead for treatments meant to preserve nerve function rather than only calm inflammation.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1240:
The Acting Secretary of State wrote to the Secretary of State on 19 July 1945. Grew's cables from Washington formed a near daily circuit with Byrnes at Potsdam. Each carried home news, pending business, and the capital's mood.

The circuit mattered because choices at the summit landed on desks in Washington within days. Taxes of detail, from names to dates, had to match on both ends. This message is one turn of that wheel. It shows the department's two chiefs keeping their shared work aligned while an ocean and a war's end lay between them.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1340:
Jefferson Caffery, the American ambassador in France, cabled the acting secretary of state on 21 July 1945. Caffery had taken up the Paris post after the city was freed in 1944. Foreign Relations of the United States, the official American diplomatic record, prints it in the second volume on the Potsdam Conference.

Paris watched the Potsdam talks from outside the room, since France had no seat at the summit. Caffery's cables told Washington how French leaders read the talks and what they feared or hoped from them. For readers, the message gives the view of a close ally. France had much at stake in choices about Germany, yet no vote in making them.
frus-1945-50-intel-d40:
James Lay, a young officer in McCormack's research and intelligence office, wrote to his chief on 2 November 1945. Lay would serve American intelligence for decades after this paper. Foreign Relations of the United States prints it in the later volume covering American intelligence between 1945 and 1950.

Staff memoranda from working officers show plans being drafted at the desk level, where phrases are chosen and charts drawn. Lay's paper belongs to the State Department's effort to design the central system it hoped to lead. Readers who know Lay's later career, at the heart of the National Security Council staff, will enjoy meeting him here at the start. The volume is full of such first appearances by men who ran the cold war's secret side.
frus-1945-50-intel-d140:
Minutes of the first meeting of the National Intelligence Authority are dated 5 February 1946. The board of secretaries created by the president's January directive here sits for the first time. It is printed in Foreign Relations of the United States, in the retrospective volume on American intelligence from 1945 to 1950.

A first meeting of a new governing body is a founding act. That holds even when the minutes run to routine: members present, officers named, first business taken up. The authority's birth had been argued over since August in the papers before this one. Readers have now crossed the volume's great divide, from contest to institution. Everything after these minutes, directives, disputes, and growth, happens inside the house that the January directive built and this meeting first occupied.
frus-1945-50-intel-d240:
A memorandum dated 27 September 1949 links two senior offices. The sender was the General Counsel (Houston) and the Legislative Liaison Officer of the Central Intelligence Agency (Pforzheimer). The reader was the Executive of the Central Intelligence Agency (Shannon). It is document 240 in the Foreign Relations of the United States volume on intelligence for 1945 to 1950. The Dulles Report had landed in January 1949, and Washington was arguing over which of its fixes the CIA should adopt.

Inside the government, memos were how business got done between meetings. One put the question and the facts in front of the reader at once. A reader can watch the system think on paper: a fact here, a doubt there, a choice asked for at the end. To read it in place is to watch the Cold War state being assembled at desk level.
frus-1945-50-intel-d340:
A memorandum dated 13 February 1948 links two senior offices. The sender was the Executive Secretary of the National Security Council (Souers). The reader was Allen W. Dulles, Mathias F. Correa, and William H. Jackson. It is document 340 in the Foreign Relations of the United States volume on intelligence for 1945 to 1950. Across Washington, the new security bodies were moving from setup work to the real business of the Cold War.

Memos like this one did the quiet work of the system. They carried facts, advice, and requests from one office to the desk that could act on them. The reply, if any came, would build on the points laid out here. To read it in place is to watch the Cold War state being assembled at desk level.
frus-1861-d40:
George Dallas, the outgoing American minister to Britain, wrote to Secretary of State William H. Seward on 22 March 1861. The dispatch is document 40 in the Foreign Relations volume for 1861.

Dallas, a former Vice President, held the London post until Adams could replace him. His March letters cover the tense gap between two governments in Washington. They show a veteran hand keeping the post warm while the Union came apart at home. Dallas had served Polk as Vice President, which lent his late reports a veteran's calm. A veteran's calm was a fair gift to a chief who had just taken his chair.
frus-1861-d140:
On 30 July 1861, William H. Seward wrote again to William Dayton in Paris. The letter is document 140 in the Foreign Relations volume for 1861.

Seward closed July with a second Paris letter in four days. The pace tells of a chief working to steady his posts after bad news. Dayton received from Washington not just orders, but a tone to copy in his talks. Tone, in such letters, was itself a form of news for the man who read it. Tone read as news is a skill this whole record rewards in its envoys.
frus-1861-d240:
16 June 1861 is stamped on a letter Seward got from James Shepherd Pike, the American minister to the Netherlands. The printed record keeps it as Document 240 in the President's message volume for 1861. The date falls in the opening months of the Civil War, when the Union fought to keep foreign powers from backing the South.

The text is the view from the post abroad: local mood, official talk, and the envoy's own judgment. Its worth grows in context, as one link in a chain of letters that kept the peace with Europe. The Foreign Relations series, kept by the State Department's Office of the Historian, preserves the full run.
frus-1862-d40:
Secretary of State William H. Seward sent a dispatch to Charles Francis Adams, the American minister in London on 1 April 1862.
