The printed record keeps it as Document 40 in the 1862 Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs volume. It belongs to the spring of 1862, a year into the war, when keeping Europe out of the war was a core task for Washington.

Outbound letters like this one told the envoy what line to take and what to report back. For students of the war, the value lies in the sequence: one dated step in a long exchange. The State Department's Office of the Historian keeps the series, called Foreign Relations of the United States.
frus-1862-d140:
Dated 12 September 1862, a report from Charles Francis Adams, the American minister in London went to Secretary of State William H. Seward. The printed record keeps it as Document 140 in the 1862 Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs volume. It belongs to the summer of 1862, the war's second year, when keeping Europe out of the war was a core task for Washington.

The text is the view from the post abroad: local mood, official talk, and the envoy's own judgment. For students of the war, the value lies in the sequence: one dated step in a long exchange. Foreign Relations of the United States, the official record series, is where the full exchange can be traced.
frus-1862-d240:
William Stuart sent Secretary of State William H. Seward a letter on 25 September 1862, printed as Document 240 in the 1862 Foreign Relations volume. Stuart was acting head of the British legation in Washington.

Stuart wrote three days after Lincoln announced the Emancipation Proclamation, which tied the war openly to slavery. British leaders now had to reckon with the politics of backing a slaveholding republic. The legation's correspondence in late September, this letter included, belongs to the moment when that new fact began to reshape British debate. Britain's first concern in Washington was the blockade and what it cost British trade.
frus-1862-d340:
William H. Seward, the Secretary of State, wrote to William L. Dayton in Paris on 3 October 1862, in a dispatch printed out of order as Document 340 of the 1862 Foreign Relations volume. The letter shares its date with Document 330.

Two Seward letters to Paris on one date, filed far apart, show how the volume's arrangement can split a single day's brief. Together they carried the Department's October line to Dayton: the Union would accept no foreign truce plan. Reuniting such pairs is basic work for any reader of this file. French mills wanted Southern cotton, and French yards watched the Union blockade with care.
frus-1862-d440:
On 23 October 1862 Secretary of State William H. Seward replied to Gabriel García Tassara, the Spanish minister in Washington. The note is Document 440 in the 1862 volume of Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs, the year's official record.

Autumn replies like this one show Seward's method with resident ministers: answer promptly, concede nothing vital, and keep the door open. Spain's questions with the United States in 1862 were practical ones, tangled with the war at sea and the French move in Mexico. The exchange with Tassara ran parallel to the Madrid file of Perry and Koerner. Together the two give the full shape of Spanish-American dealings. Those dealings filled the second year of the Civil War.
frus-1862-d540:
Roest van Limburg received this letter from Secretary of State William H. Seward on 20 August 1862. The note is Document 540 in the 1862 volume of Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs, the State Department's printed record for the year.

August 1862 was a month when Seward wrote to resident ministers with one eye on the battlefield. His other eye was on Europe's chancelleries. Intervention was being weighed in them. The Dutch minister's business was narrower and more legal: the treatment of neutral trade under the blockade. Seward answered in that narrower key, keeping the Dutch file correct while the great questions hung. The letter shows how much of a secretary's wartime day was spent on exact, limited answers to exact, limited questions.
frus-1862-d640:
On 12 July 1861 Townsend Harris sent a further dispatch from Japan to Secretary of State William H. Seward, two days after his previous letter. It is Document 640 in the 1862 volume of Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs.

Two letters in two days from Edo usually meant enclosures traveling separately. Or they meant a matter Harris wanted stated twice for safety. Any single ship's mail could be lost. The Japanese correspondence moved by infrequent vessels, and ministers wrote accordingly, in clusters. Harris's subject was the treaty relationship he had built since 1856 and the Japanese government's handling of it. The paired letter shows the mechanics of diplomacy at the greatest distance the Department attempted, where redundancy was prudence.
frus-1863p1-d40:
Judah P. Benjamin wrote this letter to Major General John B. Magruder on 17 October 1862. Benjamin ran the Confederate state office; Magruder was a Southern army commander, then bound for the command in Texas. The letter is document 40 in part one of the Foreign Relations volume for 1863.

Most of Benjamin's printed letters went to envoys abroad. This one went to a general at home, a sign of how the state office's work crossed into the war's running. The letter sits in the group of Confederate papers the Union chose to print. It shows Richmond's top men dealing with each other on paper, in the fall of 1862.
frus-1863p1-d140:
Secretary of State William H. Seward opened the new month with this letter to Charles Francis Adams on 2 April 1863. Adams was the American minister in London. The letter is document 140 in part one of the Foreign Relations volume for 1863.

April brought the ship question in Britain toward its test. A Southern-built raider's fate was in the courts' and the cabinet's hands that spring. Seward's letters armed Adams for the push. This one opens the April file from Washington's side. It shows the brief carried into a new month with no slack: claims pressed, tone held, and an envoy kept fully stocked.
frus-1863p1-d240:
On 16 July 1863, Charles Francis Adams, the American minister in London, sent this dispatch from London to Secretary of State William H. Seward. It stands as document 240 in the Foreign Relations volume for 1863. The text is preserved in the 1863 Foreign Relations volume, which gathered the year's diplomatic mail for Congress and the public. It was one of 3 letters between the same men dated that day.

Mail crossed the Atlantic by steamship, taking roughly ten days or more each way. News in a dispatch like this one was already old when Seward read it, yet it guided his next orders. Set in its place in the volume, it helps readers trace how two governments talked their way past repeated crises.
frus-1863p1-d340:
The British minister in Washington, Lord Lyons, took up his pen on 19 December 1862 to write Secretary of State William H. Seward. His note is document 340 in the 1863 Foreign Relations volume. The document comes from the Foreign Relations of the United States, the government's own published record of Civil War diplomacy.

The channel between Lyons and Seward was the main safety valve of Anglo-American relations in the war. Papers like this one are the valve at work. Kept with the rest of the 1863 papers, it forms part of the fullest record of how the Union handled its most dangerous foreign relationship.
frus-1863p1-d440:
One entry in the 1863 papers is a 2 April 1863 letter from Lord Lyons to William H. Seward. Lyons was Britain's minister in Washington, and Seward was the American Secretary of State. The letter sits in the published record of how the Lincoln government handled foreign affairs in the spring of 1863. At the time, the Union government was fighting the Confederacy at home and working to keep foreign powers neutral.

The formal tone can hide the tension, but the pace gives it away. Notes this frequent mean both capitals were watching each other closely. British subjects caught up in the war filled many pages: men arrested, goods seized, and claims for losses that London took up with Washington. The volume's editors printed it without comment; its meaning comes from the company it keeps in the file.
frus-1863p1-d540:
On 28 May 1863 a formal note passed from Lord Lyons, Britain's envoy in Washington to William H. Seward, Secretary of State. It appears in Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs, the State Department volume printed with the President's annual message for 1863. Britain had not taken sides in the American war, and holding that line was the daily work of this mail.

None of these letters worked alone. Read in sequence, they show two governments testing each other's limits while both, in the end, avoided a second war. Students of the war use this mail to see foreign policy as the men on the spot lived it, page by page. It is a small, dated piece of a very large record, and it earns its place by keeping that record complete.
frus-1863p1-d640:
The 16 October 1863 mail between Washington and London included a letter from Charles Francis Adams to William H. Seward. Adams was the American minister in London, and Seward was Secretary of State in Washington. The letter was later printed in the 1863 volume of Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs, issued with the President's annual message. Mail between London and Washington crossed the Atlantic by steamer, so each reply took weeks to complete the round trip.

British subjects caught up in the war filled many pages: men arrested, goods seized, and claims for losses that London took up with Washington. The formal tone can hide the tension, but the pace gives it away. Notes this frequent mean both capitals were watching each other closely. That is the use of such a page: not a famous text, but a firm rung in the ladder of the record.
plos-pbio-0020240:
Jan Karlseder, Kristina Hoke, Olga K. Mirzoeva, and their team studied chromosome ends in PLOS Biology in 2004. Telomeres are caps that protect chromosome tips. A protein called TRF2 sits on those caps and keeps them from being mistaken for broken DNA.

The team found TRF2 binds ATM, the kinase that sounds the alarm at true DNA breaks, and can hold that alarm back. That holding action is what lets healthy telomeres stay invisible to the damage response. If the cap fails, the alarm fires and the cell ages or dies. The paper clarifies a guard system whose faults are tied to aging and cancer.
plos-pbio-0020340:
David L. Reed, Vincent S. Smith, Shaless L. Hammond, and their team read human history from lice in PLOS Biology in 2004. Body lice live in clothing and feed on people. Their genes carry a record of their hosts' past, since lice pass from person to person by close contact.

The genetic data suggest body lice spread at a time that fits direct contact between modern and archaic humans. That is, our ancestors likely met Neandertal-like groups closely enough to share parasites. Clothing use also enters the story, since body lice need garments to live in. The study is a clever use of a humble bug as a witness to events no fossil can show directly.
plos-pone-0000140:
Stuart H. M. Butchart, H. Resit Akçakaya, Janice Chanson, and colleagues published this conservation paper in PLOS ONE in 2007. It proposes improvements to the Red List Index. The index is built from the IUCN Red List and tracks how extinction risk changes over time for whole groups of species.

Governments use the index to judge whether conservation is working. The authors address weaknesses in how the index is calculated and sampled. A more reliable index means policy makers can tell real progress from noise. Scarce conservation money can then go where the trend data says it counts.
plos-pone-0000240:
Shoshi Dorfberger, Esther Adi-Japha, and Avi Karni published this motor learning study in PLOS ONE in 2007. When people practice a movement, the memory of it becomes firm over hours, a process called consolidation, but new learning can interfere. The authors found reduced susceptibility to that interference in children before adolescence.

Young learners may hold onto a new motor skill more stubbornly than adults do. The authors compare consolidation in children and adults after training. The result bears on how physical skills, from handwriting to sports, are best taught at different ages, and on rehabilitation after injury.
plos-pone-0000340:
Bita Sehat, Sandra Andersson, Radu Vasilcanu, and colleagues published this cell signaling paper in PLOS ONE in 2007. The IGF-1 receptor receives growth signals and is a target in cancer research. The authors study the role of ubiquitination, the tagging of proteins for disposal, in how the receptor signals. They also trace how the receptor is then degraded, taken off the cell surface and destroyed.

How long a growth receptor stays active shapes how strongly a cell grows. The disposal tag is part of that timing system. The paper maps ubiquitin's role in the receptor's life cycle, knowledge needed for drugs that aim to shut this pathway down in tumors.
plos-pone-0000440:
Dimitar Dimitrov and colleagues built a brighter tool for watching voltage in living cells, reporting in PLOS ONE in 2007. Their enhanced fluorescent protein voltage sensor glows in response to changes in a cell's electrical state. Nerve and heart cells speak in voltage, so a fast, bright sensor lets researchers watch that speech directly.

The team engineered the protein and characterized how well it works. Genetic voltage sensors can be aimed at chosen cell types, something electrodes cannot easily do. Improving their brightness and speed opens the way to filming electrical activity across whole circuits, a long-standing goal in neuroscience and cardiology.
plos-pone-0000540:
Hiroyuki Yamamoto and colleagues studied antibodies that help keep HIV in check after infection, in a 2007 PLOS ONE paper. Most people's infections run unchecked, but some hold the virus down. Neutralizing antibodies, which block the virus head-on, are prime suspects in that control. The team weighed their role in post-infection control of the virus.

If antibodies made after infection can still rein the virus in, vaccine makers gain a real target. A vaccine could teach the body to make those same antibodies before it ever meets the virus. The study weighs how much of natural control these antibodies can explain, next to other arms of defense.
plos-pone-0000640:
Vinet Coetzee, Louise Barrett, Jaco M. Greeff and co-authors tested a popular idea about faces and genes in PLOS ONE in 2007. HLA genes help the immune system, and three hypotheses link them to health and to facial attractiveness. The proposed routes are avoiding inbreeding, gaining an edge from mixed gene copies, and selection that favors rare types.

Their title states a split result: common HLA alleles were associated with health, but not with facial attractiveness. That weakens the claim that good-looking faces advertise HLA quality. Evolutionary psychologists and geneticists get a careful check on a theory that is often repeated more strongly than the evidence allows.
plos-pone-0000740:
Andrew J. Spiers followed a bacterial mutant's fortunes on a flat world, writing in PLOS ONE in 2007. The Wrinkly Spreader is a bacterium whose altered form succeeds in still liquid cultures by colonizing the air-liquid interface, forming a mat at the surface. Bacterial adaptation often establishes new genotypes with significantly altered traits. Spiers moved the test to two-dimensional agar plates.

His themes are maladaptation, compensation, and ecological success. A trait that wins in liquid may cost its bearer on agar, and later changes may compensate. The microcosm is simple by design: one surface, one mutant, clear outcomes. Evolution experiments like this show adaptation's trade-offs in miniature.
plos-pone-0000840:
John S. Brownstein, Margarita Sordo, Isaac S. Kohane and colleagues asked whether routine health data could have caught a drug danger earlier. COX-2 selective inhibitors, painkillers sold as rofecoxib and celecoxib, are associated with myocardial infarction, heart attack. The team sought to determine whether population health monitoring would have revealed the drugs' effect on population-level patterns of heart attacks.

Their retrospective study used inpatients at two Boston hospitals, as the abstract reports. The playful title, The Tell-Tale Heart, covers a serious method: surveillance of ordinary records as an early warning system for drug safety. If monitoring can spot risk in real time, regulators need not wait for scandals.
plos-pone-0000940:
Godwin Ashiabi and Keri O'Neal modeled how poverty reaches children's health through hardship and parenting, in PLOS ONE in 2007. Low income alone does not tell the whole story of a child's health. Families also face material hardship, trouble paying for food, housing and care, and strain that shapes parenting.

The authors test a model with several paths running at once. They ask how much of poverty's effect travels through hardship and family factors. Answers like this decide where help does most good: raising income, easing hardship or supporting parents. The study treats child health as the end of a chain, not a single cause.
plos-pone-0001040:
Andrew Oxman, Signe Flottorp, Kari Havelserud and colleagues ran a televised, web based trial of valerian for insomnia, in PLOS ONE in 2007. The trial was part of a project to help the public use research in health decisions. Viewers could join the study and follow the process through television and the web.

Valerian is an herbal remedy widely taken for poor sleep. In a randomised trial, participants received valerian or a comparison under that public format. The design itself is the experiment's second subject: can open, broadcast trials recruit well and stay rigorous. Sleep remedies are a fair first case, since demand and doubt are both high.
plos-pone-0001240:
Eating less and dampening insulin signaling are two regimens that extend life in many organisms. Wendy Iser and Catherine Wolkow asked how the two interact in the worm C. elegans, in a 2007 PLOS ONE article. Genetic analysis had shown that dietary restriction and reduced insulin-like signaling work through distinct pathways in the worm.

The authors report that DAF-2, the worm's insulin-like receptor, modifies the effects of dietary restriction and nutrient stress on aging, stress resistance, and growth. Even distinct pathways talk to each other. Their results shape how combined interventions for aging might behave.
plos-pone-0001340:
To replicate, lentiviruses such as HIV must insert DNA copies of their genomes into host chromosomes. Heather Marshall and colleagues studied a host protein, PSIP1, also called LEDGF/p75, that guides that insertion, in a 2007 PLOS ONE article. Lentiviral integration is favored in active transcription units, which allows efficient viral gene expression after integration.

The authors examine the role of PSIP1/LEDGF/p75 in lentiviral infectivity and integration targeting. A host factor the virus depends on is a tempting drug target, because the virus cannot easily mutate its way around it. Their work clarifies how much of integration this factor controls.
plos-pone-0001440:
Danielle Kemmer and co-authors published a 2008 PLOS ONE paper on a score for how well a gene is known. Labs know a lot about some genes and near nothing about others. There was no plain scale for that gap. The team built a score that rates how deep the notes on each protein coding gene run.

Their score is drawn from text and data on what each gene does. It mirrors how people judge a gene as known or obscure. A scale like this can steer funds to the least known genes. It can also track how fast the gene map as a whole is being filled in.
plos-pone-0001540:
Der-Chih Yang and co-authors wrote a 2008 PLOS ONE study on how stem cells choose fat or bone. Stem cells from marrow can become fat cells, bone cells, and more. Fat and bone fates pull against each other, but the control was vague. The team tested a cell signal path that runs through a common messenger.

They show this path steers both fates and sets the mix of two bone signals. It works in part by curbing the hormone leptin. A single path that tips the fat bone balance has clear clinical pull. It may bear on bone loss and weight gain in aging.
plos-pone-0001640:
Emmanuel S. Onaivi and co-authors reviewed what is known about CB2 cannabinoid receptors in the brain in a 2008 PLOS ONE research article. These receptors respond to cannabis-like compounds. Addiction and major depression are the health problems in view; both are tied to stress and both often return after treatment.

Many labs had failed to find CB2 receptors in healthy brains, which made their role in mood and drug use an open dispute. Onaivi and his team pull together evidence from mouse work and human subjects on where these receptors occur and what they do. The full text weighs the detection methods and the case for CB2 as a drug target. If the receptors do act in the brain, blocking or boosting them could offer a new route to treat addiction and depression.
plos-pone-0001740:
Corinne Vacher, Dominique Piou, and Marie-Laure Desprez-Loustau analyzed a network of tree diseases in a 2008 PLOS ONE research article. Ecological networks often show compartments and nestedness, patterns whose causes are debated. The authors used a well-resolved network of host and pathogen interactions to find what shapes them. They drew on a long forest health survey from 1972 to 2005.

Their paper asks how past evolutionary history asymmetrically influences the antagonistic tree and fungus network. The full text gives the network maps and the tests of compartment structure. Knowing whether pathogens cluster by host family history helps foresters predict which trees a new disease can jump to. That is a pressing question as tree pathogens spread worldwide.
plos-pone-0001840:
Michael J. Proulx, Petra Stoerig, Eva Ludowig, and their co-authors tested a device that lets blind people 'see' through sound in a 2008 PLOS ONE research article. Sensory substitution devices translate inaccessible visual information into a format that intact senses can process. Here the translation is image-to-sound.

They tested localization of visual stimuli, LEDs and objects, using image-to-sound conversion in 13 blindfolded participants. The study separates effects of learning by doing from those of long-term sensory deprivation. The full text gives the accuracy results. Such devices could restore a measure of spatial awareness to blind users, and they test how flexibly the brain can remap one sense onto another.
plos-pone-0001940:
Zhaojie Li, Shicui Zhang, and Qinghui Liu reported a second job for a fish egg protein in a 2008 PLOS ONE study. The protein, vitellogenin, is best known as a building material for eggs and new life. It had also been tied to defense against infection in fish, but no one knew how it helped.

The team tested how the protein meets microbes in the lab, using binding tests and enzyme-linked assays. They report that it works as a broad pattern sensor that flags germs, and that it helps immune cells engulf them. A food protein that also fights germs blurs the line between growth and defense.
plos-pone-0002040:
Adinda Wellens and co-authors designed germ blockers from the shape of a bacterial grip protein, in a 2008 PLOS ONE study. Certain Escherichia coli strains cling to the wall of the human urinary tract with hair-like pili. At the tip sits FimH, a protein that grips mannose sugars on the surface, and a few clinging bacteria can then invade bladder cells.

The team used the crystal structure of FimH bound to a mannose chain to build anti-adhesives, molecules that jam the grip. Blocking attachment, rather than killing the germ, could treat urinary infections with less pressure for drug resistance.
plos-pone-0002140:
Jianhua Xing and Jing Chen revisited a classic piece of math in cell biology, in a 2008 PLOS ONE paper. In 1981, Goldbeter and Koshland showed how a simple cycle of protein changes can act like a sharp switch. A small rise in a signal molecule can flip the system from nearly off to nearly on, giving a steep, S-shaped response curve.

Xing and Chen studied that switch in its first-order region, where the response is more gentle. Asked how it behaves when the cell's inner parts move in a noisy, disordered way. Their math shows how cells can stay sensitive to signals even when conditions inside are messy and always shifting.
plos-pone-0002240:
Andrew Pask, Richard Behringer, and Marilyn Renfree brought a piece of an extinct genome back to life in mice, in a 2008 PLOS ONE paper. DNA from extinct species can tell scientists how genomes evolved and what made each species distinct. Reading the code alone, though, cannot show what a gene actually did in a living animal.

The team took a DNA control element from an extinct marsupial genome. Placed in mice, it drove gene activity in the developing limb. Their test resurrected the function of DNA that no living species carries. The approach turns museum DNA into working biology, not just sequence.
plos-pone-0002340:
Lesley Rogers and Giorgio Vallortigara showed that honeybees recall a learned smell first on one side, then the other, in a 2008 PLOS ONE paper. Bees, Apis mellifera, readily learn to link odors with sugar rewards. Recall is tested by the proboscis extension reflex: a bee that remembers sticks out its tongue at the trained odor.

The authors found that recall involves first the right antenna and then the left. Memory of the same odor shifts sides over time after learning. That lateral handover mirrors side specialization seen in vertebrate brains, and it suggests bees store the memory in stages, with each antenna taking its turn.
plos-pone-0002440:
Led by Kuehl, a team of researchers published its study in PLOS ONE in 2008. The author list runs from Hjalmar S. Kuehl, Caroline Elzner, Yasmin Moebius, and others. Its subject is the Price of Play: Self-Organized Infant Mortality Cycles in Chimpanzees. Chimpanzees have been used extensively as a model system for laboratory research on infectious diseases.

Ironically, we know next to nothing about disease dynamics in wild chimpanzee populations. Each part of the study builds on the part before it, in the order the team carried it out. Readers finish with a clear sense of the problem, the approach, and why the question was worth the team's time.
plos-pone-0002540:
Research by Leppänen and co-authors came out in PLOS ONE in 2008. The author list runs from Olli V. Leppänen, Harri Sievänen, Jarkko Jokihaara, and others. Its subject is pathogenesis of Age-Related Osteoporosis: Impaired Mechano-Responsiveness of Bone Is Not the Culprit. According to prevailing understanding, skeletal mechano-responsiveness declines with age.

What the team did, and why they did it that way, forms the core of the piece. It stands as one careful step in a longer line of work, with its question and approach laid out in full. PLOS ONE is an open journal, and the full text can be read free by anyone who wants to check the work.
plos-pone-0002640:
Work by Alison Maresh and colleagues appeared in PLOS ONE in 2008. Their subject was principles of glomerular organization in the human olfactory bulb – implications for odor processing. The full author list in the catalog record begins with Alison Maresh, and the article appeared in the open journal PLOS ONE.

The opening of the abstract sets out the basis for the work. Olfactory sensory neurons (OSN) in mice express only 1 of a possible 1. Anyone studying the topic can use the article to see how the authors framed the problem at the time of publication.
plos-pone-0002740:
Work by Rebecca Banerjee and colleagues appeared in PLOS ONE in 2008, dealing with adaptive immune neuroprotection in G93A-SOD1 amyotrophic lateral sclerosis mice. The catalog record names Rebecca Banerjee first among the authors, and the source is the open journal PLOS ONE.

The opening of the abstract sets out the basis for the work. Innate neuroimmune dysfunction is a pathobiological feature of amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS). The authors add a further point. However, links, if any, between disease and adaptive immunity are poorly understood. For readers, the value lies in how plainly the abstract sets out the problem and what the authors set out to test or describe.
plos-pone-0002840:
Work by Katherine G. Akers and colleagues appeared in PLOS ONE in 2008. Their subject was social competitiveness and plasticity of neuroendocrine function in old age: influence of neonatal novelty exposure and maternal care reliability. Authorship is credited in the record to Katherine G. Akers and co-authors, with PLOS ONE as the journal of publication.

The opening of the abstract sets out the basis for the work. Early experience is known to have a profound impact on brain and behavioral function later in life. The authors add a further point. Relatively few studies, however, have examined whether the effects of early experience remain detectable in the aging animal. Its abstract frames the work for later readers, who can judge the full text against the aims stated at the start.
plos-pone-0002940:
Gregory Mullen, Ruth Ellis, Kazutoyo Miura and co-authors ran a first human trial of a malaria vaccine mix in 2008. The vaccine targets AMA1, a surface protein of the malaria parasite's blood stage, and pairs it with the adjuvant CPG 7909 to boost response. AMA1 was a leading blood-stage candidate.

This phase 1 trial in PLOS ONE tested safety and immune response for the AMA1 vaccine on Alhydrogel plus the new adjuvant. Phase 1 is the earliest human stage, focused on safety. Malaria vaccine research needs such careful steps, since blood-stage infection is what makes people ill.
plos-pone-0003040:
Héctor Guidobaldi, María Teves, Diego Uñates and co-authors identified the sperm attractant from rabbit egg complexes in 2008. Mammalian sperm swim toward several female sources, including follicular fluid and the cumulus cells around the egg. Several substances had been confirmed as attractants, and progesterone was a candidate.

Progesterone from the cumulus cells is the chemoattractant secreted by the rabbit oocyte cumulus complex, the title reports. Published in PLOS ONE, pinning the signal to one hormone from one source clarifies the final guidance step in fertilization. It may inform fertility testing and treatment. Details of samples, measures, and analysis are set out in the full article text.
plos-pone-0003140: Mady Hornig and colleagues published a case-control study in PLOS ONE in 2008 on measles vaccine and autism. The title states the result in plain terms: no link was found between measles virus vaccine and autism with enteropathy, a gut condition, in the group studied. No abstract beyond the title was supplied, so no study details are added here.
plos-pone-0003240:
Zoe T. Richards, Madeleine J. H. van Oppen, Carden C. Wallace and colleagues test whether rare corals are hybrids in this 2008 PLOS ONE paper. Coral reefs worldwide face a variety of threats, and many coral species are increasingly endangered. It is often assumed that rare coral species face higher extinction risks because they have very small effective population sizes, with decreased genetic diversity as a predicted consequence.

The title reports that some rare Indo-Pacific coral species are probable hybrids. Readers learn that rarity can reflect origin, not just decline. If a rare coral is a hybrid, its conservation value and protection strategy need fresh thought.
plos-pone-0003340:
Yanlin Shi, Qilong Xu, Sunita V. Seemanaplli and colleagues study Lyme disease proteins in this 2008 PLOS ONE paper. As an extracellular bacterium, the Lyme disease spirochete Borrelia burgdorferi resides in the extracellular matrix and connective tissues. It also sits between host cells during infection of mammals. Decorin and glycosaminoglycans are found in plenty in those places. Its ties to those materials are thus central.

The authors assess common and unique contributions of decorin-binding proteins A and B to overall virulence of Borrelia burgdorferi. Readers learn how two similar binding proteins divide work in infection. Adhesion proteins are targets because blocking attachment can prevent disease without killing bacteria directly.
plos-pone-0007440:
Andreas Keller and colleagues published a study in PLOS ONE in 2009. Their subject was blood markers for multiple sclerosis, a chronic disease that harms the coating around nerve fibers. MS varies greatly between patients, which makes diagnosis and tracking hard. The team turned to microRNAs, tiny molecules that regulate gene activity and circulate in blood.

Their patterns separated patients from healthy people for relapsing-remitting MS, the most common form. Patient profiles differed from healthy controls accurately enough to classify them. A blood test built on such a signature could support earlier and simpler diagnosis. It might also help follow how the disease changes over time. The study makes a case for microRNA profiling as a practical clinical tool.
plos-pone-0007540:
Christophe Noll and colleagues published a study in PLOS ONE in 2009 on a gene linked to Down syndrome and its effect on metabolism. High homocysteine in the blood raises the risk of clogged arteries. People with Down syndrome, oddly, seem protected from atherosclerosis. The gene DYRK1A sits in the Down syndrome region and is overproduced there. The team tested its role in mouse models carrying extra copies of it.

DYRK1A emerged as a determinant of the methionine-homocysteine cycle. That cycle controls the very metabolite tied to artery risk. A gene that tunes the cycle could explain the Down syndrome protection. The finding links a chromosome-21 kinase to a classic cardiovascular pathway. It also suggests the cycle could be adjusted by targeting the enzyme. The study connects two distant literatures: Down syndrome biology and heart disease.
plos-pone-0007640:
Cinzia Pagliuca and colleagues published a study in PLOS ONE in 2009 on the machinery that pulls chromosomes apart. Kinetochores are the handles where spindle fibers grip chromosomes during division. Budding yeast has the simplest known kinetochores, yet they still contain dozens of subunits. The team studied a conserved complex of two proteins, Spc105p and Kre28p. They tested its roles in gripping microtubules and in running the spindle assembly checkpoint.

The complex proved important for both jobs. It helps bind the kinetochore to microtubules, and it supports the checkpoint that halts division until every chromosome is attached. One complex doing both gripping and guarding is an efficient design. Failure of either job scrambles the genome of daughter cells. The study details a critical joint in the division machinery. Yeast, once again, explains a machine all cells share.
plos-pone-0007740:
Jean-Paul Pirnay and co-authors published a study in PLOS ONE in 2009. It takes a fresh look at how the strains of Pseudomonas aeruginosa are grouped in nature. The germ causes many infections in hospitals. Its strains from sick patients look much like strains found in soil and water.

That sameness led experts to call the pattern epidemic. Strains did not seem to stick to one home or one kind of illness. The authors checked the facts behind that view. Some key points were still unsettled. Their check matters for hospitals, since it shapes how staff trace where a new infection came from.
plos-pone-0007840:
Yuta Abe and co-authors published a study in PLOS ONE in 2009. It explains how a donor blood transfusion can protect rat liver transplants. Giving donor blood before a transplant can yield long-term graft survival. Remarkably, this can happen without immunosuppressive drugs.

The mechanism behind that tolerance was not well defined. The authors show the transfusion induces regulatory T cells that express Foxp3. Those cells calm attacks on the graft. Their induction is required for tolerance to the liver allografts. Harnessing such cells could one day free transplant patients from lifelong immune suppression.
plos-pone-0007940:
Kevin Hall and colleagues measured how much food the United States throws away, in PLOS ONE in 2009. They worked from the gap between the food the nation supplies and the food people truly eat. Thrown food wastes water and fuel, and as it rots it gives off gases that warm the climate.

Their count showed waste had grown over the years, not shrunk. The lost food held a large store of energy that farms and trucks had spent real resources to make. Putting a firm number on that loss gives policy makers and shoppers a clear reason to cut waste at every step.
plos-pone-0008040:
Ming Wu and colleagues modeled liver cell signals as steps in a logic circuit for PLOS ONE in 2009. Two signal chains, one answering insulin and one raising alarms, cross inside liver cells. Systems biology wants to know how such networks move over time, not just how they are wired.

Their discrete model treats each part as on or off and steps the whole net forward in ticks. That spare style skips heavy math yet still shows which states the net settles into. The approach suits labs that need quick, clear forecasts of cell behavior.
plos-pone-0008140:
Dong Xu and Yang Zhang sped up the drawing of protein surfaces in PLOS ONE in 2009. A protein's outer surface is where drugs and partners meet it, so drug design starts with an accurate surface map. Drawing that map as a mesh of small triangles is slow for large proteins.

Their method borrows a math trick, the Euclidean distance transform, to place the mesh far faster without losing detail. Speed here is not a luxury: screening millions of drug candidates means drawing millions of surfaces. A faster mesh means wider, cheaper screens.
plos-pone-0008240:
Armand Paauw and colleagues studied a bacterial iron scavenger in a PLOS ONE paper from 2009. Some gut bacteria carry a DNA island that makes yersiniabactin. This molecule grabs iron, which bacteria need to grow. Bacteria with the island tend to be more virulent. Better iron scavenging alone might explain that edge. The team tested another effect on immune cells.

Yersiniabactin reduced the oxidative stress response of innate immune cells. That response is a burst of reactive chemicals used to kill bacteria. Blunting it would help bacteria survive attack. The study reveals a second way this molecule aids infection.
plos-pone-0008340:
Christopher A. Hamm and colleagues treated rat tumor cells with a drug in a PLOS ONE paper from 2009. Abnormal DNA methylation patterns appear in several human cancers. Local methylation can silence genes, while genome-wide loss has murkier effects. The team examined what global demethylation does to tumor growth. They used rat chondrosarcoma cells, a cartilage tumor model.

Treatment with a demethylating drug removed methylation across the genome. Afterward, the cells showed increased tumorigenicity. Losing methylation thus made these cancer cells more dangerous, not less. The result warns that methylation therapies can cut both ways.
plos-pone-0008440:
Birajalaxmi Das and co-authors look at telomeres and radiation in a 2009 PLOS ONE paper. Telomeres are caps at the ends of chromosomes. Their length is used as a sign of aging and stress. Short telomeres have been tied to cancer and long-term disease. Lab work showed radiation can shorten them. But data from people living with high natural radiation were lacking.

The team measure telomere length in adults from such an area. They compare lengths with radiation exposure in daily life. The study tests if low, steady radiation leaves a mark on cells. It adds human data where only lab data existed before.
plos-pone-0008540:
Gustavo Palacios and co-authors link a second infection to severe flu in a 2009 PLOS ONE paper. Early reports on the new H1N1 flu strain put the death rate as low. It seemed much like seasonal flu. But Argentina reported a far higher death rate in July 2009. Many cases there ended in death. The team search for what made those cases so severe. They test patients for a common lung germ, Streptococcus pneumoniae.

They find cases with both flu and that germ are more severe. Patients with the pair fare worse than those with flu alone. Germ partners also drove deaths in past flu pandemics. The work argues for testing and treating bacterial infection in severe flu.
plos-pone-0008640:
Yi-Feng Chen and co-authors study hormone receptors in a plant in a 2010 PLOS ONE paper. Ethylene is a gaseous plant hormone that ripens fruit and ages leaves. Arabidopsis thaliana perceives it with a five-member receptor family. Members are ETR1, ERS1, ETR2, ERS2, and EIN4. Gel-filtration analysis of receptors solubilized from membranes shows their sizes. The team ask if receptors exist as components of larger protein complexes.

They find ethylene receptors function within high-molecular-mass complexes. Receptors cluster with partner proteins rather than acting alone. That organization may amplify or tune the ethylene signal. It changes models of how plants sense this simple gas.
plos-pone-0008740:
Jennifer Giel, Joseph Sorg, Abraham Sonenshein, and colleagues traced what wakes a dangerous gut germ. Their study appeared in PLOS ONE in 2010. Clostridium difficile survives antibiotics as a tough spore. To cause diarrhea, the spore must sprout into active cells. Bile salts in the gut were suspected as the wake-up cue. Few details of that cue were known.

Mice handle bile salts in their own way, and germination followed that chemistry. Changing how mice process bile changed spore sprouting. The link suggests blocking the wake-up signal could prevent disease. Prevention would spare patients the antibiotics that treat active infections.
plos-pone-0008840:
Tae-Young Ha, Keun-A Chang, Jeong a Kim, and colleagues calmed an inflammation gene and eased Alzheimer-like disease in mice. Their study appeared in PLOS ONE in 2010. Alzheimer brains show inflammation, sticky deposits, and neuron loss together. Gene scans in a mouse model hunted for drivers of that damage. One gene, S100a9, stood out as a regulator candidate. The Tg2576 mouse line models human Alzheimer changes.

Knocking down S100a9 reduced memory problems in the mice. Brain pathology also eased alongside the behavior gain. An inflammation gene thus looks like a real disease lever. Silencing it, or its pathway, becomes a therapy idea.
plos-pone-0008940:
Stephen Bishop and John Woolliams wrote a methods paper for PLOS ONE in 2010 on reading genetics from farm disease records. Breeders want animals that resist disease, and field records hold huge numbers of cases. But farm data are messy: exposure to germs varies, and not every sick animal is recorded alike. Drawing genetic lessons from such records takes care.

The authors set out the ideas needed to interpret these data soundly. They explain how infection spreads through a herd can distort simple comparisons between animals. Proper models separate an animal's own resistance from the pressure of germs around it. The guidance helps breeding programmes select stock that truly resists disease.
plos-pone-0009040:
Kelli Ryckman and co-authors hunted gene variants behind early births in Norway, in PLOS ONE in 2010. Spontaneous preterm birth is a leading cause of newborn illness and death. Both the mother's genes and the baby's genes may share the blame. The team focused on two candidate genes, PTGER3 and PON1.

They tested variants in mothers and in their babies in a Norwegian population. Some variants lined up with preterm birth often enough to notice. The study also gauged how strong those links were, checking an earlier report. Gene findings like these could one day flag pregnancies needing extra care.
plos-pone-0009140:
Jennifer Davis and Joseph Metzger combined two heart-muscle mutations in single rodent cells, in PLOS ONE in 2010. Inherited cardiomyopathies weaken or thicken the heart muscle. Patients increasingly turn out to carry two faulty copies at once. Symptoms range from none to life-threatening, defying simple prediction.

The team put double mutant alleles into rodent heart cells. Their combined effect on the muscle filaments could be measured directly. Pairs of faults disrupted contraction in ways single faults did not predict. A cellular model like this helps forecast severity for real patients.
plos-pone-0009240:
Raj Kumar Pan, Nivedita Chatterjee, and Sitabhra Sinha published this worm brain study in PLOS ONE in 2010. The roundworm Caenorhabditis elegans has a tiny, fully mapped nervous system. Even so, how single neurons add up to behavior remains a deep puzzle. The authors looked between the cell level and the whole animal.

They studied the middle, or mesoscopic, scale: groups of neurons and how they cluster. That level of organization reveals limits on what the network can do. Community structure in the wiring constrains the signals the worm can produce. The analysis shows how much of an animal's behavior is written into its wiring plan.
plos-pone-0009340:
Thomas Montine and co-authors published this heart risk study in PLOS ONE in 2010. Pain drugs called NSAIDs had come under suspicion for causing heart attacks and strokes. The data came partly from ADAPT, a trial testing anti-inflammatory drugs to prevent Alzheimer's disease. The authors looked for a warning signal in urine chemistry.

They measured breakdown products of thromboxane and prostacyclin, two signals that balance blood clotting. A high ratio between them was linked to later bad cardiovascular events. Such a urine marker could flag risky patients before harm occurs. It also hints at how these pain drugs upset the clotting balance.
plos-pone-0011440:
James Bjork and co-authors used brain scans in 2010 to compare how teenagers and adults respond to rewards. Teenagers chase rewards harder and take more risks than adults, a pattern every parent recognizes. The team asked adults and adolescents to perform reward tasks inside an fMRI scanner, which tracks activity across brain regions in real time.

The scans showed age differences in how strongly motivational circuits were recruited when rewards were on offer. Teen brains and adult brains did not simply differ in strength; they engaged the network in different patterns. Mapping that neural gap gives parents, teachers, and policymakers a brain-based account of impulsive years. It also cautions that reward-based programs for teens, from grades to marketing, land on circuitry that is wired to answer loudly.
plos-pone-0011540:
Andrea Eberle and co-authors described in 2010 how yeast cells quarantine faulty gene messages and quiet the genes that made them. Cells splice their RNA messages to remove spacer sections, and mutations at splice sites leave messages unspliced and useless. The team found that such defective RNAs are held back in the nucleus by a surveillance protein called Rrp6.

Beyond holding the bad messages, the cell also turned down transcription of the splicing-defective genes themselves, as if closing a faulty production line rather than just binning its output. That two-layer quality control, retain the message and quiet the gene, keeps errors from wasting the cell's resources or making harmful protein. The circuit is a tidy model of how cells proofread at scale. Its counterparts in human cells matter for diseases where splicing goes wrong, including many cancers.
plos-pone-0011640:
Jesse Deere and co-authors measured how fast virus levels fall once treatment starts, in PLOS ONE in 2010. People with HIV must stay on combination therapy for life because the drugs suppress the virus without clearing it fully. How the virus persists during therapy remains a central question in AIDS research.

Working in rhesus macaques, the closest animal model of AIDS, the team charted viral decay after starting strong therapy. The speed of that decay reveals how long infected cells survive. Those numbers guide strategies that aim beyond suppression toward shrinking the hidden reservoirs that keep infection alive.
plos-pone-0011740:
Christopher Dibble and co-authors mapped the working part of a disease-linked protein, in PLOS ONE in 2010. Cerebral cavernous malformations are abnormal clusters of brain blood vessels that leak and can cause haemorrhagic stroke. One of the three genes involved produces a protein called PDCD10, which binds a specific membrane lipid.

The team defined PDCD10's functional domain by studying its interaction with that lipid, PIP3. Pinpointing which part of the protein does the binding gives a foothold for understanding its role in vessel stability. It also suggests where disease mutations may break its function.
plos-pone-0011840:
Sébastien Rodrigue and colleagues presented in 2010 a pipeline meant to open up metagenomics, the study of DNA taken from whole microbe communities at once. Sequencers at the time forced a trade-off: cheap machines gave huge numbers of very short reads, while longer reads cost far more. Short pieces are hard to assemble when thousands of species are mixed together.

Their combined lab and computer method was designed to make those short reads usable for community samples from places like soil, water, and the gut. If short reads can be trusted, far more labs can afford to survey mixed microbes instead of single grown cultures. That widens the study of the vast share of microbes that never grow alone in a dish.
plos-pone-0011940:
Antoine de Morrée and colleagues described in 2010 a fast-acting protein switch at the center of muscle remodeling. The switch is calpain 3, a protein-cutting enzyme that is unusual among its family: when its gene is faulty, people develop limb girdle muscular dystrophy. The enzyme is unstable, which had kept its targets and mechanism obscure.

The team's work shows calpain 3 acting as a rapid, one-way proteolytic switch, cutting targets in a burst that cannot easily be undone. A switch design explains how muscle can remodel quickly during growth and repair. It also clarifies what is lost when the switch is broken by disease mutations.
plos-pone-0012040:
Marion Cornelissen and co-workers reported in 2010 a careful search that found none of a much-debated virus in the semen of men with HIV. The virus, short-named XMRV, had just been found as a kin of mouse leukemia viruses, and no one knew how common it was or how it spread. Its traces in the prostate gland had raised the thought that it might pass from man to woman in sex.

Men with HIV who lived in the Netherlands gave samples, and the team's tests found no sign of the virus in the fluid part of their semen. If the virus passed in sex, that is just where it should show up, so the blank result weakens the claim. With other blank searches, it helped deflate a scare that had drawn wide fear.
plos-pone-0012140:
Kathryn Swoboda, Charles Scott, Thomas Crawford, and colleagues reported a clinical trial in spinal muscular atrophy for PLOS ONE in 2010. This inherited disease weakens muscles by killing the nerve cells that drive them. Valproic acid, a drug long used for seizures, had shown promise for this disease in lab and animal work, and the trial added a supplement, L-carnitine, beside it.

Children and young patients joined in two groups: those who could sit but not walk, and those who could still walk. Half received the real treatment and half a dummy one, with neither side knowing which. Trials reported this carefully, part by part, give families and doctors trustworthy ground for judging a hoped-for therapy.
plos-pone-0012240:
Umberto Castiello, Bruno Giordano, Chiara Begliomini, and co-authors studied how touch sounds steer the reaching hand, in PLOS ONE in 2010. Research on hearing and vision usually asks how sound changes what people perceive, not how it changes what their hands do. The team recorded the small sounds fingers make on contact as volunteers reached to grasp objects, and fed those sounds back in altered form.

Hearing the contact sound changed how the grasp itself unfolded, even though the task was guided by sight. The hand, it turns out, listens as it reaches. That insight matters for prosthetic hands and surgical tools, where restoring sound feedback might restore some of touch's guidance too.
plos-pone-0012340:
Igor Itskovich and Brad Roudebush proposed resampling methods for mortality studies in PLOS ONE in 2010. Such studies compare deaths in one group with deaths in the wider public. A factory's workers are a common example. The gap is summed up in a single ratio. A range around that ratio decides if an excess looks real. The usual range rests on fixed rules of thumb. One rule is an arbitrary choice of confidence level. These rules can mislead when deaths are few.

Resampling builds the range from the data itself. It does not lean on those fixed rules. Health verdicts at work sites can hinge on such ranges. They can be worth large sums in pay-outs and rules. A more honest range protects both sides at once. Workers gain when real risks are not dismissed. Employers gain when false risks are not believed.
plos-pone-0012440:
Michael Bonsall modeled how fast parasite breeding inside a host shapes the evolution of virulence, in a 2010 PLOS ONE theory paper. A parasite's harm to its host is set by forces at two scales: growth within one body and spread across a population. Studies often treat the two scales apart, missing how they feed back on each other.

Bonsall's model links within-host replication to population spread, including varied hosts and parasites. Faster replication can push toward nastier disease, but population structure can brake that push. The framework helps explain why some parasites stay mild and others turn deadly, and it informs control programs that change transmission.
plos-pone-0012540:
Corinne Jud, Antoinette Hayoz and Urs Albrecht tested body clock resetting in mutant mice, in a 2010 PLOS ONE paper. Circadian clocks let organisms adjust to the daily light cycle, and two clock genes, Rev-Erb alpha and Per1, help set the rhythm's length and stability. Mice missing both genes offer a test of how the clock handles sudden light shifts, like jet lag.

The double mutants showed unusually strong phase resetting — their rhythms jumped by large amounts after light pulses. A clock that resets too easily is as flawed as a stubborn one. The work clarifies how the two genes steady the clock, with relevance to shift work and sleep disorders.
plos-pone-0012640:
Van Soolingen, Hernandez-Pando, Orozco and co-authors revived an old drug idea against drug-resistant tuberculosis. Some TB bacteria now resist the main drugs, and few replacements are close to ready. Their 2010 study tested thioridazine, a mental-health drug long known to kill TB bacteria in the lab.

In mice infected with resistant TB, the drug showed real promise as a treatment. Reusing an approved drug can reach patients far faster than building a new one. The work gives clinics in poor regions a possible extra weapon against a growing threat.
plos-pone-0012740:
Jamali, Salzmann, Perroud and co-authors tested a variant in an immune gene for links to epilepsy and childhood fever fits. Temporal lobe epilepsy is the most common form of partial epilepsy, and early febrile seizures often come before it. Their 2010 study read a working variant in the promoter of the complement C3 gene.

Complement is part of the immune system's first response, so a link would tie brain seizures to immune variation. Genetic clues of this kind may one day sort which children with fever fits need watching. The study adds patients sorted by seizure history.
plos-pone-0012840:
Yang, Ke, Tan and co-authors examined what happens to the plague bacterium when a key regulator is removed. In gut-infecting Yersinia relatives, the RovA regulator controls invasin, a protein for entering host tissue. In Yersinia pestis, the plague agent, invasin is already inactive.

Their 2010 study found that without RovA the cell membrane is damaged, while the type III secretion system, a needle for injecting host cells, is turned up. One regulator thus balances surface safety against attack machinery. That balance may shape how plague bacteria survive in fleas and mammals.
pmc-3021840:
Oostenveld, Fries, Maris, and co-authors describe FieldTrip, open-source software for analysing brain recordings. FieldTrip handles MEG, EEG, and invasive electrical recordings from the brain. It is built as a MATLAB toolbox with a complete set of consistent, user-friendly functions.

Inside, the toolbox covers the full path from raw signals to statistical results. Open code lets labs share analysis steps exactly, so findings can be checked and reused. FieldTrip became a standard environment in cognitive neuroscience, shaping how brain activity data are processed across many labs.  Shared pipelines also make multi-site brain studies far easier to compare directly.
pmc-4320440:
Moher, Shamseer, Clarke, and many colleagues issued the PRISMA-P statement in 2015. Systematic reviews should rest on a protocol that sets out the reason, the hypothesis, and the planned methods in advance. Few reviews at the time reported whether such a protocol even existed.

PRISMA-P lists what a review protocol should describe, item by item. Well described protocols make a review's methods easier to understand and judge. They also limit quiet changes of plan after results are seen. Journals and funders use the checklist to raise the quality of reviews that guide medical practice and policy.
pmc-5139140:
Ouzzani, Hammady, Fedorowicz, and their co-authors presented Rayyan in 2016, a web and mobile app for systematic reviews. A systematic review can summarize the effects found in many randomized trials and give numerical answers on whether a treatment works. Screening search results to find the right trials is slow work.

Rayyan was built to speed up that filtering step. Reviewers can screen titles and abstracts on the web or a phone, alone or as a team. No single earlier method met the priority needs of reviewers, the authors note. Faster screening frees time for the analysis and writing that give a review its value.
pmc-5866840:
Mohammad Saklayen reviewed the global epidemic of metabolic syndrome in 2018. The syndrome groups belly fat, insulin resistance, high blood pressure, and abnormal blood fats. Definitions vary a little between health bodies, but the pattern is the same.

The review traces how this cluster raises the risk of diabetes and heart disease. It links the worldwide rise to urban living, rich diets, and low activity. Rates now climb in poorer countries as well as rich ones. Readers get a clear picture of why doctors treat the cluster as one warning sign rather than separate small problems.
pmc-6602440:
Zefang Tang, Boxi Kang, Chenwei Li, and coauthors launched GEPIA2 in 2019. GEPIA is a web server for studying gene expression in tumors and normal tissue. It draws on the large TCGA cancer and GTEx normal data sets.

The new version adds finer tools, including analysis by cancer subtype and by gene signature. Users can compare survival between high and low expression groups with a few clicks. No programming is needed, which opened cancer data to many clinicians. GEPIA2 became a quick first check for whether a gene behaves oddly in cancer.
pmc-8387240:
Kathryn Tunyasuvunakool and colleagues at DeepMind reported in 2021 that they had predicted structures for nearly the whole human proteome, the full set of human proteins. A protein's shape reveals how it works and where a drug might grip it. After decades of effort, experiments had covered only part of the residues in human protein sequences.

Using the AlphaFold method, the team computed models for the great majority of human proteins and released them openly. The article describes the coverage achieved, how confidence in each model is reported, and the limits users should keep in mind. For medicine, an atlas of human protein shapes offers starting points for drug design and for understanding disease mutations.
plos-pone-0351640:
Dayron Leyva Rodriguez and Michelle Visser published this research article in PLOS ONE in 2026. It studies Treponema denticola, a bacterium involved in gum disease. The authors examine oncostatin M released by neutrophils, immune cells first on the scene, and its contribution to endothelial cell dysfunction, harm to the cells lining blood vessels.

Linking a gum bacterium to vessel lining damage connects oral infection with wider inflammation in the body. Neutrophil-derived signals during this interaction may be one bridge between the two. Periodontal researchers and scientists studying how mouth infections affect general health are the readers for this mechanism work.
plos-pone-0354740:
Viet Ngu Nguyen, Thi Minh Tam Le, Duc Hung Pham, and Huu Cuong Nguyen wrote this 2026 PLOS ONE research article on robot control. It presents a reinforcement learning method of the actor-critic kind, robust and aware of disturbances, for robotic manipulators with multiple degrees of freedom, arms that bend at several joints. Robust means the controller keeps working when conditions push against it.

Disturbance awareness means the learning system takes outside forces into account instead of being surprised by them. Factory and laboratory robots face loads and contacts that shift constantly, so control that expects disturbance is safer and steadier. Robotics engineers are the audience for an actor-critic method built this way.
plos-pone-0359940:
Jinlian Zhang and eight colleagues wrote this 2026 PLOS ONE research article on the chemical bisphenol A, a plastic ingredient people meet daily. It examines BPA's neurotoxicity in the pathogenesis of depression, how the chemical might help cause the illness, using three combined methods: molecular docking, dynamics simulations at the molecular level, and network toxicology.

These computer methods map which body systems BPA touches, how it binds to proteins, and how those bonds behave over time. Building a mechanism in silico is a first step before animal or human studies. Toxicologists and mental health researchers share the audience for a chemical-depression link explored this way.
plos-pone-0358840: Mohammed and four co-authors published a 2026 PLOS ONE study on two plants used in West African folk care. They tested leaf extracts from bitter leaf and from Senna siamea against harmful bacteria. The tests checked both germ killing and the power to break up biofilms, the slime layers that shield bacteria from drugs. Results of this kind guide the search for plant-based options as drug resistance grows.
plos-pone-0358540: Xiao and three co-authors published a 2026 PLOS ONE study comparing drugs for advanced breast cancer. All the cancers were HER2-positive and had spread. The team weighed one drug, T-DXd, against other HER2-targeted options used after first treatment failed. They used a Bayesian network method that pools many trials at once. Rankings like this help doctors choose when no single trial compares every option.
plos-pone-0358640: Bendaoued and seven co-authors published a 2026 PLOS ONE paper on an antenna shaped like a flower for future phone networks. The design carries four ports and works in two bands at the very high frequencies used by 5G millimeter-wave links. A feature called DGS, a pattern cut into the ground plane, is new in their design. Compact multi-port antennas are key parts for fast, crowded city networks.
plos-pone-0358740: Jiang and six co-authors published a 2026 PLOS ONE study on rehab after stroke. Patients practiced with restricted blood flow in the limb plus training guided by visual feedback. The team tracked lower limb function and blood levels of two growth factors, BDNF and VEGF. Combining methods that push both muscle and brain recovery is a live hope in stroke care.
plos-pone-0345340: Robinson and two co-authors published a 2026 PLOS ONE study on light, eyes, and color vision. LED light can dull how well people see color differences. The title reports that exposure to infrared light improved color vision that LED light had weakened. The result is surprising enough to draw wide notice, since infrared is invisible to the eye yet seems to restore what visible light disturbed.
gao-gaoreports-gao-08-40: GAO published its findings on social Security Disability: Better Planning, Management, and Evaluation Could Help Address Backlogs in 2007. GAO digs into federal programs at Congress's request and reports back what it learns. The library keeps it in the public record of federal watchdog work.
europmc-pmc7175140: Published in 2020, this research paper takes on tgf-β signaling (cell-to-cell messaging). The authors lay out their methods and results in full. Pinning down the inner workings gives drug makers a concrete target to aim at. The full text sits with this description in the library.
europmc-pmc7204940: A fresh look at coronavirus Disease-2019: knowledge, attitude, and practices of health care workers at makerere university teaching hospitals, uganda arrived with this 2020 research paper. Coronavirus disease-2019 is an new public health problem threatening the life of over 2-4 million people globally. Findings like these get picked up, tested, and built on by other teams.
europmc-pmc8656040: Published in 2021, this research paper takes on ketone bodies: from enemy to friend and guardian angel. The authors lay out their methods and results in full. Each solid result like this one becomes a stepping stone for the next round of research.
europmc-pmc7145640: A fresh look at IPD-IMGT/HLA database (large data store) arrived with this 2020 research paper. The IPD-IMGT/HLA database (large data store), http://www.ebi.ac.uk/ipd/imgt/hla/, currently contains over 25 000 allele (gene version) sequence for 45 genes, which. Findings like these get picked up, tested, and built on by other teams.
europmc-pmc8280040: Yoshiji and co-authors published this research paper in 2021 on evidence-based clinical (in patients) practice guidelines (official advice) for liver cirrhosis (liver scarring) 2020. The team describes what it did and what it found, step by step. Findings like these get picked up, tested, and built on by other teams.
europmc-pmc9007740: Pereira and co-authors published this research paper in 2022 on SLEAP: a deep learning (layered computer learning) system for multi-animal pose tracking. The team describes what it did and what it found, step by step. Findings like these get picked up, tested, and built on by other teams.
europmc-pmc9820240: Doctors and scientists took on discogenic low back pain: anatomy, pathophysiology and treatments of intervertebral disc degeneration in this 2022 research paper. The authors lay out their methods and results in full. If later work backs it up, the finding could open a new path for treating the illness.
europmc-pmc9664440: A fresh look at Muscle5: high-accuracy alignment ensembles enable unbiased measuring of sequence homology and phylogeny (evolutionary history) arrived with this 2022 research paper. Multiple sequence alignments are widely used to infer gradual-change relationships, enabling inferences of structure, function, and phylogeny (evolutionary history). Findings like these get picked up, tested, and built on by other teams.
europmc-pmc7658740: NCD and co-authors published this research paper in 2020 on height and body-mass index trajectories of school-aged children and adolescents from 1985 to 2019 in 200 countries and territories: a pooled analysis. The team describes what it did and what it found, step by step. Findings like these get picked up, tested, and built on by other teams.
europmc-pmc8387240: A fresh look at highly accurate protein structure forecasting for the human proteome arrived with this 2021 research paper. Protein structures can provide invaluable information, both for reasoning about biological (from living things) processes and for enabling treatments such. A sharper test or warning sign can change outcomes, since earlier care usually works better.
europmc-pmc7393740: Doctors and scientists took on "they look at us like junkies": influences of drug use stigma on the healthcare engagement of people who inject drugs in this 2020 research paper. The authors lay out their methods and results in full. If later work backs it up, the finding could open a new path for treating the illness.
europmc-pmc8143540: A fresh look at oxidative stress (cell damage from unstable oxygen) in cancer cell metabolism (how cells turn food into energy) arrived with this 2021 research paper. Reactive oxygen species are important in regulating normal of cells processes whereas deregulated ROS leads to the growth. Findings like these get picked up, tested, and built on by other teams.
europmc-pmc7072240: A fresh look at control of Nrf2 by mitochondrial (tied to the cell's energy plants) reactive oxygen species in physiology and pathology arrived with this 2020 research paper. Reactive oxygen species are byproducts of aerobic respiration and signaling (cell-to-cell messaging) molecules that control various of cells functions. Findings like these get picked up, tested, and built on by other teams.
europmc-pmc7794640: This 2021 review paper covers a rapid review of the impact of COVID-19 on the mental health of healthcare workers: implications (what the findings mean). Health and social care workers have carried a heavy burden during the COVID-19 crisis and, in the challenge to control. Having the evidence weighed in one place saves busy doctors from sifting through dozens of papers alone.
europmc-pmc7382540: Wafa and co-authors published this research paper in 2020 on the burden of stroke in Europe: thirty-year projections of incidence (new cases), prevalence (how common a condition is), deaths, and disability-adjusted life years. The team describes what it did and what it found, step by step. With firm counts in hand, planners can size the problem and track whether it grows or shrinks.
europmc-pmc8584040: This 2021 research paper covers mechanism (how it works) of antimicrobial (germ-killing) peptides (small proteins): germ-killing, anti-inflammatory (calming swelling) and antibiofilm activities. Antimicrobial (germ-killing) peptides (small proteins) are regarded as a new generation of antibiotics (bacteria-killing drugs). Pinning down the inner workings gives drug makers a concrete target to aim at.
europmc-pmc9085840: Published in 2022, this research paper takes on mitochondrial (tied to the cell's energy plants) autophagy (cell self-cleanup): mechanisms (the inner workings) and implications (what the findings mean). The authors lay out their methods and results in full. Pinning down the inner workings gives drug makers a concrete target to aim at.
europmc-pmc7511340: A fresh look at recent advances (new steps forward) in the growth of protein-protein interactions (how parts affect each other) modulators: mechanisms (the inner workings) arrived with this 2020 research paper. Protein-protein interactions (how parts affect each other) have pivotal roles in life processes. Once the chain of events is mapped, future treatments can be built to break it.
gao-gaoreports-gao-08-240: The Government Accountability Office dug into supply Chain Security: US Customs and Border Protection Has Enhanced Its Partnership with Import Trade Sectors, but Challenges Remain in Verifying Security Pr in this 2008 report. Its findings feed into Congress's hearings and new laws. Findings like these push agencies to fix the problems GAO reports.

europmc-pmc7228340: A fresh look at COVID-19: what we know? arrived with this 2020 research paper. In late December 2019, a cluster of unexplained pneumonia (lung infection) cases has been reported in wuhan, China. Findings like these get picked up, tested, and built on by other teams.
the-moravians-in-georgia-1735-1740: A scholarly history by Adelaide Fries of the Moravian settlers who came to colonial Georgia in the 1730s. the-playboy-of-the-western-world-a-comed: J. M. Synge's 1907 comedy about Christy Mahon, who wins an Irish village's admiration by claiming to have killed his father.
