the-tempest-pg1540: Prospero's island of magic fills this edition of Shakespeare's farewell play: a staged storm, a shipwrecked court, and a wronged duke weighing revenge against mercy. Ariel's songs and Caliban's curses sound around the great choice. The most beautiful goodbye in all the theater.
much-ado-about-nothing-pg2240: Beatrice and Benedick wage their merry war in this edition: "I will not send you." Tricked into love by their friends, the witty pair spar toward marriage while Claudio's jealousy nearly ruins Hero. The wittiest comedy in English, sparkling from first to last.
st-martin-s-summer-pg2640: Sabatini's tale of St. Martin's summer: an aging rake finds one last love in old France. Gallant and tender, it shows the swashbuckler's softer side. Romance with a rapier's grace, romance with a rapier's grace.
plos-pone-0341940:
Laurence Taggart leads a team of eight testing a mentoring scheme serving older people who have intellectual disabilities, in PLOS ONE in 2026. The question is whether the scheme is ready for a full trial. The MATILDA intervention matches each participant with a community group and mentors, aiming at participation, confidence, and less loneliness. The UK feasibility study randomized fifty-seven people, close to nine tenths of its recruitment target, and followed them for a year after the six month program.

Every intervention participant who started was matched to a group. Most were still attending at six months, and about two thirds remained at a year. Anxiety scores eased slightly in the intervention group. Judged against the study's progression criteria and a reach and adoption review, the procedures worked well enough to justify a definitive trial. The report is a model of testing the plumbing before promising the water.
plos-pone-0358940:
Qiu Zhu leads a team of eight reviewing a new way of studying symptoms in stomach cancer, in PLOS ONE in 2026. Instead of treating each symptom as a lone score, network analysis maps how symptoms reinforce one another. It reveals which sit at the center of a patient's suffering and which bridge between clusters. The review searched nine databases in English and Chinese and gathered studies applying the method to gastric cancer patients through early 2026.

Nine studies qualified. One symptom inventory, a Chinese version of the Anderson gastrointestinal module, dominated the field, appearing in seven. Across studies, nine core symptoms recurred, with fatigue named central most often, in five. Ten bridge symptoms were reported, but they varied between studies, unlike the steadier core list. The authors say the map is consistent enough to guide precision symptom care, while calling for standard methods so bridge findings can accumulate.
plos-pone-0358240:
Zhijie Zhou and colleagues published a 2026 methods paper in PLOS ONE on diagnosing machine faults when sensors sit at many different points on the equipment. A model trained at one monitoring point often fails at a new point, because the vibration data look different and labeled fault examples are scarce there. Their network, UCTL, learns from a labeled source point and adapts itself to an unlabeled target point without human tagging.

Inside, a reshaped transformer reads raw one-dimensional vibration signals directly and picks out patterns at several time scales. A new alignment method then pulls source and target data together, balancing average and spread differences so fault classes are less likely to mismatch. Across six transfer tasks on public bearing and gear datasets, the method averaged accuracy above ninety-nine percent. Starting from a pretrained model also cut training time, easing deployment across large monitoring systems.
plos-pone-0356240:
Takondwa Connis Bakuwa, Gillian Saloojee, and Wiedaad Slemming interview caregivers and physiotherapists who ran a home training program in rural Malawi. The program serves children with cerebral palsy. In the program, trained caregivers teach other caregivers, a model suited to places with few professionals. Their interviews, held after a seven-week trial run, were sorted with a standard framework for what helps or blocks new practices.

Daily routines helped: training folded into normal caregiving, parents stayed engaged, and a community group handled logistics. Peer teachers stood out, since expert caregivers taught in shared language and earned trust professionals could not match. Barriers also emerged in the accounts. Bakuwa and colleagues say any scale-up must fund the peer layer and protect caregiver time, not just print manuals.
plos-pone-0349740:
Meeyoung Kim and colleagues track how the brain's internal excitability shifts across Ramadan in healthy fasting adults. Daytime fasting for a month resets eating, sleep, and blood sugar rhythms, any of which could tune brain circuits. Volunteers received paired magnetic pulses to the brain's movement area before, during, and after Ramadan, while a small non-fasting group provided comparison points, alongside sleep, sugar, and thinking measures.

Excitability rose by mid-Ramadan and partly stayed up afterward, a broad shift across all pulse timings rather than a change in one circuit type. Blood sugar and sleep time both fell mid-month. Kim and colleagues read the pattern as a general retuning tied to the fasted state, useful baseline knowledge for brain stimulation research scheduled around fasting.
plos-pone-0357040:
Peisheng Yang and co-authors paired a deep learning flood model with Jiangxi Province's staged warning system. The work focused on the Xiangshui River Basin in China. Floods gather fast in this small mountainous catchment. Their 2026 study trained a bidirectional memory network on twenty past flood events. It tested the network on six held-back events, against three established approaches.

The new model forecast flood flows more accurately than all three rivals. It was strongest one hour ahead, though its skill faded by six hours out. Rainfall from upstream stations in the previous two hours mattered most. The authors map the model's output onto the province's six-three-one hour response stages. They use weather forecasts for the longer leads. That gives local officials a clearer chain from prediction to evacuation orders.
plos-pone-0342140:
Shristi Sharma and co-authors reviewed forty-four population studies to chart how the mental health of middle-aged and older adults moved through the COVID-19 pandemic. Their 2026 scoping review divides the timeline into the crisis phase through 2021 and the transition years after, recording which symptoms rose, which eased, and which personal factors mattered.

During the crisis phase, depression, anxiety, stress, and loneliness climbed broadly. By 2022 and 2023 some studies showed symptoms settling or improving. Women, the oldest adults, the unemployed, and people in poor physical health or isolation fared worst. The authors note almost no research tied mental health to population-level factors like local case rates, leaving a gap for planning the next emergency.
plos-pone-0355540:
Eugênio Simão, writing in 2026, tackles a gap in how scientists model living cells. In older models, small molecules are treated either as raw material for chemical work or as simple on-off switches. Real cells use the same molecules, such as ATP, for both jobs at once, and Simão builds a formal system that can handle that double role.

His method extends a classic modeling tool called Petri nets, adding special arcs that let a signal molecule be used up as it passes information upward through layers of control. He proves that signal flow cannot run in circles and that draining a lower layer blocks higher steps. Tested on spore formation in a common bacterium, the model explains why a slow build-up triggers far more spore formation than a sudden pulse.
plos-pone-0355940:
Eva Débora de Oliveira Andrade and seven colleagues review whether learning to cook actually improves adults' diets, in this 2026 systematic review. Cooking programs are often funded on the assumption that skills lead to healthier eating and better nutritional status. Searching five databases, the team gathered fifteen studies of healthy adults and graded their methods and the certainty of their findings.

Better cooking skills and cooking more often were linked with better diet quality, especially more fruit and vegetables and greater confidence in the kitchen. No evidence connected skill development to nutritional status measures like weight. The certainty behind the positive findings was low or very low, and most studies carried serious risks of bias. The authors say cooking education looks promising for eating habits but needs proper randomized trials before stronger claims can be made.
plos-pone-0356340:
Filipe Sousa and three colleagues issued this correction in 2026 to their study comparing a three-minute all-out running test with classical laboratory benchmarks for aerobic fitness. A data entry error had put one participant's maximal oxygen uptake value from a verification bout in the wrong place. That also distorted a figure's analysis and some error statistics in the results text. The notice supplies the corrected figure and data file.

After rerunning the analyses, the statistical picture shifted only slightly, and the authors state that the interpretation and conclusions are unchanged; an editorial board member reviewed the correction and agreed. A post-hoc power analysis, added after a reviewer raised the small sample size, indicated the key comparison was adequately powered. Readers should use the corrected values and figure when citing the study's test comparisons.
plos-pone-0355740:
Jonathan Williams Ramirez and seven colleagues release a free artificial intelligence tool that automatically outlines brain tissue in photographs of sliced postmortem brains, in this 2026 paper. Brain banks routinely photograph coronal slabs, and new methods can rebuild three-dimensional maps of disease from those photos, but someone first has to trace the tissue in every image by hand. Their model, built on a standard segmentation network, was trained on more than fourteen hundred hand-traced photographs from two sites, covering fresh and fixed tissue and varied diagnoses.

On unseen photographs the tool matched human tracings closely, with overlap and boundary errors approaching the agreement between human raters themselves. The authors have made the model and its training data public. They argue removing the tracing bottleneck should let far more laboratories adopt three-dimensional neuropathology and mine their existing photo archives.
plos-pone-0356140:
Shane Lewis and colleagues designed a wireless scheme to keep vehicle-to-vehicle messages reliable in crowded city streets. Their 2026 paper combines a reconfigurable intelligent surface, which can steer radio signals, with spatial modulation using dual-polarized antennas. Only one radio chain stays active at a time, which saves power and hardware.

Simulations using standard vehicle channel models tested signal strength, error rates, and energy use against a full multi-antenna setup. The new design used far less energy while keeping error rates close to the bigger system. Signal quality measures also improved, thanks to the surface shaping signals around blockages. The authors present it as a practical option for future connected vehicles.
plos-pone-0355840:
Elijah Sunday Okwuonu and colleagues screened cave bats near homes in southeastern Nigeria for blood parasites called trypanosomes. Caves hold large mixed bat colonies, and their parasite traffic near settlements is poorly known in West Africa. Their 2026 study tested blood and parasite samples from fifty-seven bats of ten species caught in nine caves and one house.

Parasite DNA appeared in well over a third of the bats, spanning six species in four families. Family trees placed the parasites in a group known from African bats, an early branch near the lineage that causes Chagas disease. Okwuonu and colleagues say peri-domestic roosts deserve monitoring, since bats, parasites, and people meet closely there.
plos-pone-0354840:
Emiliano Serviole and colleagues use in 2026 chemical profiling of leaves to sort out tangled naming in alpine brambles, the group that includes raspberries and blackberries. These plants breed without normal sex and cross freely, creating many forms with blurry borders. Leaves from nine forms were sampled over two years along a mountain height gradient in the French Alps.

Profiles split the forms into three broad super groups, with the true raspberry standing apart. Dozens of compounds were named, some new to the group, and classes such as plant pigments and tannins marked each group. Chemical fingerprints could aid naming and matter for drug and cosmetic uses.
plos-pone-0352640:
Øivind Tøien and co-authors test in 2026 automatic scoring of sleep in American black bears, including during hibernation, when body temperature cycles up and down. Years of brain, eye, and muscle recordings from captive bears were far too many to score by hand. Two learning classifiers were trained in different ways and checked against careful hand scoring by three experts.

Both tools matched hand scores closely, with top scores in a high range, and training apart for hibernation worked best. Bears slept about twice as much in hibernation as in summer by both methods. Some files challenged both tools alike, pointing to hard cases rather than tool failure.
plos-pone-0350040:
Van Minh Nguyen and five colleagues published this 2026 systematic review of programs that help people living with HIV quit smoking. Smoking is common in this group and compounds their health risks, while most live in poorer countries. The reviewers gathered thirty-two intervention studies and combined results, also hunting for any study of costs.

Medicines and intensive, tailored counseling helped people quit, with early positive signs from poorer countries, where most trials are still missing. No cost-effectiveness studies turned up at all. Nguyen urges future programs in HIV clinics to build in economic evaluation from the start.
plos-pone-0353240:
Shanila and colleagues, in a 2026 experiment, find the salt level at which giant freshwater prawns grow best. Salt in the water shapes molting, growth, and stress in prawns, a valuable farmed species in Bangladesh and beyond. Young prawns were raised for eight weeks at five salt levels, from fresh water up to a third of seawater strength, each in triplicate tanks.

Growth, weight gain, feed use, and survival all peaked at the lowest added salt level, a mildly brackish mix. Math fitted to the results put the sweet spot for growth close to that level. Gene checks matched the picture: at that level, a hormone that blocks molting fell, a shell-building gene rose, stress genes quieted, and immune genes woke up. The authors conclude that a touch of salt, not none and not much, helps these prawns thrive, a cheap lever for farmers whose water they can adjust.
plos-pone-0354240:
Morantes and colleagues, in a 2026 laboratory study, test cocoa leftovers against chikungunya, a mosquito-borne virus that causes fever and lasting joint pain. The husks around cocoa pods and the shells around beans are farm waste. Yet cocoa is rich in compounds that fight both viruses and oxidative stress, the chemical damage the virus provokes in cells.

Extracts of both leftovers were added to infected human liver cells. The extracts barely harmed the cells themselves. Above a threshold dose, they cut the amount of viral genetic material and the number of live virus particles, most clearly half a day after infection. Harmful oxygen chemicals inside the cells also fell. The authors read the two actions as linked: calming oxidative stress may be part of how the extracts slow the virus. They recommend deeper work to pin down the active compounds before any remedy is claimed.
plos-pone-0354140:
Priyanka Renita D'Souza and Princia Rolita D'Souza present a protocol, published in PLOS ONE in 2026, for mapping research on a mother's drinking and her child's skin disease. Alcohol in pregnancy is best known for harming brain development, but it may also shape the developing immune system. Their planned review covers eczema of the atopic kind in children whose mothers drank before or during pregnancy.

Following standard scoping methods, two reviewers will screen five databases plus grey literature for original English-language studies. They will chart exposure timing, how eczema was diagnosed, and proposed biological pathways, then check their findings with practising clinicians. The aim is to show where evidence exists and where it is missing.
plos-pone-0353840:
Cesar Augusto Inoue and seven colleagues map what Brazil knows about viral hepatitis, in this 2026 PLOS ONE scoping review. The country aims to eliminate these liver infections by 2030, but progress is uneven. Searching seven databases, the team gathered two hundred studies covering more than fourteen million people, and charted rates for hepatitis types A through E across regions and social groups.

Hepatitis B drew the most research, then C. Exposure was highest among prisoners, immigrants, and transgender people, while hepatitis D clustered in the Amazon. The authors found most studies small and one-off, rarely connecting infection to social conditions. Their evidence map is meant to steer policy and better-designed research.
plos-pone-0344140:
Kazuto Suda and seven colleagues grow miniature gut tissue from children with Hirschsprung's disease to test a natural fat molecule, in this 2026 PLOS ONE study. In this birth condition a section of bowel lacks nerve cells and is removed by surgery, yet dangerous gut inflammation can still strike the remaining bowel. The team grew organoids from the healthy-segment tissue of patients and from comparison tissue, then exposed them to the molecule, called 12-HHT.

The patient organoids started with weaker barrier genes than the comparison tissue. The molecule strengthened those barrier proteins and blunted inflammatory signals triggered by an immune provocation, and less tracer dye leaked through the tissue wall. The findings point to a possible protective treatment worth pursuing.
plos-pone-0353740:
Burle and colleagues tested blue light treatment in mice infected with a common parasite in a 2026 study. The parasite can pass from a pregnant mother to her unborn young and cause serious harm. Blue light had been proposed to kill the parasite in tissues, but its effects on animal behavior were unknown.

Infected mice rested more and groomed less than healthy mice, with or without the light. Treated infected mice showed more odd behaviors, while healthy treated mice ate and drank more and moved more. Long light exposure seemed to act as a mild stressor. Light may lower parasite load, but dosing needs care to protect animal welfare.
plos-pone-0352440:
Filip Jevic and three colleagues check whether nerve damage from a chemotherapy drug is really the same on both sides of the body. Their 2026 study covers forty-seven children treated for acute lymphoblastic leukaemia. Vincristine, a backbone drug for this cancer, frequently injures peripheral nerves. Doctors usually assume the injury is symmetric. The team ran nerve conduction studies on both sides of each child and compared them carefully.

Motor nerve readings agreed only fairly to moderately between sides. Signals from the leg and arm nerves matched worst of all. Sensory timing, by contrast, was excellently symmetric. Whole-nerve verdicts for motor damage also differed side to side. A one-sided test, still common in clinics, can therefore misjudge a child's motor neuropathy. Testing both sides gives survivors fairer monitoring, and rehabilitation plans that fit the limb that actually struggles.
plos-pone-0352140:
Olufemi Akande, Adesike Olayinka, and Moses Adebayo field-test maize bred to withstand the fall armyworm. Their 2026 trials ran in Nigeria's derived savanna. The armyworm caterpillar devastates maize, worst in the minor cropping season. Twenty-six resistant hybrids grew alongside six commercial checks in a replicated lattice design. Yield, plant appearance, ear quality, diseases, and worm damage were all scored across the season.

The hybrids differed significantly on nearly every trait. Five experimental crosses stood out from the pack. They combined high grain yield with handsome plants and ears and low leaf damage from the worm. Superiority rankings held across the trial environments. Two further leaf diseases were scored as part of the screen. Before release, the winners must prove stable in wider agro-ecologies. If they hold up, Nigerian farmers gain seed that fights the pest genetically, cutting reliance on sprays they can barely afford.
plos-pone-0352340:
Yan-Shing Chang and three colleagues survey British mothers about the burdens of multiple births during COVID-19. Their 2026 cross-sectional study recruited women up to six months after delivery, in late 2021. Over eight hundred fifty mothers answered, fifty-three of them with twins or more. Social circumstances, obstetric history, pandemic experiences, and feeding support were all examined. This was the first British study to ask which factors travel with multiple births in the pandemic context.

Twins' familiar complications dominated the adjusted results. Multiple births were far likelier to involve formula feeding, preterm delivery, and caesarean birth. Socioeconomic and COVID-specific factors, by contrast, showed no association in simpler comparisons. Postnatal depression and feeding support patterns also differed for these mothers. Services planning for the next crisis should note the practical lesson. Mothers of multiples need feeding and mental health support designed for their situation, not postnatal care stretched thinner.
plos-pone-0351540:
Ali Ibrahim, Shaikha Alshehhi, and Nikolaos Tsingilis surveyed over a thousand teachers in the United Arab Emirates. They asked how much leadership in each school is shared beyond the principal. They also asked how attached teachers feel to their schools. Schools in all seven emirates took part, both public and private. Shared leadership is a favorite reform idea, and this study tested its link with teacher commitment.

Teachers said leadership was widely shared. Public schools reported slightly more sharing. Where sharing ran stronger, commitment ran stronger too. The link was strongest for emotional attachment and duty. It was weakest for staying only because leaving costs too much. Giving teachers a real voice seems to build teachers who want to stay.
plos-pone-0352240:
Seungwoo Han read three decades of South Korean newspapers to chart how the country's media feel about its two giant neighbors, the United States and China. Word-level analysis scored the emotional tone and intensity of coverage from nineteen ninety-two to twenty twenty-five. How a middle power's press warms or cools toward rival giants matters, since public feeling constrains what governments can do.

The two portraits diverged steadily. Coverage of the United States stayed fairly stable, mildly warm and low in emotional heat. Coverage of China grew more negative and more heated over the years. Han ties the durable gap to the American alliance, historical memory, and the media landscape itself. The long record warns against reading any single headline storm as the story: the emotional drift is slow, structural, and one-directional so far.
plos-pone-0351740:
K S Athira, Raju Attada, and Sulekha Komeravelli charted winter cold stress across north India over nearly forty years. They used a comfort index that blends temperature, wind, and sun into how cold a body feels. Cold waves kill people in India, yet they draw far less study than heat. The team mapped when stress starts each evening and how it deepens overnight.

January brought the worst stress. The far north, Jammu and Kashmir and Ladakh, suffered most. Cold waves stretched the stress across the whole region. Over the decades, hours of slight cold stress grew. Stronger stress eased into the slight band rather than new cold arriving. Winters are softening on average, but the maps still tell relief teams which nights turn dangerous, and where.
plos-pone-0351840:
Tzu-Fei Wang and colleagues asked whether the language a dying patient speaks shapes the end of life. The study covered home care patients in Ontario, Canada, who died of cancer. Records held nearly thirty-four thousand people. Their preferred languages were English, French, or another tongue. The team tracked deaths in hospital, emergency visits, and heavy treatment in the last thirty days.

Patients who preferred another language died in hospital more often. They also had more emergency visits and more aggressive care near the end. French speakers died in hospital more often than English speakers too. The gaps held after other factors were weighed. Care that a patient cannot fully understand may default to the hospital, wanted or not.
plos-pone-0351940:
Tímea Popucza surveyed fifteen hundred six care and human service workers about emotional demands and burnout. The study rests on a well-known model of job demands and resources. It asks whether resources such as control, support, and meaning buffer the harm of demands. Two kinds of emotional demand were measured. One is the strain workers feel inside. The other comes from contact with clients.

Both demand types fed both sides of burnout: exhaustion and pulling away. The buffering effect did not appear. Resources linked to less burnout on their own. But meaning in work and social support made the demand-exhaustion link stronger, not weaker. Caring more can deepen the wound when the emotional load stays high. Managers should hear that before they prescribe more engagement as the cure.
plos-pone-0350140:
Feeling a buzz on one finger is easy; the brain must also combine buzzes across fingers. Shasha Wei and colleagues measured that combination with detection tests and brain recordings from the scalp, in this 2026 PLOS One study of touch.

Doubling the buzzing fingers improved detection only slightly, matching a model where each finger offers a separate chance to notice. Adding a distracting buzz to neighboring fingers made detection worse, showing fingers suppress each other. Brain signals summed when fingers shared a rhythm and shrank when rhythms differed. The weight of this suppression sits between what vision and hearing show, the authors report.
plos-pone-0351140:
Akiko Katayama and colleagues compared two ways that vessel lining cells grow old, and how each affects blood clotting. Cells can age by dividing until worn out, or by early stress damage. Ageing raises clot risk, yet the two paths may not act alike. Lab tests mixed aged cells with plasma and measured clot forming drive, backed by gene reading.

Worn out cells surprisingly lowered clot drive in dishes, while stress aged cells did not. In live mice, though, both natural ageing and stress aged vessel cells worsened vein clots, and their gene patterns looked alike. Dish results alone mislead here: stress driven ageing matches the aged body pattern best.
plos-pone-0350840:
Xiaoyuan Jin and colleagues present an ultra light detector for small targets in drone photos, where tiny objects drown in clutter and scale swings. Their design swaps heavy maths blocks for lean ghost style ones, adds a two path attention step that damps background noise, and focuses channel weights on faint small target cues.

On a public drone photo set, accuracy nudged above a strong compact rival while the model held under one million settings. That tiny size suits on board drone chips with strict power limits. Traffic counts, crowd checks, and small vehicle spotting from the air all need exactly this mix of lightness and sharp small target vision.
plos-pone-0350740:
InHo Lee and colleagues built a screening index in 2026 for judging whether workers are fit for confined space jobs. Such work risks low oxygen, toxic gases, and heavy strain, so fitness checks need structure rather than gut feel.

Health exam and function data from one hundred eleven workers were sorted into body, function, and lifestyle risk groups. A statistical method that shrinks weak factors set the index weights. The index sorted most workers as suitable, some as caution, and a few as unsuitable, closely matching independent specialist judgment in checks. A standard score could make fitness calls fairer across sites.
plos-pone-0350440:
Expression of Concern: the journal warns that this article may not be trustworthy. It deals with calcium signals in visceral leishmaniasis, a disease caused by a parasite. Until the doubts are resolved, its findings should be read as unverified.

Editors found a control image that looks like images in other papers. Those papers used the image for quite different tests. The stated methods also do not fit tests with more than two groups. Promised raw data were never supplied. The first author disputes the image point and says the files are gone. With no source data, the journal cannot check the results.
plos-pone-0349140:
Carol A Hitchon, Lisa M Lix, and co-authors followed Canadians with rheumatoid arthritis, inflammatory bowel disease, or primary depression and anxiety to see how mood symptoms move quality of life over time. Chronic physical disease and mental symptoms often travel together, but within-person change is rarely separated from differences between people. Their 2026 cohort study saw more than seven hundred participants yearly for three years, testing mood, fatigue, function, and quality of life.

When a person's own depression or anxiety worsened, their mental quality of life fell clearly. Rising fatigue and worsening thinking scores dragged physical quality of life down, while better physical function lifted it. Most participants saw meaningful swings in quality of life across the study. The authors argue that tracking mood changes inside each patient, not just comparing patients, reveals where support can help most.
plos-pone-0345540:
Weihong Zhao and Chunlu Hu tackled a core language problem: judging when two sentences mean the same thing, even when worded very differently. Word-counting methods fail when a short sentence is rephrased with new words. Their model uses twin neural networks that read both sentences, follow the order and context of words, and learn deep patterns of meaning.

Trained on sentence pairs, the model beat word-frequency methods and standard machine learning regressors, with lower errors and steadier results. The twin-network design also allows some explanation of why two sentences scored as similar. Search engines, automatic essay grading, summarizers, and question-answering tools all lean on this kind of similarity judgment, so a more accurate and explainable model has wide use.
plos-pone-0347040:
Natalia Heredia and colleagues evaluated a culinary medicine program for people living with type 2 diabetes who also carry excess weight, recruited from clinics in low-income neighborhoods. Over five weekly ninety-minute sessions, a dietitian taught basic cooking skills wrapped in practical nutrition education. Eighty-nine people enrolled, about two-thirds in the program and the rest in a comparison group.

Most program participants attended and finished the follow-up surveys. Compared with the comparison group, they showed significant gains in how they perceived their diet and related measures, and interviews after the program added texture on what changed at home. Teaching people to cook, rather than only telling them what to eat, is the program's wager, and the early results support testing it at larger scale.
plos-pone-0345040:
Shahrzad Jahangiri and Samira Sarikhani created a clear plastic composite that resists heat better, aimed at optical coatings and sensor windows. The base is a specialty acrylic blend, and the reinforcement is zirconium phosphate platelets treated with sulfur-bearing groups so they bond well and spread evenly at very low loadings. A battery of imaging and thermal tests characterized the material.

Even at one percent filler or less, the composite kept high visible transparency while its softening point rose and the temperature where breakdown begins climbed by roughly thirty degrees. Heat resistance and optical clarity usually trade against each other, because fillers cloud the plastic. Beating that trade-off without silicon-based ingredients opens options for protective layers and electronic packaging.
plos-pone-0349040:
Guanlin Zheng and colleagues traced how a protein that reads chemical tags on RNA helps heart muscle cells mature. Earlier work showed that losing this reader protein stalls heart development, but which of its target messages mattered was unknown. Working with rat heart precursor cells coaxed to mature with a vitamin A relative, the team fished out the messages the protein physically holds.

One message stood out, carrying instructions for an enzyme that edits DNA marks. Removing the reader lowered that enzyme's output without lowering its message, showing the reader boosts translation into protein. Adding the enzyme back partly rescued the stalled maturation. The team also found a previously unknown rat variant of the gene. The work names a concrete link between RNA tagging and the making of a working heart.
plos-pone-0347640:
Santiago Jijón and co-workers join two natural health compounds, curcumin from turmeric and pigments from colorful vegetables, into new combined molecules. Both parents fight cell damage from oxygen, and curcumin has other wide effects. Their 2026 chemistry study links the two in two ways, then measures how well each new molecule resists oxidation in alcohol and in salty water.

Most linked versions beat their parent pigments at fighting oxidation. Merged versions with two of curcumin's active ends looked best as drug candidates on paper. A catch appeared too: the fat-loving molecules clumped together in water, so test values there describe clumps, not single molecules. A good delivery system would be needed to carry them into the body.
plos-pone-0348840:
Muzlifa Mohamed Yusoff and co-workers study how actively patients with type two diabetes in Malaysia take charge of their own care. Active patients tend to manage blood sugar better over time. Their 2026 study surveys four hundred fifty patients at a public clinic in Penang, scoring their confidence and skills for self-care alongside views of their treatment and doctors' support.

Two-thirds of patients scored at a high level of engagement with their care. Men scored slightly higher, while older patients scored lower. Higher long-term blood sugar readings went with lower engagement, and patients on tablets alone scored below others. Clinics may lift self-care most by focusing support on older patients and those whose sugar control is already slipping.
plos-pone-0348440:
Yiming Zhang and co-workers capture the first detailed shapes of a human channel that lets calcium into cells. The channel, called Orai1, opens when internal calcium stores run low, and faults in it cause immune and muscle disease. Their 2026 study freezes the purified human protein and images it with a cryo-electron microscope.

The map confirms the channel is built from six matching parts arranged in a ring. Surprisingly, particles appeared in two different symmetry patterns, which hints the channel flexes and rearranges as it works. Resolution was moderate, so fine detail awaits sharper maps. Even so, having the human form gives drug designers a real target instead of a stand-in from flies.
plos-pone-0348140:
Imen Zghab and co-workers create a family of new molecules and test whether they can block enzymes tied to blood sugar and skin darkening. Blocking the two sugar enzymes could help diabetes care, while blocking the third interests cosmetics. Their 2026 study builds the compounds from a simple acid base and checks them in lab dishes against standard drugs.

One compound blocked both sugar enzymes far more strongly than the standard diabetes drug used for comparison. A sister compound led on the skin enzyme, beating a common reference agent. Computer models of how the molecules dock into the enzymes matched the dish results. The pair stand out as starting points for medicines that do several jobs at once.
plos-pone-0347140:
Xiao Wang and co-workers test whether what a chief executive says in sustainability reports helps predict how the company will perform. Their 2026 study gathers more than twelve hundred listed Korean companies across eight years. It mines the bosses' report messages for strategy themes. Those themes are sorted by a sustainability scorecard. They are then joined with standard financial measures.

Eight learning models were tried, from simple neighbors to deep sequence readers. Models fed both money numbers and strategy themes beat money-only models across the board. A transformer design scored highest overall, with its close cousins next. Investors gain a hint that the words in the front of the report carry real signal about the numbers that follow.
plos-pone-0330140:
Ádám Fésüs and colleagues tested two styles of hip training in young women whose knees cave inward when they land, a pattern tied to knee injuries. Twenty active college students trained their hip abductor muscles three times a week for four weeks, one group working the muscles mainly as they lengthen under load, the other as they shorten. Motion cameras measured knee position during jumps and landings.

Both groups grew stronger and jumped better. The lengthening-style group, though, reduced the inward knee collapse more during single-leg jumps, though not during drop landings. Strength gains alone did not explain the improvement. The pilot study suggests how the hip is trained matters, not just how strong it gets.
plos-pone-0348240:
Sema İncekara and Ahmet Şahin studied whether happiness at work keeps teachers in Türkiye's private schools committed to their schools. Teaching in the competitive private sector is stressful, and unhappy teachers leave. Their 2026 mixed-methods study surveyed two hundred ninety-nine teachers and interviewed eight more about emotions, fulfilment, and loyalty to their employer.

Teachers reported strong positive feelings, fulfilment, and emotional commitment, but weaker intention to stay when leaving would be costly. Feeling good and fulfilled predicted every form of commitment, while negative emotions dragged all of them down. Interviews echoed the numbers. The authors advise school leaders to protect positive working conditions and actively reduce sources of daily frustration.
plos-pone-0347540:
J. K. Owaresat and co-authors compared how human neural progenitor cells, the stem cells that build the brain, respond to dengue virus and Zika virus. Both infect these cells, with Zika notoriously damaging developing brains. Using gene network analysis on infected cell samples, the 2026 study separated the genes each virus rallies for its own replication from the defences the cell mounts.

Each virus leaned on distinct helper pathways, dengue on a growth signalling route and Zika on the cell's protein-making machinery, while sharing stress responses in the cell's folding workshop. Their defences diverged too. The authors say the map points to drug targets tailored to each virus.
plos-pone-0343140:
Mordicai Atinga and colleagues surveyed four hundred rugby players from ten clubs across Kenya for this 2026 PLOS ONE study of injury and mental health. Rugby brings frequent muscle and joint injuries, yet little research has asked what those injuries do to players' minds in African settings, where mental health support is limited.

More than half the players reported a significant injury in the previous two years, most often to the knee, ankle, or shoulder. Injured players scored worse on a general mental health questionnaire and reported lower physical functioning than uninjured teammates. The authors argue that treating a rugby injury in Kenya should include attention to mood, identity, and substance use, not only the damaged joint.
plos-pone-0346340:
Anna Sophie Kebke and colleagues used chemistry locked in whale skin to work out what long-finned pilot whales eat off Scotland, in this 2026 PLOS ONE paper. The tissue came from fifty adults and juveniles that stranded together on the Isle of Lewis in July 2023.

Carbon and nitrogen markers in the skin pointed to feeding along the continental shelf edge and slope, on prey from deep-water food webs. The whales' feeding zone overlapped only slightly with those of six dolphin species used for comparison, and males and females overlapped fully, though females ranged more widely. Such baselines help conservation planners protect the waters these whales depend on.
un-sc-res-united-nations-security-counci:
A broken ceasefire in the Sinai produced a new kind of UN force in 1973. On 25 October, the Council adopted Resolution 340. Fourteen members voted yes and none voted no. China took no part. The truce ordered by Resolution 338 three days before was being breached again and again. UN observers still could not reach both sides of the line.

The text demands a full and instant ceasefire. Both sides must return to the lines held when Resolution 338 passed. More observers are ordered at once. The big step comes next. A United Nations Emergency Force is set up under the Council's own command. Its troops come from member states, but not from the five permanent members.

A theater full of hostages in Moscow drew the Council's swift word in 2002. On 24 October, it adopted Resolution 1440 without dissent. Chechen gunmen had seized the hall a day before, mid-show. Hundreds of playgoers and cast members were held inside. The seizure came amid a string of terror attacks in many lands.

The text condemns the hostage-taking in the strongest terms. It demands the instant, free release of all hostages, with no conditions. Deep sympathy goes to Russia's people and leaders. It goes to the victims and their families as well. All states must help Russia hunt down those behind the attack. That duty rests on the terror rules of Resolution 1373.

Indonesia's independence struggle drew UN mediators after the Second World War. Dutch forces were fighting to restore colonial rule. A Committee of Good Offices tried to broker peace. Resolution 40, adopted on 28 February 1948, gave that committee a specific assignment. Eight members voted in favor. Argentina, the Ukrainian republic, and the Soviet Union abstained.

The committee was told to watch political events closely. Its focus was western Java and Madura, two restive regions. Reports had to reach the Council frequently. The task was fact-finding, not enforcement. Still, steady reporting kept world attention on Indonesia. That pressure helped push the Dutch toward the transfer of sovereignty completed in 1949.

What if a terror band built a gas bomb or stole a nuke? That fear drove one of the Council's boldest texts. Trade in parts for such arms had shown black paths round the law. States had gaps in their books. Resolution 1540 passed with no dissent on 28 April 2004. It speaks to all states at once, with the Charter's teeth.

No state may aid lone groups that seek such arms. Each state must pass laws to bar the work. Goods that could feed such arms must be tracked and locked down. Borders and ports must watch for banned trade. Shipments in and out need strict checks. A team of the whole Council would track the work for two years. First word from each state was due in six months. Few texts reach so deep into each land's own law books.

Nepal's peace deal gets a UN mission in Resolution 1740, adopted on 23 January 2007. The government and the Maoist party had signed a comprehensive peace agreement on 21 November 2006, ending a decade of civil war. Both sides asked the UN to help with the trickiest parts: managing the arms and fighters of both armies, and monitoring elections.

Answering that request, the Council established the United Nations Mission in Nepal, UNMIN, for an initial twelve months. Its monitors would watch cantonments and weapons storage, and support the vote for a constituent assembly. The text notes the strong public desire for peace and restored democracy, and calls for attention to women, children, and groups long shut out of power.

Resolution 1940, passed on 29 September 2010, sweeps away the last UN bans on Sierra Leone. The bans dated from 1997, when a junta seized power by force. As elected rule came back, the bans were trimmed year by year. In a letter of 9 September 2010 the state's envoy brought fresh news and asked for the last bans to go. The bans team's final report backed the step.

The Council ended the last bars that same day. It praised the UN peace team's work in the land's revival. It urged all states to keep aiding the war crimes court set up for Sierra Leone. One task named was to bring a key indictee to court if he still lived. A long war file thus closed.

Resolution 1640, passed on 23 November 2005, takes Eritrea to task for curbs on UN troops. In October, Eritrea had banned all UN flights by air in its skies. Fresh curbs on the UN team's ground moves came on top of that. The team watched the border with Ethiopia. The curbs crippled its work and put its staff at risk. Ethiopia, for its part, still balked at the border ruling in full.

The demands ran to both sides. Eritrea had to lift the flight ban and the ground curbs, with no strings tied. Ethiopia had to take and apply the border panel's ruling, which both had sworn to treat as final. With no line marked on the ground, the Council warned, no real peace could last in the region.

Resolution 1140, adopted on 28 November 1997, is a two-line procedural text on the former Yugoslav Republic of Macedonia. Recalling its Resolution 1110 (1997), the Security Council decides to extend the mandate of the United Nations Preventive Deployment Force, UNPREDEP. The extension is for one additional short period ending on 4 December 1997. The Council also decides to remain actively seized of the matter. The force was the UN's first preventive deployment, stationed to watch the country's northern borders.

Haiti's military regime is ordered out by force if needed in Resolution 940, adopted in July 1994. The de facto regime had defied the Governors Island Agreement, blocked the UN Mission in Haiti, worsened the humanitarian crisis, and expelled the international civilian mission's staff. Letters from Haiti's president and its UN envoy were before the Council.

Acting under Chapter VII, the Council authorizes member states to form a force under unified command. The force may use all necessary means to make the military leadership leave, secure the return of the legitimately elected President, Jean-Bertrand Aristide, and restore Haiti's lawful government. A UNMIH advance team of up to 60 goes in with the force. Once a stable environment exists, UNMIH takes over with 6,000 troops, to keep security, professionalize the armed forces, create a separate police force, and help prepare legislative elections. Sanctions are to be lifted on Aristide's return.
un-ga-res-united-nations-general-assembl:
Resolution 140 (II) was approved by the General Assembly on 1 November 1947. It placed the island of Nauru under the United Nations trusteeship system. Nauru is a small island in the Pacific. It had been run by Australia under a League of Nations mandate. Australia ran it on behalf of Australia, New Zealand, and the United Kingdom. The agreement replaced that mandate.

The three governments were named joint administering authority. Australia was to carry out the day-to-day rule, lawmaking, and courts. They promised to guard the rights and land of Nauru's own people. They promised to aid their progress in schooling, health, and public life. They promised to protect free speech, worship, and assembly. All this was under the watch of the Trusteeship Council.

General Assembly Resolution 40, adopted on 13 December 1946, took up the use of the veto in the Security Council. Members disagreed over how Article 27 of the Charter should be read and used. The Assembly earnestly asked the permanent members to work in talks with each other and with the Council's other members. The aim was that their special voting privilege would not hold up prompt decisions.

The Council was urged to adopt habits and ways of working, within the Charter, that would ease the strain around Article 27 and let it act fast and well. In shaping them, it was to weigh the views members had voiced during the session.

Resolution 69/40 of the General Assembly, 'Reducing nuclear danger,' focuses on accident and miscalculation rather than arsenals themselves. It calls for a review of nuclear doctrines. It calls for immediate steps to cut the risk of unintentional or accidental nuclear use. In particular, weapons should be taken off hair-trigger alert and de-targeted. The five nuclear-weapon states are asked to carry out such measures. The Secretary-General is asked to push the Advisory Board on Disarmament Matters' seven recommendations for reducing the risk of nuclear war.
un-sc-res-united-nations-security-counci:
Security Council resolution 1040, adopted on 29 January 1996, addresses the worsening crisis in Burundi. The Council says it is deeply concerned at the continued deterioration of the situation and the threat to regional stability. It condemns those responsible for the rising violence, including attacks on refugees and aid workers. It stresses Burundi's responsibility for the safety of international personnel.

The Council demands restraint from all concerned. It backs a comprehensive political dialogue in support of the Convention of Government of 10 September 1994. It invites states to help identify and dismantle radio stations that incite hatred and violence. It asks the Secretary-General for contingency planning and a full report by 20 February 1996. It warns that it is ready to consider an arms ban and travel restrictions. Those would target leaders who keep encouraging violence.

Choosing judges for the war crimes tribunal for the former Yugoslavia takes a formal step forward on 8 February 2001. The tribunal, set up in 1993, tried people accused of crimes in the Balkan wars. Its permanent judges are elected by the General Assembly, but only from a list the Security Council forwards.

That forwarding is the whole of this text. It sends the Assembly the nominations the Secretary-General had received by 31 January 2001: 26 candidates put forward by countries across Europe, Africa, Asia, and the Americas. From that list, the Assembly would elect the judges who would hear the tribunal's trials and appeals.

Madagascar's entry into the United Nations begins with this short text of 29 June 1960. Having examined the application of the Malagasy Republic, the Council recommended to the General Assembly that the republic be admitted to membership. That recommendation is the Charter's required first step. Only after it can the General Assembly vote on admission, which makes this brief resolution the formal doorway to the new state's seat in the world body.

Fighting in the Middle East continued in the autumn of 1967, months after the Six-Day War had ended. The Council had ordered a cease-fire, but its orders were being broken. Reports from the Secretary-General documented the violations one by one. Resolution 240 was adopted unanimously on 25 October 1967.

The Council condemned the cease-fire violations. It expressed regret over the deaths and the damage to property that they caused. It reaffirmed that the cease-fire resolutions had to be strictly obeyed. The member states concerned were told to halt all prohibited military action in the area at once. They also had to work fully and without delay with the United Nations Truce Supervision Organization. That observer body was the United Nations presence on the ground.

The war between Iran and Iraq was in its third year in the autumn of 1983. A mission sent by the Secretary-General had inspected civilian areas in both countries. Those areas had come under military attack. Resolution 540 was adopted on 31 October 1983.

The Council deplored the conflict and its heavy toll. Civilian lives were being lost, and cities and industry were badly damaged. All violations of international humanitarian law were condemned, above all breaches of the Geneva Conventions. Attacks on civilian targets had to end. The text affirmed the right of free navigation and trade in international waters. Both sides were told to stop hostilities at sea. The Secretary-General was asked to keep mediating toward a full settlement, and to consult both parties on ways to sustain and verify a cease-fire.
un-sc-res-340:
Fighting in the October 1973 Middle East war had outrun two ceasefire orders. On 25 October 1973 the Security Council demanded a complete ceasefire at once. It told the parties to return to the positions held on 22 October. United Nations observers still could not reach both sides of the line. The Council wanted more of them, fast.

The resolution also creates a United Nations Emergency Force on the spot. Its troops would come from member states, but not from the permanent members. The Secretary-General had twenty-four hours to report on the first steps. That force, known as UNEF II, then stood between the Egyptian and Israeli armies.
un-sc-res-1440:
Chechen gunmen held hundreds of hostages in a Moscow theater in October 2002. On 24 October 2002 the Security Council condemned the seizure in the strongest terms. It called the act heinous. It treated it, like all international terrorism, as a threat to peace. The Council acted one day after the attack began. The standoff was still under way as members voted.

The resolution demands the immediate and unconditional release of all hostages. It sends deep sympathy to Russia's people and government. It also goes to the victims and their families. All states must help Russia find and punish those behind the attack. That duty flowed from the counter-terrorism rules set in resolution 1373.
un-sc-res-40: Indonesia's political future in two regions drew the Council's eye in February 1948. On 28 February 1948 it asked its Committee of Good Offices to watch western Java and Madura closely. The committee had to report to the Council at frequent intervals. Political events in those areas were the focus. The whole resolution is a single sentence. It formed part of the Council's close watch on the Dutch-Indonesian dispute.
un-sc-res-1540:
Weapons of mass destruction in private hands drove this landmark text of 2004. On 28 April 2004 the Security Council ruled that spreading such weapons threatens world peace. It acted under Chapter VII, so its orders bind every state. The fear was that terrorist or criminal groups might build nuclear, chemical, or biological arms. States had to cut off every path to that outcome.

No state may help non-state actors seek such weapons in any form. Every state must pass laws that bar private work on them. States must also build tight controls over dangerous materials. Stockpiles had to be counted and guarded. A committee would track how states carried the rules out. The text made non-proliferation a duty for all, not just treaty members.
un-sc-res-1740:
Nepal's peace agreement gained a United Nations mission on 23 January 2007. The government and the Communist Party of Nepal (Maoist) had signed a Comprehensive Peace Agreement on 21 November 2006. Both sides asked for United Nations help with arms monitoring and election watching. An advance team of monitors and electoral staff was already going in. The Secretary-General's report of 9 January 2007 set out the plan.

The Council established a United Nations political mission in Nepal, UNMIN. Its mandate covered watching the management of arms and armed personnel of both sides and helping monitor the coming constituent assembly election. The mission was sized to Nepal's special setting and to the parties' own ownership of the peace. The Secretary-General had to keep the Council informed of progress. The parties were asked to guard United Nations staff and keep the process moving.
un-sc-res-1940:
Sierra Leone's sanctions chapter closed on 29 September 2010. The government in Freetown wrote on 9 September asking for the measures to be lifted. Its letter updated the Council on the country's recovery. The Council had long said it would end the measures once the government held full control and all other forces stood disarmed. The peacebuilding office in Sierra Leone drew its praise.

Acting under Chapter VII, the Council terminated the measures in paragraphs 2, 4, and 5 of resolution 1171 (1998) with immediate effect. Those terms carried the arms and travel limits left from the war years. The Council also dissolved the sanctions committee set up in 1997 under resolution 1132. States were urged to help the Special Court, or any court taking its cases, bring Johnny Paul Koroma to justice if he lived. Lifting the last measures marked Sierra Leone's formal exit from the Council's sanctions list.
un-sc-res-1640:
Eritrea and Ethiopia faced twin demands over the stalled border peace on 23 November 2005. Eritrea had banned UNMEE helicopter flights on 5 October and tightened other limits since. The move cut the mission's ability to work and put its staff at risk. Ethiopia still refused to accept the Boundary Commission's final ruling without conditions. An envoy had visited both capitals from 6 to 9 November.

The Council deeply deplored Eritrea's continued restrictions on UNMEE. It demanded that Eritrea reverse its steps and give the mission full freedom of movement. Both parties were called to show maximum restraint and to pull their forces back from the border zone. The Council demanded that Ethiopia accept the Boundary Commission's decision fully and without delay, and start the talks needed for marking the border. The Secretary-General would watch both sides' compliance and report. Further measures were held in reserve.
un-sc-res-940:
A Council decision on Haiti took shape as Resolution 940, adopted on 31 July 1994. A military regime held power against the Governors Island Agreement. Rights abuses grew, refugees fled, and the joint civilian mission had been expelled. The elected president, Jean-Bertrand Aristide, asked for help from abroad.

Acting under Chapter VII, the Council lets member states form a multinational force under one command. The force may use all necessary means to remove the military leaders and bring Aristide back. A small United Nations advance team of up to sixty will link with the force. After calm returns, the United Nations Mission in Haiti takes over at 6,000 troops. Sanctions will end once Aristide returns.
europmc-pmc10011140:
Brain gene activity and its links to disease are mapped by de Klein and a large team in a 2023 study. The group combined RNA data from more than eight thousand brain samples across many datasets. They built a shared resource called MetaBrain to make the merged data usable by other labs.

With that resource, the team tracked how gene variants change gene activity in the brain. They then pointed to genes that may drive brain diseases. The work helps turn raw genetic hits from past studies into clear targets for new research.
europmc-pmc10024440:
Hu and colleagues report that a circular RNA carried in exosomes weakens killer T cells and helps liver cancer resist a key drug class, in a 2023 study. The RNA is called circCCAR1. Killer T cells that stop working well are a main reason liver tumors escape the immune system and shrug off PD-1 blocking drugs.

The team shows how tumor parcels deliver this RNA to T cells and blunt their attack. Blocking the RNA restored T cell strength in their tests. The finding names a new target for making liver cancer drugs work better.
europmc-pmc10307640:
Kruse and a large team report that CD4 T cells can control tumors that evade standard immune attack, through inflammatory cell death, in a 2023 study. Most cancer immunotherapy relies on CD8 killer T cells that spot tumor markers directly. Tumors often escape by losing those markers, which leaves such therapy powerless.

The team shows that helper CD4 T cells can instead trigger a fiery form of death in tumor tissue. That death engulfed even marker-free tumor cells nearby. The finding opens a path to treat tumors that hide from killer T cells.
europmc-pmc10468540:
Wang, Zhao, and Wan reviewed in 2023 how one signal family steers two rival T cell types. The family is TGF-beta, a set of growth signals found across animals. The two cell types are Treg cells, which calm immune attack, and Th17 cells, which can stir it. Both types guard the fine line between tolerance and rejection.

When that line breaks, autoimmunity, cancer, or infection can follow. TGF-beta sits at the core of both cell types, despite their opposed acts. Wang maps the signal web that lets one family guide both. The web is built from ordered, linked steps that share parts. Two decades of work feed into this account of the balance.
europmc-pmc10585440:
Meskó wrote a tutorial in 2023 on prompt engineering as a new skill for medical staff. The craft means shaping the text prompts that steer a large language model. ChatGPT drew over 100 million users in two months, a record pace. As patients and staff turn to such tools, the skill gap grows hard to ignore.

Good prompts can lift the quality of a model's output on a task. Poor prompts can yield vague or false text, a risk in care. Meskó sums up the state of research on the craft so far. The piece then gives hands-on tips for a wide range of health workers. Tips cover clear task framing, context, and checks on output.
europmc-pmc10632140:
Taylor and co-authors showed in 2023 that brain tumours borrow the brain's own learning tricks. Gliomas are cancers that grow inside brain circuits. Nerve cells feed their growth through synapses, the links that pass signals between cells. Those links push tumour cells to divide.

A growth factor called BDNF tunes synapse strength in the healthy brain. Taylor found that it tunes the tumour links the same way. It sends more signal receivers to the tumour cell surface, which boosts the current each signal makes. Stronger currents drove faster tumour growth in their tests. Blocking the BDNF receptor, TrkB, cut these effects and stretched survival in mouse models of child brain cancers.
europmc-pmc11275440:
Yi and colleagues review signal proteins as targets for cancer therapy in this 2024 paper. Cytokines are proteins that regulate immune responses and cell behaviour. Families include interleukins, interferons, tumour necrosis factors, and chemokines, which guide cell movement. Growth factors such as TGF-beta, VEGF, and EGF belong to the same broad set. These molecules can push tumours either way.

Depending on context, a cytokine can promote or suppress tumour growth, the authors stress. It can also reshape the tumour's surroundings and change how well treatments work. Recent agents aim to modulate these pathways to slow progression and beat resistance. The review summarises current understanding of each family in tumour biology. It then details the new drugs built on that knowledge. The dual nature of cytokines is treated as both the central challenge and the central opportunity.
europmc-pmc1238740:
Gutierrez and co-authors revisited the deep origins of tuberculosis bacteria in 2005. The TB germ shows very little genetic variety today. That sameness suggested a narrow origin about 35,000 years ago. New isolates from East Africa told a broader story.

Gene trees for those isolates did not agree with each other. Some genes looked like mosaics stitched from different sources. Gutierrez argues the modern germ descends from a wider ancestral pool. Gene swapping shaped that pool long before clonal spread. The bacteria may have lived with early humans far longer than thought.
europmc-pmc1240840:
Hoppin, Brock, Davis, and Baird checked urine test stability for phthalates in 2002. Phthalates are chemicals found in plastics and cosmetics everywhere. Some forms harm reproduction in animal studies. Judging human exposure needs reliable measures.

These chemicals clear the body in about twelve hours. The team collected first morning urine on two straight days. Samples came from 46 women in the Washington area. Seven breakdown products plus a dilution marker were measured. Four products appeared in every sample. Hoppin tests how steady single spot checks really are. Levels were measured with liquid chromatography and mass spectrometry.
europmc-pmc1241340:
Lovekamp-Swan and Davis reviewed how phthalates harm female reproduction in 2003. Phthalates are mass-produced chemicals in plastics and consumer goods. Survey data suggested women face a distinct exposure pattern. Their lab studied these chemicals in animal models of the ovary.

One phthalate, DEHP, cut blood estrogen and halted egg release in rats. Its active breakdown product lowered a key enzyme message in ovary cells. That enzyme, aromatase, makes estrogen in the ovary. The product also switches on fat-sensing receptors called PPARs. The authors propose those receptors suppress aromatase and drive the harm.
europmc-pmc12535840:
GBD 2023 Disease and Injury and Risk Factor Collaborators audited world health in 2025. The Global Burden of Disease effort has run for over thirty years. It counts health loss from disease, injury, and risk factors. Coverage spans 204 countries plus 660 subnational locations.

Burden was estimated for 375 diseases and injuries. Eighty-eight changeable risk factors got linked burden estimates. More than 120,000 sources fed this round of estimates. Healthy life expectancy was computed alongside illness burden. GBD 2023 Disease and Injury and Risk Factor Collaborators frame post-pandemic gaps in plain numbers. Burden was counted as years of life lost and years lived with illness.
europmc-pmc1311140:
Steele and co-authors tested how lung immune cells recognize a fungal invader in 2005. Aspergillus fumigatus spores are inhaled daily and cleared by lung macrophages. Which recognition receptor matters was disputed. The fungus wall is rich in beta-glucan sugars, pointing to one receptor.

Blocking tests showed the response depended on dectin-1, the beta-glucan receptor. Without it, cells made far fewer inflammatory signals. Eight signaling molecules were measured in the response. Swollen spores and early sprouting forms triggered the strongest reaction. That strength matched how much beta-glucan they exposed. Steele settles the receptor question for this fungus.
europmc-pmc1473040:
Proteins with many partners, called hubs, are more often vital than loners. He and Zhang asked in 2006 whether the web's shape explains that rule. They proposed a plainer cause: some protein links are themselves vital for life. A hub simply holds more links, so it more likely holds a vital one.

Their math suggests about three percent of yeast protein links are vital. Those links account for about 43 percent of vital genes. Vital links also changed less over evolution than others. He argues the yeast web is sturdier than random webs, yet far from the best possible. The rule may owe less to design than to counting.
europmc-pmc1905940: MicroRNAs: novel regulators involved in the pathogenesis of psoriasis? — a 2005 science paper on tiny RNAs in psoriasis. It asks if they drive the skin ills for labs. The paper is the tiny-RNA study: the notes on skin ills, filed here in full session today.
europmc-pmc1989740: Grand challenges in global health: community engagement in research in developing countries. — a 2005 science paper on health research in poor nations. It guides the community engagement. The paper is the engagement guide: the findings on global health, filed here in session.

europmc-pmc2684740: Alterations in vitamin D status and anti-microbial peptide levels in patients in the intensive — a 2008 science paper on vitamin D and peptides. It finds the altered peptide levels. The paper is the peptide study: the findings on vitamin ills, filed here in session.

aldrovandi-serpentum-draconum-1640:
Ulisse Aldrovandi, the tireless naturalist of Bologna, devoted his Serpentum et draconum historiae to serpents and dragons. The two Latin books appeared in 1640, after his death, from his vast museum and notes. Aldrovandi aimed to record everything known about a creature, ancient report and fresh sighting alike.

Vipers and common snakes share his pages with basilisks and sea serpents. Each creature gets a careful picture in the Renaissance manner. Aldrovandi stands halfway between true science and honest marvel, and knows it not at all. His serpent book founded learned serpent lore in print. Collectors still prize its plates.
regino-prum-de-synodalibus-causis-latin-:
Regino, abbot of Prüm, compiled his two books on synodal cases around 906. Bishops used the collection when judging clergy and laity in their courts. This text follows Wasserschleben's edition of 1840, the standard scholarly printing of Regino's Latin.

Regino's gathering is famous above all as the transmitter of the Canon Episcopi. That canon, set among his cases, taught that witches' night flights were demonic illusions. His books also treat magic and superstition across many headings. The collection is a foundation of canon law on such matters. Through Regino, an early medieval ruling of doubt shaped church courts for the next six hundred years.
plos-pone-0004940:
Transplanted organs often fail years after surgery. Their blood vessels slowly narrow and clog. The process is called chronic allograft vasculopathy. Standard immune-suppressing drugs fail to prevent it. Zhiliang Wang and colleagues tested a different strategy in PLOS ONE in 2009. They targeted dendritic cells inside the recipient's body. The treatment used dying cells taken from the donor.

Dendritic cells take up these donor cells. They then present donor material in a calming way. That restrains indirect allorecognition, the slow immune route driving vessel damage. In tests, the approach eased the vessel disease. It suggests tolerance can be taught, not forced with lifelong drugs.
plos-pone-0005040:
New genes can be born from copied RNA. A copied message pasted back into DNA forms a retrogene. Deng Pan and Liqing Zhang surveyed retrogenes across mammals. Their PLOS ONE paper appeared in 2009. They examined eight mammalian genomes. Four non-mammalian genomes served as contrast.

They found a burst of young retrogenes. Each retrogene formed independently in its lineage. Retrogenes are a live engine of new gene formation. Some later gain real jobs in the body. The pattern shows mammals keep inventing fresh DNA. The work charts that invention across the mammal family tree. It helps explain how genomes stay creative over evolutionary time.
plos-pone-0005140:
Diagnosing lung TB in children is difficult. It often requires hospitalization and repeated sampling. Nasher Al-Aghbari and colleagues tested a shortcut in Yemen. Their PLOS ONE paper appeared in 2009. They collected specimens from different body sites in one day. The samples went for smear microscopy, the standard field test.

They compared the one-day yield with samples collected over several visits. Multiple sampling in a single day optimized the microscopy results. Children could be diagnosed without long hospital stays. That matters where beds and money are scarce. It also spares families repeated travel. The finding offers a practical protocol for pediatric TB. Clinics can adopt it without new equipment.
plos-pone-0005240:
Freeze-drying could let cells be stored and shipped at room temperature, but most cells die in the process. Earlier work showed freeze-dried cells kept for years could still guide development in cloning. Natan and colleagues tested cord blood cells in PLOS ONE in 2009.

The team freeze-dried mononuclear cells from umbilical cord blood and then checked colony formation. Colonies growing after rehydration prove that some cells kept real function, not just intact DNA. Progress here could ease the cold storage burden for cell therapies and blood banks. Cells that can be kept dry and shipped in a box would change how blood banks plan for war zones and far-off clinics with no freezer.
plos-pone-0005340:
Asking people about risky sexual behavior face to face can invite false answers. Audio computer-assisted self-interview, or ACASI, lets people answer privately by computer. Van der Elst and colleagues compared the two methods in sex workers in Mombasa, Kenya, in PLOS ONE in 2009.

Female and male sex workers answered through both ACASI and face-to-face interviews. ACASI may elicit more honest reporting of sensitive behaviors. Knowing which method tells the truth matters, since risk assessments guide HIV programs for these communities. Health teams can plan HIV care well only if the facts on risk are true,. A method that wins trust gives them facts they can act on with more faith.
plos-pone-0005940:

Their PLOS ONE paper maps the immunoproteome of Neisseria meningitidis, meaning the full set of its proteins that the immune system can see.

A map of that kind is a menu of targets for a vaccine meant to cover more strains. Germs of this species still cause blood poisoning and meningitis around the world despite current shots. By listing the proteins the body reacts to, the team gives vaccine makers a grounded place to start the search for wider protection.
plos-pone-0006040:
Cell lines are the workhorses of cancer research, but a mislabeled line poisons every result built on it. Janyaporn Phuchareon, Yoshihito Ohta, Jonathan Woo and colleagues audited six lines in 2009. The audit found cross-contamination and misidentification among the six, the title reports. Work done with a wrong line cannot be trusted, however careful it was. The study is both a warning and a service: it names the suspect lines, ACC2, ACC3, ACCM, ACCNS, ACCS and CAC2, so labs can check their own stocks.
plos-pone-0006140:
Kenya's parks are famed for wildlife, yet most animals live outside their fences. David Western, Samantha Russell and Innes Cuthill compared those two worlds over thirty years in 2009. Their PLOS ONE paper compiles more than two hundred seventy wildlife counts to compare population trends in protected areas with those in adjacent ecosystems and across the country.

Separating human-caused change from natural swings is the study's care. If wildlife falls as fast inside parks as outside, fences alone are not saving it. The long count record gives conservation a rare honest mirror, and it argues for protecting the lands between parks where most animals actually roam.
plos-pone-0006240:
Learning from a mistake means adjusting within seconds, and single brain cells take part. Thomas Michelet, Bernard Bioulac, and Dominique Guehl recorded individual neurons in the medial prefrontal cortex in a 2009 PLOS ONE paper. One idea is that attention systems are retuned right after an error.

plos-pone-0006740:
Quentin Vicens and co-authors prepared self-splicing RNA molecules for study in PLOS ONE in 2009. Group I introns are RNA segments that cut themselves out. They applied it to twenty-three group I intron variants. The introns ranged from about two hundred fifty to three hundred forty nucleotides. Some variants still contained their exons. Consistent purification across sizes makes experiments comparable. Reliable samples support both biochemical tests and crystal structure work on these catalytic RNAs.
plos-pone-0006840:
Adi Tabib and colleagues split one protein's two ends into opposite immune instructions in PLOS ONE in 2009. The protein is thrombospondin-1. The team tested the protein's two ends separately. The N-terminal domain induced a phagocytic state in dendritic cells. The C-terminal domain induced the tolerizing phenotype instead. One protein thus carries two distinct messages. Splitting the messages could let medicine use each effect alone.
plos-pone-0006940:
Gail Kilroy, David Burk, and Z. Elizabeth Floyd tackled a laboratory problem in PLOS ONE in 2009. Fully grown fat cells, called adipocytes, resist standard gene silencing methods. plos-pone-0007040:
Jin Yu, Ngan Huang, Kitchener Wilson, and colleagues tested nicotine's effect on stem cell therapy in PLOS ONE in 2009. Many heart patients carry risk factors such as smoking. plos-pone-0007140:
Anasuya Sarkar, Srabani Mitra, Sonya Mehta, and colleagues traced a cell death message in PLOS ONE in 2009. Apoptosis usually starts inside the doomed cell itself. The team found monocytes release tiny vesicles loaded with caspase-1. Those microvesicles deliver the death message to target cells. A packaged enzyme acting as a letter is a new twist in cell death biology. It may operate in sepsis, where monocytes and vessel damage collide.
plos-pone-0007240:
Athuluri Divakar Sai Krishna, Raj Kumar Mandraju, Golla Kishore, and colleagues designed targeted drug carriers for cancer in 2009. They test the carriers as an efficient targeted delivery route. Their approach aims to concentrate drugs in tumors while sparing healthy tissue.
plos-pone-0007340:
Claudia B. M. Bijen, Karin M. Vermeulen, Marian J. E. Mourits, and colleagues reviewed surgery costs and effects for hysterectomy in 2009. They compare abdominal hysterectomy with laparoscopic hysterectomy, the keyhole approach. openalex-w2130707940: Five trillion plastic pieces float in the oceans. A 2014 paper estimated more than 5 trillion plastic pieces weighing 250,000 tons afloat at sea. The global count drew on data from far-flung seas.
plos-pone-0006340:

openalex-w2157165940: Every decision we make carries a quiet second judgment: how sure am I? openalex-w2169574440: A famous rule of chemistry, Sabatier's principle, says the best hydrogen catalysts bind hydrogen neither too strongly nor too weakly — plot activity against binding energy and you should get a volcano-shaped curve. openalex-w2471350540: Thousands of papers claim progress in sentiment analysis, and startups sell opinion-mining products — but which methods actually work best? europmc-pmc2860140: Muscles that shrug off insulin drive diabetes, and this 2010 review asks why. The authors trace the pathogenesis of insulin resistance in skeletal muscle. Their overview connects faulty signaling to the disease. The review remains a primer on muscle's role in diabetes.
europmc-pmc2872640: The genome's dark matter, mysterious RNA transcripts, mostly maps to known genes after all. This 2010 paper shows most dark matter transcripts associate with known genes. The authors' analysis shrank the mystery. Their result refocused the hunt for truly novel RNAs.
europmc-pmc2888740: Drink's link to stroke is not one-size-fits-all. This 2010 review and meta-analysis weighs alcohol against the risk of illness and death from different stroke types. The authors find the risk varies by stroke kind. Their careful split refined drinking advice.

europmc-pmc2920840: Iron is life's contested prize. This 2010 review narrates the battle for iron between bacterial pathogens and their vertebrate hosts. europmc-pmc2954140: Computer programs can ease anxiety and low mood. This 2010 pooled study finds online therapy works well and suits patients with anxiety and depression. europmc-pmc3113940: Protein changes got a stability predictor. This 2011 paper brings PoPMuSiC 2.1, a web server that predicts how mutations shift protein stability.
