europmc-pmc3146540: E. coli's size got measured for modelers. This 2011 paper measures condition-dependent cell volume in E. coli. The authors provide conversion data. Their work aids systems biology. Cell size shifted with growth rate. Modelers now use the tables. The data is freely shared.
europmc-pmc3177840: A brain parasite raised dopamine. This 2011 paper shows Toxoplasma gondii boosts dopamine metabolism. The authors reveal the manipulation. Their work illuminates behavior science. arxiv-2606-16040: The one-time pad is the only provably unbreakable cipher, but it is famously impractical. This paper explores a new twist: a "mixed-radix" one-time pad that encodes messages in mixed number bases, an old type of cipher given new life. The author presents the design and argues it opens fresh possibilities for unbreakable-by-math encryption.
arxiv-2606-16140: Small language models are cheap to run, but can they reason reliably? VibeThinker-3B is a 3-billion-parameter model built to explore "verifiable reasoning" — reasoning steps that can be checked, not just trusted — at small scale. The paper reports what the authors found at the frontier of making tiny models think carefully.
arxiv-2606-16240: What happens when you give a language model a "directorial persona" — a strong creative identity — and pit it against another? This paper studies persona steering and competition in large language models, exploring how directorial framing changes the model's creative output. It is an AI-creativity study aimed at researchers of model behavior.
arxiv-2606-16340: The Moon's gravity doesn't just move oceans — it tugs on Earth's deep interior too. This geophysics paper studies resonant lunar tides in Earth's core and the basal magma ocean, the molten layer above the core. The authors model how tidal forces slosh these hidden layers, targeting researchers of Earth's deep dynamics.
arxiv-2606-16440: Training Transformers usually needs giant GPU clusters, but what if chips could train locally? NeuronFabric is a software reference architecture for on-chip Transformer training with local adaptive methods — updating weights where the data lives. The paper targets hardware and AI researchers pushing training onto specialized chips.
arxiv-2606-16840: Crypto markets crash together but rally apart — or so traders say. This paper tests that with dynamic conditional tail dependence: measuring how extremely the coins move together in crashes vs rallies. It is for financial econometricians who study crypto risk closely.
arxiv-2601-07440:
Fiona Redmen and colleagues wrote a 2026 arXiv preprint. The work covers variational autoencoder with normalizing flow for x-ray spectral fitting. ArXiv posted the preprint in 2026 under its PAPERS collection. Black hole X-ray binaries (BHBs) can be studied with spectral fitting to provide physical constraints on accretion in extreme gravitational environments.

Traditional methods of spectral fitting such as Markov Chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) face limitations due to computational times. The authors introduce a probabilistic model, use a variational autoencoder with a normalizing flow, trained to adopt a physical latent space. The work gives specialists a compact account of the problem and one proposed way to handle it.
arxiv-2601-08140:
Amit Pathak reports searches for new physics with baryons at the BESIII experiment. His 2026 arXiv paper, written for the BESIII Collaboration, uses the clean setting of the BEPCII collider. The dataset holds ten billion J/psi events, a huge sample for rare-decay searches.

The searches probe links between baryons and a dark sector, plus baryon-number violation. Channels include Sigma decays to a proton plus an invisible particle, and Xi decays to a pion plus an invisible particle. The team also searches for Lambda and anti-Lambda oscillation. Null or positive results here would sharpen what physicists know about matter's hidden rules.
arxiv-2601-08340:
Dorothea Strecker, Heinz Pampel, and Jonas Hofting survey how German research organizations track publication costs. Their 2026 arXiv paper reports a 2024 survey of research performing organizations in Germany. Of 583 invitees, 258 completed the questionnaire, a 44.3 percent response rate.

The authors call it the first comprehensive study of publication cost recording at these organizations. Knowing what papers cost is basic to open access planning and funder talks. Yet many institutions lack clean records of article charges and related fees. The survey shows how data are collected now, which reveals where reporting breaks down. Funders and libraries can use the findings to push for clearer cost tracking.
arxiv-2601-07540:
Farhad G. Zanjani, Hong Cai, and Amirhossein Habibian work on making realistic driving scenes for testing self-driving cars. Autonomous systems depend on multi-view camera images to perceive the road. Developers need closed-loop simulators to test perception and planning safely. Their 2026 preprint, ViewMorpher3D, generates new camera views of a scene.

Reconstruction methods like Gaussian Splatting can build simulators, but their new views often show artifacts. Problems grow when views stretch beyond the original cameras or observations are sparse. ViewMorpher3D is a 3D-aware diffusion framework for multi-camera novel view synthesis. It aims for views that stay consistent across cameras. Better synthetic views mean safer, cheaper testing of driving software before real roads.
arxiv-2601-07840:
Yuhan Gu and Wen Zheng prove uniqueness for a family of vertex operator algebras built by a classic construction. The GKO construction builds new algebras from known ones and generalizes the 3A and 6A algebras. The authors prove the algebra structures are unique under nonzero assumptions on some braiding matrix elements. They also show each algebra is generated by its weight two subspace. That subspace is the Griess algebra. Their 2026 preprint settles the family's structure.

Vertex operator algebras formalize the algebra of two-dimensional conformal field theory. Uniqueness results pin down a construction that might have allowed several outcomes. Generation by the Griess algebra links these algebras to the theory of the Monster group. The paper serves mathematicians in algebra and mathematical physics. It gives later work a firm object to build on.
arxiv-2601-06940:
Hengyu Liu and six co-authors wrote a 2026 arXiv paper on ships and the tracks they leave. Ships send out their place and speed by a system called the Automatic Identification System. Those tracks guide safe travel at sea. Yet tracks often have gaps, from lost signals or from crews who switch the signal off.

Past tools fill the gaps but give few clues as to why they fill them as they do. The new tool, called VISTA, uses large language models to fill gaps. It also brings in facts about ships and seas. That mix helps the fill stay true to how ships move. It also helps later tasks, such as spotting odd tracks or planning routes. Readers can see the grounds for each fill, not just the fill itself.
arxiv-2601-07240:
Mohammad Rowshan wrote a 2026 arXiv paper on how to read out quantum codes with fewer slips. The codes in view are called CSS codes. The read-out tool is belief propagation, or BP, which passes odds along a graph as it works. The graph is called a Tanner graph. Noise in these codes is often biased, so slips lean one way more than the next.

That lean can pile up flaws along set paths in the graph. Rowshan calls this pile-up directional degeneracy. He puts weights on the edges of the graph to mark which way each edge points. The weights merge into one weight per qubit. He then defines a count that sums how the pile-up spreads. The count guides a form of BP that knows the bias in the noise, for a read-out that fails less often.
arxiv-2601-08840:
Xiaoqi Han and five co-authors work on how to make a chat model forget one named thing. A model may hold facts on a firm, a star, or a drug that must be wiped. The wipe must take all facts on that thing, yet leave the rest of the model sound. Past wipes need costly full retrains, or prompts that fail when a ask is rephrased.

The team gives an edit method that keeps facts in line as it wipes. If one fact goes, facts that rest on it are dealt with too. That care stops half wipes that leave clues. A reader who must scrub a model gets a more firm wipe plan. It aims for low cost and few side harms.
arxiv-2601-08940:
B. Agis-Gonzalez and a large team read old light echoes round a galaxy core named GSN 069. The core gives off soft X-ray bursts that repeat on a set beat. Such bursts are a new puzzle in how cores feed. Signs hint a star tear event came first, where a star was torn by the core pull.

The team uses the slant of light, called polarization, as a probe. Slant can hold a print of past bright acts long past the act. Echoes in slant may show a past burst of core life that direct light has lost. A reader in core work gets a new probe for a strange source. It may tie the bursts to a past tear event.
arxiv-2601-09440:
Yi Gao and five co-authors built DepRadar, a tool that judges how library bugs affect user code. Their 2026 arXiv paper, bound for ICSE 2026, targets deep learning libraries such as Transformers and Megatron. When these libraries ship defects, downstream users struggle to tell whether their own programs are hit.

The defects range from silent wrong answers to small slowdowns. DepRadar uses coordinated agents to reason about the context of each defect and each user program. Matching the two gives a focused impact analysis instead of a blanket warning. The goal is to help developers patch what matters and ignore what does not.
arxiv-2601-09640:
David Miller and Rémi A. Chou extend secret sharing to groups that grow over time. Their 2026 arXiv paper builds schemes on correlated randomness and public communication. Secret sharing splits a secret so that only approved sets of participants can rebuild it.

Earlier correlated-randomness models assumed a fixed access structure. The new additive version lets any subset of participants join the approved set at each time step. The dealer learns of each change only when it happens. Such flexible schemes fit real teams, where who is trusted changes as projects evolve.
arxiv-2601-09840:
Alberto Domínguez Corella and Trí Minh Lê settle a corner case in the theory of best extensions. Their 2026 arXiv paper studies absolutely minimal Lipschitz extensions in finite metric spaces. Such extensions stretch a function to a whole space while keeping its slope as small as possible, pointwise.

In endless spaces these extensions are known to exist. The finite case is less settled. For spaces of at most four points, the authors show every function on a nonempty subset admits one. Small cases anchor a theory: if the claim failed anywhere, it might fail at four points first.
arxiv-2601-09940:
Joseph Marrow and Andrew Misseldine move a known ring idea to a new base. Schur rings were first built on groups. They split a group ring into parts with strong rules. Those rules make them of use in codes and graphs.

The pair now build Schur rings on semigroups. A semigroup has a product rule but may lack inverses. They show that key facts from the group case still hold. They also give cases where the two worlds part ways. Some semigroup types get fresh results of their own. The work widens where Schur ring tools can be used.
arxiv-2601-10240:
David Gruner, Sydney Barnes, Ansgar Reiners, and a large team make the case for a vast star survey. The survey would take light spectra of stars again and again over time. Such repeats can date a star. A star's spin and acts shift with age in known ways.

To date stars well, the field needs a large time based set. The white paper sets out that case. It lists the gear and sweep the task needs. It also names the gains for star birth and growth work. The paper is a plan pitch to the field, not a data report.
arxiv-2601-10740:
Anas Hajbi proposes Neuro-Symbolic Activation Discovery, a way to give neural networks activation functions drawn from science itself. Standard networks use generic activations like ReLU, GELU, or SiLU. Those shapes ignore the math structure inside scientific data. Hajbi's framework mines that structure with genetic programming, which evolves formulas that fit the data.

The found formulas are readable, and they are injected into the network as custom activations. The title frames a transfer from physics to ecology: structure learned in one field may serve another. If it works, networks could need fewer parameters for the same skill. The approach blends symbolic math with deep learning in a concrete, testable way.
arxiv-2601-11040:
Changhao Yi certifies the entanglement dimensionality of quantum states by random Pauli sampling. The Schmidt number measures how many dimensions a pure state's entanglement truly spans. Certifying it tells whether a state can power tasks that need high-dimensional entanglement. Yi's protocol uses Pauli measurements, the workhorse measurements of quantum labs.

The method achieves average-case sample complexity that grows mildly with qubit count and the square of the Schmidt number. That beats a prior worst-case bound that grew exponentially. Cheaper certification matters: labs must verify states without measuring them to death. The protocol helps experimentalists prove they made the rich entanglement their protocols presume.
arxiv-2601-11740:
Graham Hesketh gives full math forms for four-wave mixing in glass fibre. In this effect, light waves in a fibre act on each other and make new waves. The work deals with waves that are close to steady in time.

He writes the forms with a set of named math functions due to Weierstrass. The forms give the full wave shape for all four waves, for any start state. A chain of shifts then shows a clean core form with no free scale terms. Such forms let users test code and see the shape of the effect with no need to run a full sim each time.
arxiv-2601-12040:
Murilo da Luz, Bruno Brandão, Luana Martins, and their co-authors give language models a way to reason in parts, guided by doubt. Models still fail at multi-step maths and logic. Full chains of thought can wander or cost too much.

Their method, named PREGU in the work, uses partial reasoning. It searches and refines steps where doubt is high. That focus spends effort where it helps most. A doubt-led search could lift logic skill at lower cost than blind full search.  That focus may cut wasted steps in hard proofs.
arxiv-2601-11240:
Angelo El Saliby proves a claim about rigid graphs in this 2026 preprint. A graph is a web of points joined by edges. It is globally rigid when its shape is forced by edge lengths. That holds when near all placements match up to plain moves.

A graph is vertex-transitive when its symmetry group is rich. Any point can be sent to any other by a symmetry. The title claim joins the two traits in one result. Rich symmetry of that kind, with high regularity, forces global rigidity. Such graphs matter where shape must be pinned by few lengths. Sensor webs and molecular frames are classic use cases of that need.
arxiv-2601-11440:
Francisco Giral and four coauthors rebuild city wind fields from sparse sensors. Their 2026 preprint names the frame GenDA, for generative data assimilation. Wind maps of cities guide air quality and heat work. They also shape how comfortable streets feel for walkers.

Dense wind data over a whole city are rarely at hand. Sensors give only sparse points in a complex area. GenDA uses a diffusion model to fill the gaps. Classifier-free guidance steers the build toward the sensor data. The output is a high-resolution field on unstructured meshes. Such meshes fit real street layouts and building shapes. The frame could help planners test designs before building.
arxiv-2601-11640:
Yingda Yu and five coauthors correct data, not models, for weed detection. Their 2026 preprint gives a data-centric framework named MDDC. Agricultural weed detection often runs on edge devices. Those devices cap model size, compute, and latency hard.

Scaling the model or ensembling is off the table there. Model-Driven Data Correction improves the data instead. It iteratively diagnoses flaws in the training data. Deficiencies in quality are corrected round by round. Confident learning is the frame named in the title. Better labels can lift a small model past a bigger one. The approach suits field robots with strict power budgets.
arxiv-2601-13140:
Renana Opochinsky and Sharon Gannot bring a fresh tool to speech clean up. Diffusion models can rebuild a clean image from a noisy one step by step. Like ideas have been used on speech, where a time and pitch map is treated as an image.

Most phones and aids now carry more than one mic. The team uses that fact. Their method takes in feeds from many mics at once. It aims to use the gaps between feeds to pull speech out of noise with more care. For users of aids and call tools, more mics plus a strong rebuild model may mean speech that is far more clear.
arxiv-2601-13340:
Feliks Raczka settles a question on when a smooth quadric is D affine in plus characteristic. Work over a closed field whose characteristic is at least three. A quadric is a smooth form cut by a degree two law in projective space.

Raczka shows a sharp fail case. If the dim is an even count of at least four, the quadric is not D affine. D affinity ties to how differential operators act on the form, a deep mark in this field. Clean fail cases bound where a prized trait can hold. For algebra staff, the result closes a case that general tools left open.
arxiv-2601-12440:
Teng Huang and Pan Zhang link curvature bounds to a global shape number of a manifold. The number is the Euler characteristic, a classic invariant of closed Riemannian manifolds. Their route goes through operators of Schrodinger type. At the center sits a twisted Dirac operator whose index equals that Euler characteristic.

Index theory turns hard geometry into operator data that can be bounded. Integral curvature bounds are weaker than pointwise ones, so they cover more manifolds. New links of this kind show how much global shape is forced by average curvature alone. The work speaks to geometers who study what curvature can and cannot control. It also adds a fresh use for Dirac operators in topology.
arxiv-2601-12540:
Tingxuan Han, at Tsinghua University, studies rerandomization for quantile treatment effects. Random assignment is the gold standard for causal inference in experiments. Even so, chance can leave treatment groups unbalanced on key traits in a finite sample. Rerandomization checks the draw and redraws when balance is poor, which sharpens estimates.

Most rerandomization work targets mean effects, the average impact of a treatment. Han turns to quantile effects, which show how a treatment shifts the whole spread of outcomes. A treatment may help the worst off more than the median case, and quantiles reveal that. Better balance should boost precision for these effects too. The work extends a trusted design tool to a richer class of questions.
arxiv-2601-12640:
Jingge Zhu and Matthias Frey, at the University of Melbourne, study communication where the goal is a function, not the message itself. A transmitter holds a binary message and sends a codeword. The receiver wants a Boolean function of that message, not the full text. The function is unknown to the transmitter, but it comes from a known class.

This setup goes beyond identification, where the receiver only tests one property. Computing a function through a channel may need fewer bits than full recovery. The question is how much can be saved, and with what codes. Results here inform sensor networks and distributed computing. In many such systems, only a summary of the data ever matters.
arxiv-2601-12740:
Zijian Zhang and seven co authors present TreeWriter, an AI assisted system for long form writing. Long documents pose many challenges to current writing tools. Keeping consistency across sections is hard as a draft grows. Planning and writing efficiently also get harder with complexity. Users need AI help that integrates well, not help that fights the draft.

TreeWriter organizes writing hierarchically, like a tree of sections and subsections. That structure supports planning at the top and drafting at the leaves. AI assistance can then act at the right level for each task. Long reports, theses, and books all fit this pattern. A hierarchical tool could keep long projects coherent from outline to final text.
arxiv-2601-14040:
Mirko Torresani classifies a family of geometric structures on simple 3D spaces in 2026. The structures are tight contact structures, a kind of plane field on a space. The spaces are 3-space, the 3-ball, and the 3-sphere. The structures are invariant under an involution, a symmetry that flips the space.

That involution is conjugated to the standard rotation around the x-axis. Unlike the classical scenario, a new integral torsion appears. It dictates a splitting between equivalence classes of structures. Classification results tell geometers exactly which structures can exist. The proof sorts the full set of such forms for these three spaces. Few fields get so clean a full list.
arxiv-2601-14140:
Tong Xie and a large team harden embodied AI systems against faults across design layers in 2026. Embodied AI bridges AI with the physical world. Modern systems often combine a language model planner for high-level tasks. A reinforcement learning controller handles low-level action generation in the same stack.

Their CREATE framework characterizes resilience across layers and optimizes it. The aim is efficient yet reliable embodied AI systems. Faults can enter through sensors, planners, controllers, or hardware. Cross-layer views catch weak points that single-layer checks miss. Each layer gets its own checks, from the lens to the plan. Weak spots that hide in one layer show up when the layers are read as one.
arxiv-2601-14240:
Marc Windsheimer, Simon Deniffel, and André Kaup bring local rate control to neural video compression in 2026. Local rate control generalizes compression for challenges like video coding for machines. Traditional hybrid coding adapts the local rate-distortion trade-off via a local quantization parameter. No such approach is currently available for learning-based video compression.

Their LRC-DHVC aims toward local rate control in neural codecs. Regions that matter could get more bits, and dull regions fewer. Machine viewers need detail in task areas, not in backgrounds. Local control could cut bandwidth for camera networks and analytics.
arxiv-2601-14440:
Saeed Khaki, Ashudeep Singh, Nima Safaei, and Kamal Ginotra study a gap in AI math skills in this 2026 paper. Vision-language models lag behind text-only models on math reasoning. The gap shows when the same problem is given as an image, not as text. The team names this the modality gap and measures it.

They trace the gap to compounded failures. Models misread dense formulas, layout, and mixed symbolic and diagram context. Their answer is VisTIRA, which closes the gap through structured tool integration. Tools let the model work on the problem in steps. Readers get both a diagnosis of a clear weakness and a tested style of fix.
arxiv-2601-14540:
Payaswini Saikia leads a team of twelve authors on a black hole binary in this 2026 paper. IGR J17091-3624 is a distinctive black hole X-ray binary. It shows exotic variability, including complex heartbeat oscillations in its X-ray light curves. A famous system, GRS 1915+105, shows similar structured, rapid variability. That system is heavily obscured at optical wavelengths, though.

IGR J17091-3624 is less obscured, so it is a more accessible target for optical investigations. The team studies its exotic optical variability. Readers get a view of heartbeat-like behavior in visible light, from a source where such a view is rarely possible.
arxiv-2601-15740:
Jordi José offers a primer on stellar explosions in a 2026 arXiv paper. Nuclear astrophysics seeks the cosmic origins of chemical elements. It also studies the processes that power stars. The field is truly multidisciplinary, he stresses. It joins theoretical astrophysics with observational astronomy. Cosmochemistry and both branches of nuclear physics add their tools. His primer covers three kinds of explosions.

Type Ia supernovae, classical novae, and type I X-ray bursts make the list. Each forges elements in its own way. Each runs on distinct physics, from white dwarf blasts to surface bursts on neutron stars. A primer serves newcomers crossing into the field. It also gives specialists a shared map of how the three explosions compare in their element-making roles.
arxiv-2601-15940:
Antonio Casares, Christof Löding, and Igor Walukiewicz present a canonical model for automata over infinite words in a 2026 arXiv paper. Layered automata are a subclass of alternating parity automata. They extend deterministic automata. With a consistency property, these automata are history deterministic. They also show 0-1 probabilistic behavior. The authors prove a strong normal form result for them.

Every omega-regular language is recognized by a unique minimal consistent layered automaton. That form can be computed in polynomial time. It can be built from any layered or deterministic automaton for the language. Canonical forms are prized in this field. They let programs check equivalence and shrink models safely. Verification of systems that run forever leans on such tools.
arxiv-2601-14840:
Abdelrhman Bassiouny and six co-authors present a knowledge engineering framework in this 2026 paper. KRROOD is designed to bridge the integration gap between modern software engineering and knowledge representation and reasoning systems. Object-oriented programming is the standard for developing complex applications. Existing reasoning frameworks often rely on external ontologies and specialized languages, though. Those are difficult to integrate with imperative code.

The title states the approach: implementing knowledge representation and reasoning with object-oriented design. Rules and facts would live inside the same classes programmers already write. The tools are meant for coders. Rules can sit in the same files as the rest of the app, with no new tongue to learn. If the tool feels like plain code, it will be used; if not, it will not. Readers get a framework that lets an ordinary software team add reasoning without adopting a foreign stack.
arxiv-2601-16140:
Sylvestre-Alvise Rebuffi and coauthors hide marks in the deep code of image models. Their 2026 preprint deals with marks that tag AI made pics. Past marks are oft put on the pic at the end. End marks add cost and can leave flaws in the pic. The team puts the mark in the latent code in its place.

Their tool, named DistSeal, works for more than one model type. It fits both spread type and step type image models. A mark in the code should leave less trace on the pic. It should also save the cost of an end step. The work seeks marks that hold up in real use.
arxiv-2601-16340:
Zhentao Yu and three coauthors build a matrix reply model for brain pics through time. Their 2026 preprint deals with scans of one brain at more than one time. Such scans track form and act shifts in the brain. Shifts can give early marks of ill brain change. Each scan is a full matrix of values, not a lone count.

The model treats each matrix as the reply in a mixed model. Mixed terms hold both fixed group acts and lone brain acts. Good fits can flag small shifts ere they grow large. They also cut noise that hides true brain change. The work aids long term brain scan studies.
arxiv-2601-16640:
Jakob Stokke, Kundan Kumar, and Florin Radu build tools for tasks that mix more than one kind of physics. Flow in rock, heat in metal, and stress in beams can all mix. Such mixed tasks are split into parts and solved step by step. Each step leans on the last one's output. Their 2026 preprint asks how to tell if a step plan will work.

The authors give a broad frame for such step plans. Their frame yields tests that judge a plan after each pass. A failed test warns that the split was a poor choice. Users can then fix the plan and run it once more. This can save time on large screen models of real sites.
arxiv-2601-17040:
Hala Neji, Javier Nogueras-Iso, Javier Lacasta, Miguel Latre, and Francisco García-Marco read old Latin texts by machine. Their texts date from the 1400s and 1500s. Old script holds marks with sense of their own. Lose those marks, and the text's true sense shifts. Their 2026 preprint builds a full-page read pipe that keeps them.

The pipe treats the whole page at once, not line by line. That grip helps it keep odd marks in place. Such reads open vast old stores to search. Schools and vaults can then share lost works wide. Faithful marks keep past texts true for new eyes.
arxiv-2601-17240:
Shaoze Zhou and seven co-authors study how to help small groups talk face to face. Group talk is live and fast. People must give it full focus. They cannot pause to fix what they said. They must also read tone, face, and gesture cues. The team looks at mixed reality tools that offer help in the moment.

The study asks what kind of proactive support people need. It also asks what design choices could meet those needs. Help could mean facts, prompts, or cues shown at the right time. Done well, such tools could help each person join in more. The work speaks to designers of smart glasses and group aids.
arxiv-2601-17940: Luca Colagrande and Luca Benini report early results on giving a small open-source RISC-V core a second issue slot. Their 2026 preprint builds on the Snitch core, a light in-order design used in machine learning accelerators. Limited dual-issue execution lifts the mean instructions per cycle by a factor of 1.6. It also raises energy efficiency, a key gain when thousands of small cores share one chip.
arxiv-2601-18140:
Yan Zhu, Boru Chen, Christopher W. Fletcher, and Nandeeka Nayak recast chip simulation as a tensor problem. Their 2026 preprint presents RTeAAL Sim in an extended version. RTL simulation on CPUs is a standing bottleneck in hardware design. Today's simulators bake the circuit into the program itself. That makes builds slow, and the run is bound by the CPU front end, with heavy pressure on the instruction cache. The team instead states RTL simulation as a sparse tensor algebra problem.

Tensor form lets algebra engines and accelerators do the heavy lifting. Sparse structure matches how circuits actually wire up. Faster simulation means more design checks per day. In chip work, that speed can decide who ships first.
arxiv-2601-18940:
Jacek Gatlik and three co-authors shrink a hard wave problem down to a few key numbers. A kink is a stable twist in a field, and the phi-four model is a classic home for such twists. Their work extends an effective theory first built for a cousin model, the sine-Gordon model.

Three reduced models track the kink by its place, its width, and the strength of its inner mode. The team checks each reduced model against full numeric solutions, with pushes that vary in space and time. A good small model lets researchers guess kink motion fast, without solving the full field each time.
arxiv-2601-19040:
Junwei Deng and five co-authors grow fresh training data for time series models while they train. Time series foundation models, trained once and reused widely, often improve when fed synthetic extra data. Older ways to make that data rest on fixed rules and set plans that never adapt during training.

Their method, OATS, makes the extra data online, inside the training loop itself. Data made on the fly can chase the model's current weak spots instead of a fixed guess. Smarter extra data could lift forecast skill for energy, health, and finance series without new real data.
arxiv-2601-19440:
Mark Colley and four co-authors test how self driving cars should signal the people around them. With no human driver to wave or nod, automated vehicles may need external displays to talk to pedestrians, drivers, and cyclists. Past work mostly studied one kind of road user at a time.

The team tests such external interfaces for all three groups at once, inside virtual reality. VR lets them stage risky crossings safely and repeat them exactly. Signals that read clearly to a walker and a cyclist in the same scene are what real streets will demand.
arxiv-2601-19540:
Yuansong Xu and nine colleagues study how doctors judge advice from artificial intelligence. Large language models can suggest diagnoses and support clinical reasoning. Yet doctors often struggle to tell when a model's advice is sound and when it is not. Trust that is too high or too low can both harm care.

The authors look at how users perceive these systems during real diagnostic work. Most past tests used fixed benchmarks and set tasks, which say little about daily practice. This study focuses on the human side of the exchange. Knowing how trust forms helps designers build tools that doctors can calibrate. The goal is AI support that clinicians use with clear eyes, neither blind faith nor blanket doubt.
arxiv-2601-19640:
Hao Chang and five colleagues build tools for governing cities from the air. Low-flying drones and cameras can watch traffic, crowds, and public spaces. City managers need systems that flag unusual events, not just detect objects. Current pipelines detect things well but reason weakly about what an event means for governance.

The team introduces GovLA-10K, a benchmark of low-altitude scenes built for management questions. It is the first benchmark of its kind for this task. Alongside it they present GovLA-Reasoner, a vision-language framework tuned for governance-aware perception from the air. The framework aims to read a scene the way a city officer would. Such tools could help cities respond faster to problems seen from above.
arxiv-2601-20240:
Anthony Peruma and three colleagues survey how developers in the npm ecosystem build packages securely. npm hosts a vast store of reusable code for modern software. Yet flaws in third-party packages have led to serious breaches in the applications that depend on them.

The authors ask developers about their practices, their challenges, and their recommendations for safer package development. First-hand accounts show where tools and habits fall short in daily work. Their findings can guide platform owners and teams who want security steps that developers will actually follow. Their answers point to habits that tools and team leads can fix.
arxiv-2601-20440:
Adam Bobrowski and Andrey Pilipenko revisit Portenko's classical theorem on the approximation of skew Brownian motion. Skew Brownian motion is a diffusion that behaves like a one-way membrane at a point. Portenko's theorem says it arises by concentrating the drift of a diffusion process around that point, creating the effect of a semi-permeable barrier.

The authors reflect on the theorem from the viewpoint of operator semigroup theory. Revisiting classic results with modern tools can widen their reach and clarify their assumptions. Skew diffusions model barriers in finance, physics, and biology, so a firmer base has wide use.
arxiv-2601-18540:
Niels-Ole Frerick, Michael Roemelt, and Eric Fischer use high-grade maths to re-check a claim about a bond swap in strong light fields. The swap is a classic move in which one part takes the place of a next part at a silicon core. When the stuff sits in a tuned box of light, the light and the stuff can join as one. That join was said to shift how the swap runs.

Past claims on how the shift works did not agree. The team weigh in with strict maths that need no tuned facts. They ask if a push from the box on the core counts, and if a named stretch of the core helps form the joint state. Their check may help end the row on what fields in a box can and cannot do to bond swaps.
arxiv-2601-21240:
Shu-Min Wu and four co-authors study how a mirror-like boundary changes the way quantum coherence can be pulled from empty space. Three still detectors sit near an endless flat wall that reflects a light scalar field. The detectors are placed either side by side along the wall or in a line away from it.

The team tracks how much shared coherence the three detectors can gather in each setup. Their energy gaps are set in a fixed order from low to high. The results show that the wall is not a passive backdrop. Its position and the layout of the detectors shape how much coherence can be harvested.
arxiv-2601-21340:
Lang Cao, Qingyu Chen, and Yue Guo help language models use long patient records without losing key facts. Health records hold rich evidence spread over years of visits. That history often runs past what a model can read at once, and simple search can drop vital events or their order.

Their system improves retrieval for long records before the model answers. It keeps clinical events and their timing in view rather than chopping the record blindly. Better grounding should mean answers that rest on the patient's real history. The work targets safer, more faithful AI help in medical decisions.
arxiv-2601-21540:
Iris Yazici, Mert Kayaalp, Stefan Taga, and Ali H. Sayed test whether classic opinion models can predict how groups of language models settle on a view. Agents trade text messages over varied network layouts for several rounds. Each message is scored for its stance by sentiment tools.

The frame is the DeGroot model, where each agent averages the views it hears. The question is whether that simple math tracks real model behavior. If it does, designers can forecast group drift before running costly trials. If it fails, the gaps show where model talk departs from classic social dynamics.
arxiv-2601-21640:
Naeem Desai, Oliver Graham, Sean Holman, and William R.B. Lionheart recast radar-style imaging as a tensor tomography problem. Travel-time imaging rebuilds a picture of a scene from the timing of signals that bounce through it. In multistatic setups, senders and receivers sit in different places.

The scene's reflectivity may also vary with direction, which is the anisotropic case. Framing the task as tensor tomography brings a mature set of tools to bear. The reformulation clarifies what can and cannot be recovered from the timing data. It serves radar, sonar, and medical imaging, where richer direction data keeps arriving.
arxiv-2601-22440:
Bhada Yun, Renn Su, and April Yi Wang test how well chatbots read, show, and explain a user's own values. Their 2026 preprint takes a practical line: whatever the deep truth, users do judge whether a model gets their values. They built a toolkit, VAPT, to study those judgments.

Twenty people texted a chatbot for a month, then judged its take on their values. The work shows where models seem to grasp what matters to a person. It also shows where the show of grasp falls flat. Such insight can guide more honest, personal AI. It keeps the user's view at the center.
arxiv-2601-22740:
Sin Kyu Kang, Ranjeet Kumar, and Hiroshi Okada build one model that tackles neutrino mass, flavor, the strong CP problem, and dark matter at once. Their 2026 preprint generates neutrino masses by radiation, inside an axion model. A modular symmetry shapes the flavor pattern.

Joining four puzzles in one frame is bold; each piece constrains the rest. The axion at the core could also be the dark matter. Such unified builds are prized when they stay testable. The work gives experimenters joint targets to hunt. It is theory with many doors.
arxiv-2601-21940:
Yihui Fu and Tim Fingscheidt work on making noisy speech clear in a single step. Diffusion methods that clean speech by working on discrete audio codec features can rebuild the speech parts well. But they need many passes of a reverse process, which makes them slow.

They also show an odd split: scores that need no reference recording look good. While scores against a clean reference look poor, as the process can drift from the original. The authors' 2026 preprint, DISCONTSE, uses joint discrete and continuous embeddings to enhance speech in one step. Fast cleanup matters for hearing aids, calls, and voice interfaces, where delay is as much a flaw as noise.
arxiv-2601-22040:
Reza Batley and Sourav Saha question how small language models spend their parameters. Scaling analyses usually treat all parameters as interchangeable, an assumption that predicts loss from compute well. In small models below a billion parameters, though, embedding matrices eat most of the parameter budget.

The authors argue that this allocation is as suboptimal as it is counterintuitive. Their 2026 preprint proposes a separable architecture for continuous token representation, splitting how tokens are represented so parameters go where they earn their keep. Small models run on phones and embedded devices, so squeezing more ability from the same budget has direct practical value.
arxiv-2601-22140:
Akash Jain adds quantum rules to the theory of flow. Flow theory tracks how things that are kept, like heat or charge, spread and drift. Jain builds a quantum form of this theory for one kept trait. The rules guide how the trait moves when it is spread thin and pushed by chance kicks.

A key rule set links the kicks a system feels to the drag it shows. A named law, the KMS law, makes that link hold in the math. Jain finds that this law forces some clear quantum marks to show up. One mark is a long tail in how the kicks line up in time. Such marks show in hot quark soup and in cold atom clouds.
arxiv-2601-20740:
Jian-Bo Cheng, Zi-Yang Lin, Jun-Zhang Wang, and Shi-Lin Zhu investigate two mysterious particles in the charm sector. Their 2026 paper decodes the states known as Zc(4430) and Zc(4200). These are hidden-charm tetraquark candidates, built from four quarks rather than the usual two or three. The team works within the hadronic molecular picture. In that picture, the state is a loose bound pair of mesons. The emphasis falls on systems made of an S-wave meson pair.

One meson of the pair carries charm; its partner carries anti-charm. How such pairs bind decides what the Zc states really are. Molecular and compact tetraquark pictures predict different patterns. Careful study of these two states can separate the pictures. The paper adds theoretical detail to a long-running puzzle. Exotic hadrons test whether our quark rulebook is complete.
arxiv-2601-20840:
Juan-Juan Niu and Hong-Hao Ma compute how a rare particle could be made with light. Their 2026 paper studies a baryon that mixes bottom and charm quarks. A baryon is a particle built from three quarks. This blend is heavy and rare. The team focuses on its P-wave states. They work in nonrelativistic QCD, the standard tool for heavy quark systems.

Two channels are treated. In one, two photons collide and create the baryon plus anti-matter partners. In the other, a photon and a gluon do the job. Such math tells search teams where to look. It also says how much signal to expect. The baryon has not been seen yet, so rate estimates guide the hunt.
arxiv-2601-21040:
Nikolaos Kidonakis and Kaan Simsek use a rare top quark process to probe physics beyond the standard model. Their 2026 paper studies single-top production with a W boson at the LHC. The probe is the dimension-6 Standard Model Effective Field Theory, or SMEFT. SMEFT packages possible new physics into a set of extra interactions. Collider data can then bound each one. Precision is the key to tight bounds.

The team computes the process at several accuracies. They work at leading order, next-to-leading order, and approximate next-to-next-to-leading order in QCD. Each step sharpens the prediction for the signal rate. Sharper predictions turn the same data into stronger limits. The paper serves the global effort to find cracks in the standard model. It shows how theory precision and collider data advance together.
arxiv-2512-01240:
Shaddin Dughmi, Yusuf Kalayci, and Xinyu Liu study choice under doubt with costly checks. In packing tasks, each item has an unknown gain. Checking an item costs time or money. The key choice is which few items to check first.

Their work looks for sparse sets that still lead to near-best plans. Past work scored sparsity by how many items were checked. The team seeks sets that come close to the best score with few checks. Good sparse sets save cost in tasks like hiring, ads, and stock choice, where each check has a real price.
arxiv-2512-01340:
Yingjie Zhou and a large team work on judging fake talking faces. Speech-driven tools can make a still face seem to talk. New tools can move two or more faces at once. That adds life to calls and shows, but quality drops as faces are added.

Judging that quality by eye is slow and uneven. The team built EvalTalker to learn the judging task itself. It scores clips made from real face photos with more than one subject. Fair scores help builders spot flaws fast. They also give users a clear sign of which tools to trust.
arxiv-2512-01540:
Zipeng Wang and Dan Xu speed up 3D rebuilding from many photos. Feed-forward methods now beat slow per-scene tuning. Top models attend to all image tokens at once. That full attention is sharp but costly as views pile up.

Their model, FlashVGGT, squeezes descriptor attention to cut that cost. It keeps global links between views while work drops. Fast, scalable rebuilding serves in robots, mapping, and virtual scenes. Lower cost also lets smaller teams run state-of-the-art geometry tools on plain hardware. Squeezed attention also lowers memory load, so longer view sets fit on one card where full attention would spill and fail.
arxiv-2512-00840:
Tamanna Jain and Piero Rettegno compute a key force for gravitational wave science in a 2025 paper. When two compact objects orbit each other, they lose energy to gravitational waves and slowly spiral inward. The radiation reaction force captures that loss and drives the orbit's change.

Most studies of modified gravity theories assume near-circular orbits. Real future detections may catch eccentric ones, where the orbit is stretched into an oval. Jain and Rettegno derive the force for nonspinning eccentric orbits in massless scalar-tensor theories. They use the effective-one-body formalism, which maps two bodies onto one, up to a stated accuracy order.
arxiv-2512-01040:
Vladislav Shishkov studies how light reaches thermal balance inside molecular films in a 2025 paper. When molecules absorb and emit light, low-frequency vibrations of the molecules shape the spectra. Those vibrations set the linewidths of absorption and emission peaks, and the gap between them known as the Stokes shift.

In cavities that use a molecular film as the active medium, the same vibrations help light thermalize, or settle into equilibrium. That settling can enable Bose-Einstein condensation of light. Shishkov computes the thermalization rate for weakly coupled molecular systems. Knowing the rate helps design cavities that actually reach the condensed state.
arxiv-2512-00040:
Sagar Sudhakara and Pankaj Rajak assign network users to slices using large language models. Network slicing splits physical infrastructure into virtual slices tuned for different needs, like high bandwidth or low latency. Allocating users optimally is a constrained problem usually solved with complex algorithms.

The authors test whether language models can handle the radio resource allocation directly. A model that respects constraints in plain reasoning could simplify slice management. The study probes a new role for language models in live network operations. High bandwidth and low latency slices illustrate the competing service requirements the allocation must respect simultaneously.
arxiv-2512-00140:
Xin Li, a computer scientist at the University at Albany, proposes a theory linking computation, memory, and brain inference in a 2025 study. The starting point is a classic result: nondeterministic search takes exponential time but can be simulated in polynomial space. Li asks whether the brain exploits a related trade.

The proposal, called Memory-Amortized Inference, suggests the brain physically carries out an inverse form of that trade. In this picture, stored memory turns chaotic exploration into a geometry of certainty. The work is speculative theory, aimed at readers who enjoy bold connections between computing limits and how minds reach conclusions. The geometry of certainty in the title names the end state the theory aims to explain.
arxiv-2512-00240:
Hotel managers lose revenue when guests cancel, so predicting cancellations has direct business value. Yingdong Yang presents a Bayesian analysis of hotel booking cancellations in 2025, using hierarchical modeling in PyMC. Three model specifications of increasing complexity are compared.

The study investigates how lead time, special requests, and parking requirements affect cancellation probability. It also explores interaction effects with hotel type. A hierarchical Bayesian approach shares information across groups while showing uncertainty honestly, which helps managers set deposit and overbooking policies with clearer eyes. Hierarchical models suit hotels, since chains, cities, and property types all shape behavior. The comparison of three specifications shows what the added complexity buys. For a front desk team, the gain is plain. Fewer shocks at check-out time, and a clear view of which kinds of stays are most apt to fall through.
arxiv-2512-00640:
Tire degradation decides Formula 1 strategy as surely as engine power does. Cole Cappello and Andrew Hoegh present a state-space approach to modeling tire degradation in racing in 2025. Tire wear is one of the most important factors in Grand Prix race planning.

State-space models track a hidden wear state through noisy lap-time observations, updating estimates as the race unfolds. A good degradation model tells a team when to pit before the tires fall off a performance cliff. The study is a tidy case of statistical modeling meeting a live, high-stakes decision problem. State-space models are built for exactly this mix of hidden state and noisy data.
arxiv-2512-03340:
Medical papers are hard for many readers to use. Rohan Charudatt Salvi and co-authors build a data set for controllable medical summaries in this 2025 work. Automatic simplification can raise health literacy, but most tools assume one generic audience.

Readers differ widely in medical knowledge and in what they need. The authors' data set, PERCS, is guided by personas that stand for different user groups. Persona-guided summaries could tailor the same paper for a patient, a nurse, or a student. That tailoring may make research more usable. Persona control could also help clinicians write summaries matched to each reader's needs.
arxiv-2512-03440:
Noise bursts, called glitches, pollute gravitational wave data. Tabata Aira Ferreira, Gabriela González, and Osvaldo Salas analyze LIGO glitches in this 2025 work. They use data from the first part of the fourth LIGO-Virgo-KAGRA observing run.

The team applies t-SNE, an unsupervised method that maps data into clusters for viewing. That view shows how groups of glitches behave. Knowing glitch families helps separate real cosmic signals from detector noise. Cleaner data raise the odds of spotting black hole and neutron star mergers. Cluster views help engineers group glitches by cause and fix the worst sources.
arxiv-2512-03540:
Recipe photos should match each cooking step in order. Ruoxuan Zhang and co-authors present CookAnything in this 2025 work. Cooking is sequential and visual, with each step carrying procedural logic and visual meaning.

Diffusion models generate strong single images but struggle with structured multi-step scenes. CookAnything aims for flexible and consistent images across a recipe's steps. Consistent step images could help cooking apps and learners. They also test whether image models can follow real-world procedures faithfully. Consistency across steps is the hard part, since one wrong pan or color breaks the recipe's visual story for learners following along.
arxiv-2512-02040:
A system of equations can demand even more discipline from its solutions than a single equation does. Junfeng Xu, Sujoy Majumder, and Debabrata Pramanik study in 2025 the exact form of entire solutions, functions defined on the whole complex plane, to a system of Fermat-type partial differential-difference equations.

The system couples two unknown functions, mixing their partial derivatives with shifted values of each other. The authors restrict to solutions of finite order, a growth condition that keeps the search manageable, and pin down their precise form. Results like these extend complex analysis's catalogue of which coupled functional equations admit solutions at all.
arxiv-2512-02240:
Language models solve narrative tasks by writing out long chains of thought, and those traces can be trained with reinforcement learning to be more useful. Alexander Gurung, Nikolay Malkin, and Mirella Lapata study in 2025 a lighter alternative: latent reasoning, where the thinking happens inside the model's hidden states rather than in words.

Treating the reasoning trace as a latent variable means the model can learn to think in a compressed internal form. Optimizing that ability directly could cut the cost and length of explicit chains of thought. For storytelling and other narrative work, where fluent output matters, a quiet internal reasoning step may preserve quality while keeping responses concise.
arxiv-2512-02440:
Galaxies are not one color: their centers and outskirts differ, and that gradient records how they assembled. M. Martorano and nine co-authors trace in 2025 how ultraviolet-to-near-infrared color gradients evolve with redshift and stellar mass, using Hubble and Webb telescope data on more than ten thousand galaxies.

Their sample spans the era when galaxies were forming stars most vigorously, with masses above a billion suns. Radial gradients in two rest-frame colors separate age, dust, and composition effects across each galaxy. Knowing how gradients depend on mass reveals whether galaxies grew inside-out or outside-in, a basic question in galaxy evolution.
arxiv-2512-02540:
Francisco Monteiro and five co-authors study liquid sloshing inside partly filled fuel tanks. When a tank is shaken up and down near twice its natural sloshing frequency, the liquid can resonate strongly. That parametric resonance drives large waves, breaks the surface, and mixes the liquid hard.

The team maps the regimes of this behavior for horizontal cylindrical tanks under vertical acceleration. Knowing which regime a tank sits in helps predict loads on its walls. Such maps matter for vehicle design, since violent sloshing can harm stability and crack structures over time. Tank tests on the ground are far cheaper than repairs once a fleet is in daily use.
arxiv-2512-02740:
Waleed El-Geresy and Deniz Gündüz turn an attacker into a training tool for an autoencoder. An autoencoder squeezes data into a small latent code, then rebuilds the original from it. For the code to behave well, its spread should match a chosen bell shaped distribution.

A wireless jammer tries to disrupt recovery of a Gaussian source sent over the channel. Fighting that jamming pushes the encoder to shape its latent space as desired. The setup joins learning with adversarial pressure, a trick that may help design robust communication codes. Noise is most often the foe in radio work, so a scheme that puts noise to work stands out from the pack.
arxiv-2512-02840:
Tom Zehle and four co-authors package prompt optimization so practitioners can actually use it. Tuning prompts has become crucial for getting the best from large language models across many tasks. Research code proving the point often sits isolated and unmaintained, which blocks adoption.

Their framework, promptolution, is unified and modular, gathering prompt tuning methods in one maintained home. Users can swap parts in and out instead of rebuilding each experiment. Shared tooling of this kind helps prompt research leave the lab and serve real products. Shared racks get patched and kept, while lone code rots, and that gap is why the field needs this kind of home.
arxiv-2512-02940:
F. S. Luiz and three co-authors cover graph vertices with the fewest guards, guided by a quantum walk. The minimum vertex cover problem asks for the smallest set of vertices touching every edge. It is a classic hard problem across scheduling, networks, and biology.

Their heuristic lets a quantum walker spread coherently over the graph. Transition probabilities then flag highly influential vertices for the cover. The method aims to scale to larger graphs than exact solvers handle. Quantum heuristics of this kind may one day speed real optimization work. Walk based picks lean on the shape of the graph, not on brute force. That is why they may grow where brute force stalls out cold.
plos-pone-0010040:
Marc Burian, Christiane Wolz, and Christiane Goerke studied a common nose germ in 2010. Staphylococcus aureus lives in the human nose, often with no symptoms at all. Carrying it there is still a known risk, because the germ can later infect its own host. Their study appeared in PLOS ONE.

The team measured bacterial gene activity in nose swabs from persistent carriers. They asked how the germ adjusts its controls while living quietly in people. Those adjustments may explain why the same germ can sit harmlessly for months and then cause serious illness.
plos-pone-0010140:
The authors were Xulin Xu, Min Jiang, Yuhong Wang, and others. Their 2010 PLOS ONE study fed rabbits fish oil and watched their hearts. Trials had suggested fish oil can protect some patients from abnormal heart rhythms. The mechanism behind that benefit was not entirely clear, despite wide use of fish oil supplements.

After four weeks of supplementation, rabbit hearts showed changed channel protein levels. The authors call the pattern cardiac electrical remodeling, a rewiring of the heart's signals. Those channel changes offer a concrete explanation for how fish oil might steady heart rhythm.
plos-pone-0010240:
The authors were Virginia Espina, Brian Mariani, Rosa Gallagher, and others. Their 2010 PLOS ONE study examined early breast cancer that stays inside the ducts. Most invasive breast cancer is thought to start from this stage, called DCIS. DCIS cells survive in ducts that are low in oxygen and nutrients, a harsh setting that should kill many cells.

The team found that malignant precursor cells already exist within DCIS lesions. Those cells require autophagy, a self-eating survival process, to stay alive there. Blocking autophagy might starve early lesions before they turn invasive.
plos-pone-0010340:
Sheri Weiser, David Tuller, Edward Frongillo and others studied hunger and HIV care in Uganda for PLOS ONE in 2010. Taking AIDS drugs on schedule is vital, yet many patients miss doses. Lack of food was emerging as one reason, in Africa and beyond. Little was known about exactly how hunger leads to missed doses. The team set out to trace those steps through patients' own accounts.

They held deep, open-ended talks with people on treatment. Patients described skipping doses when food was short, fearing side effects on an empty stomach, or choosing food for family over clinic trips. Such detail turns a broad link into concrete barriers. Programs that pair food support with medicine could act on each one. The study gives those programs a human map.
plos-pone-0009840:
People spot symmetry in a pattern almost instantly, even in clutter. Chien-Chung Chen and Christopher Tyler modeled what helps or hurts that skill. Their study appeared in PLOS ONE in 2010. Symmetry is a basic cue the visual system uses everywhere.

The model weighed three influences: masking noise, axial cueing, and salience. Masking noise hides the pattern, cueing points to its axis, and salience makes it stand out. Balancing the three predicts when symmetry will be seen. The work helps explain a core talent of human vision. The model turns those effects into testable predictions.
plos-pone-0009940:
A claimed network of tiny vessels, distinct from blood and lymph, has sparked debate for decades. Jung Sun Yoo and colleagues characterized that system in the abdomen of lung cancer mice. Their study appeared in PLOS ONE in 2010.

The primo-vascular system is said to thread through organs and body cavities. The team described its features in the abdominal cavity of the cancer model. They also laid out its differences from the lymphatic system, the drainage network it is often confused with. Careful description is the first step in judging the claim.
